stories.Headline: Are Boutique AI Firms India’s Next Big Thing?
stories.Summary:
Prateek Jogani spent a decade building product-led startups in fintech and insurance before setting out in 2025 to find his next problem. He found that almost no enterprise had AI doing meaningful work inside the business, even though the models were powerful. Legacy IT services firms struggled to keep pace with AI and were absent from those conversations. Seeing an execution vacuum, Jogani launched Parallel Loop this month as an AI enablement and execution firm, backed with $6.6 million from Paytm CEO Vijay Shekhar Sharma, CRED Founder Kunal Shah, AEOS Labs Founder Varun Mayya and a cohort of VCs.

Parallel Loop uses AI-native engineers and a software factory of AI agents rather than large coding teams. Jogani said one customer received a quote of five months from a services company, while Parallel Loop delivered the app in 10 days. The firm deploys its AI stack inside the customer's own infrastructure, and its commercial model combines a monthly licence fee, packages of forward-deployed engineering hours, one-time software development fees and recurring maintenance charges. It has secured eight enterprise AI clients within months of incorporation, with $2 million in booked revenue.

Akhil Verghese, co-founder and CEO of boutique firm Krazimo, said traditional IT services deliver against a specification while his firm sells an outcome. Krazimo offers a cancellable monthly subscription for exploratory projects and a fixed price tied to delivery milestones for clearly defined work, and clients can exit without payment during the first 30 days. Verghese said clients typically break even within three to six months, with profits rising by an average of 17%. He spent six years at Google working on Gemini projects, and he and co-founder Mridul Nagpal left in July 2025 after the company hit $50,000 in monthly recurring revenue.

Forrester VP and Principal Analyst Leslie Joseph said boutique AI firms are strongest where incumbents would have to cut their own revenue to compete. Infosys reported that fixed-price contracts were 58% of its revenue in FY2026, while Wipro drew 45.6% from fixed-price and volume-based contracts. Coforge said outcome-based contracts contributed 6-7% of its $2.5 billion revenue run rate, and TCS reported a shift toward outcome-based commitments. Joseph said AI shrinks billable work in these contracts and clients expect the savings passed back, though he added that outcome-based pricing remains unproven for large transformation programs.

India's IT industry employs an estimated 5.95 million people in 2026, and firms are hiring far fewer fresh graduates as AI changes the skills employers seek. TCS hired more than 110,000 engineering graduates four years ago, but its intake in financial year 2026 was less than half that level, while Infosys recruited about 80 per cent fewer fresh graduates in financial year 2025 than three years earlier. Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum on Oct 13 that AI was taking over coding tasks traditionally handled by junior engineers. Mansee Singhal of Marsh Workforce & Rewards said the old model of hiring graduates in bulk and developing them over time is giving way to expectations that graduates arrive with greater technical depth.

stories.Headline: Obscure neocloud lenders, not Nvidia, are where the AI bubble could burst first
stories.Summary:
Neocloud firms, the data centre companies that lease computing power to major AI developers, have become the focus of investor concern about the AI boom. CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN, Applied Digital and the British firm Nscale are among the companies involved, according to the BBC. CoreWeave carries about $50 billion in debt, and its bonds due in 2031 have traded with yields above 16%. Credit default swaps on CoreWeave have implied a nearly 63% probability of default within five years.

Applied Digital launched a $2.35 billion senior secured notes offering on top of debt obligations already over $2 billion, and its interest payments now run close to its entire annual revenue. Nscale hoped a US listing would value it at $30 billion, but after Microsoft walked away from a major data centre leasing agreement, investors reportedly priced the IPO closer to $16 billion. CoreWeave is also pricing a $3.55 billion dual-currency junk bond deal led by JPMorgan, including the first euro-denominated high-yield note from a US AI infrastructure company. Gartner expects 80% of neocloud companies to stop operating independently by 2030.

CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator has said the market is acting irrationally and has expressed confidence in its business model. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent downplayed concerns on CNBC, calling neoclouds a small component of the overall ecosystem. Elon Musk suggested on social media that more than 200 neoclouds could face what he called guppy-level death and consolidation, adding that some will make it through but not many. Analyst Cory Johnson of The Quiet Period said there is reason to worry.

Several neocloud firms began in crypto mining, including CoreWeave, which was founded in 2017 to mine Ethereum, while Nebius was formerly Yandex NV and changed its name in 2024. Shares in Nebius, IREN and Applied Digital fell sharply through October and into November, leaving the group down nearly 30% from mid-October highs. Microsoft and Google recently forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, and shares in several neocloud firms tumbled. Australia's Firmus shelved plans to sell shares to the public, and Gartner estimates more than $3.5 trillion in global AI infrastructure spending could face impairment risk by 2030.

stories.Headline: 2 Industrial Stocks That Win Whether the AI Bubble Pops or Not
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the U.S. company behind the Claude chatbot, filed for an initial public offering on Oct. 26, 2026, according to a 335-page registration statement. The filing gave the public a first official look at the company's business operations and ownership. The statement did not state a valuation, but some investors have guessed it could be as high as $2 trillion. That would make it the biggest IPO ever, and a large IPO could inflate what is sometimes called an AI bubble.

A bubble is overinvestment in a space that will not see a positive return, eventually creating market instability. Rob May, author of the 2026 book "Investing in AI," pointed to the 19th century railroad infrastructure bubble and the 1990s dot-com bubble as examples. He said people make a mistake when they think of the AI bubble as one consistent thing, because different areas, from data centers to model providers to startups, could see different returns. Dennis Kelleher, CEO of the nonprofit Better Markets, said that if the bubble bursts, companies lose money, debt and loans are not repaid, some companies and banks go bankrupt, stock markets crash and the economy contracts. He compared that to the 2008 economic crash, and said that if it is not a bubble, the economy could benefit depending on which companies win the AI race.

Experts disagree on whether an AI bubble exists. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in August that he is happy to pay hundreds of millions of dollars a year to use AI services. Others worry the money spent on AI is not seeing the expected return, and in 2024 Sequoia Capital estimated that gap at $600 billion. May said he sees pockets of bubbles but does not expect a violent pop, and he predicted that in the next 18 months investors will stop pumping money into startups and model labs. The article says Anthropic is expected to start trading, but it does not say what happens next beyond that.

stories.Headline: NAVER CEO Urges Spread of Industrial AI to Smaller Firms
stories.Summary:
NAVER chief executive Choi Soo-yeon met Siemens Group Chairman Roland Busch on Oct. 31 at the Grand InterContinental Seoul Parnas in Seoul, during the 19th Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business, known as APK 2026. The two held a dialogue on industrial artificial intelligence, and NAVER announced the meeting on Nov. 2. APK began in 1986 and is co-hosted by the Korean-German Chamber of Commerce and Industry and Germany's Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy. After the dialogue, Busch visited NAVER's second headquarters, called 1784, with senior Siemens executives.

Choi said the base for AI use must widen to small and medium-sized enterprises and suppliers for industrial AI to spread. She said the true tipping point will come when even small companies can use AI easily, and that wider use lets individual gains lift productivity across an industry. She also said AI results should be judged by real improvements in work, not by the technology itself, and that human checking grows more important as AI handles more tasks. Busch said industrial AI has reached an important turning point, and that its value is complete only when it is used safely and reliably in the field and spreads across industry. He stressed combining German engineering with Asia's strengths in semiconductors, AI models and digital platforms.

At the 1784 visit, those present included Choi, NAVER LABS CEO Suk Sang-ok, Siemens Head of M&A Dagmar Mundani, Siemens Korea Chief Executive Jung Ha-joong and Stephanie Frank, who heads Siemens Korea's Digital Industries division. The executives shared cases where NAVER's digital twin technology was used at real industrial sites. They discussed extending that technology to global markets with Siemens' industrial solutions, and possible cooperation in robotics and robot foundation models NAVER is developing. The group then toured the building to see NAVER's technologies at work.

In a separate session at APK 2026, moderated by journalist Jennifer Moon, the two CEOs urged companies to move beyond AI pilot projects toward measurable productivity gains. Choi said firms must first organize scattered information into formats AI can use, and should measure whether AI cuts waiting times, improves efficiency or removes repetitive tasks. Busch said adoption has to come from the top, and cited a Japanese automaker that used Siemens technology across 10,000 machines with a payback period of under three months. Choi noted NAVER has run more than 200 delivery robots at its 1784 headquarters for over four years. In an audience poll, 41 percent named data sharing and interoperability as the biggest barrier to scaling industrial AI across regions.

stories.Headline: ProHance Launches AI Adoption Index to Show What AI Is Changing at Work
stories.Summary:
ProHance, an AI-led productivity platform, launched the AI Adoption Index on November 2, 2026, in Sydney. The company described it as an AI realization scorecard that helps enterprises measure AI usage and confirm it is on approved tools, applied to real work and turning into delivered value. The launch comes as unmanaged AI use draws closer scrutiny. A 2026 industry study of data breaches found that incidents involving shadow AI, meaning AI tools used by employees without IT approval, accounted for 43% of all breaches, up from 20% in 2025. Among organizations reporting an AI-related security incident, 92% lacked adequate AI access controls.

The Index lets leaders map how AI is used across teams, from AI-Aware to AI-First, measure which teams are behind on adoption, and detect shadow AI while keeping a permanent audit trail. ProHance said usage analytics stop at activity, while governance and security tools control approval and spend but cannot show whether AI changes how work gets done, and a separate set of tools tracks output shipped. The Index brings all three views together in one place, across every AI tool and every team. It follows ProHance's launch of an outcome measurement layer for Outsourcing Performance Management, which gives enterprises independent evidence of what their outsourced and contingent teams deliver.

Ankur Dhingra, CEO of ProHance, said the company aims to solve the problem of assessing AI's impact on the workforce by helping leaders understand how to reskill and reshape their workforce with AI, measuring the actual impact of AI and humans together. He said the Index shows leaders who is using what, how deeply, at what cost, and where AI is running without approval, measured from the work itself, so they can decide where to act. In a separate interview, Cathy Rowe, executive vice president and segment leader for the U.S. Professional Market at Wolters Kluwer, said AI is helping firms balance growing client expectations with limited professional capacity. She said the future belongs not to firms that use AI to replace talent but to those that use it to amplify talent.

Rowe said most firms recognize the value of expanding advisory services, but many professionals spend most of their time on compliance work, and AI helps change that equation by freeing capacity for strategic conversations throughout the year. She said firms seeing the greatest success build a strong technology foundation rather than simply adding more tools, starting with connected systems that bring tax, financial, client and workflow data into a unified environment. She also said firms need trusted AI that provides transparent, explainable recommendations grounded in authoritative sources, and that technology alone does not create transformation. Firms that realize the greatest value redesign workflows, invest in training and help professionals develop new skills, and many are creating new career paths and revisiting engagement models to encourage year-round client relationships.

stories.Headline: AI finds expanding uses in traditional medicine, hurdles remain: report - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
A report released on Sunday at the World Conference on Traditional Medicine 2026 in Beijing said artificial intelligence is transforming traditional medicine worldwide, and China leads global patent filings for related applications. The report was publicized at the conference held over the weekend in Beijing. It was initiated by the Global Alliance for Traditional and Integrative Medicine. Qin Huaijin, vice chair and secretary-general of the alliance, said AI-enabled traditional medicine has moved beyond the conceptual stage.

Since 2000, 3,030 patents for AI applications in traditional medicine have been published worldwide, and 6,882 high-quality academic papers have been released since 1990, according to the report. China accounts for 80.4 percent of the published patents and 84.2 percent of the granted patents, and 47 percent of the academic papers. China's 2026-2030 development plan calls for wider adoption of smart technologies in traditional Chinese medicine and the creation of high-quality datasets. Major economies including China, India and the Republic of Korea have integrated AI applications for traditional medicine into national health and science strategies.

Li Haiyan, head of the Institute of Information on Traditional Chinese Medicine under the China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences, said AI tools can turn accumulated practices into knowledge and data that can be stored, programmed and validated. Chen Jianxin, a professor at Beijing University of Chinese Medicine, highlighted three advances: quantifiable tongue and pulse readings, computable TCM theories, and faster drug screening. Huang Luqi, a TCM expert and academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, said AI-assisted diagnosis could make TCM diagnostic information more objective and quantifiable. Premier Li Qiang told the conference's opening ceremony on Saturday that China will promote the digital and intelligent transformation of TCM.

The report says a semantic gap remains between the experience-based language of traditional medicine and the standardized, quantitative data required by AI systems. It adds that the reliability and explainability of AI models in traditional medicine need to be improved, and that digitized traditional knowledge faces the risk of unauthorized extraction and reuse. The report calls for unified coding standards for datasets, cross-disciplinary professionals, and global governance mechanisms balancing data security and knowledge sharing. In late 2025, the World Federation of Chinese Medicine Societies issued guidelines for international TCM terminology translation, and China has rolled out national standards for English translation of TCM terms.

stories.Headline: Nasdaq 100 losing momentum as AI trade divides
stories.Summary:
On Friday, October 30, 2026, the Nasdaq 100 fell 3.46 per cent to close at 28,384.85, after touching an intraday low of 28,093.24, which was 10.0 per cent below the October 6 record close of 31,224.47. That low briefly put the index in correction territory during the session, but buyers lifted it back before the close, leaving it 9.1 per cent below the record. The selling began in chip stocks, with Intel dropping 28.6 per cent after guiding fourth-quarter revenue to US$15 billion to US$16 billion, below the US$16.5 billion it had just reported. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 7.2 per cent, its worst day since June 23, and lost 15.4 per cent for October. The VIX hit 23.93 during the session but closed at 19.41, up 12.91 per cent.

The Federal Reserve held its policy rate at 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent on October 28, a pause after September's hike, on a split vote with multiple dissents. Chair Kevin Warsh struck a balanced but hawkish tone, played down any influence from the midterm elections and left a December increase on the table. Third-quarter GDP grew at a 3.4 per cent annualised pace, headline PCE inflation accelerated to 3.6 per cent in September, and jobless claims held near multi-decade lows, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield back towards 5 per cent. Alphabet fell around 10 per cent after results as search growth disappointed and cash burn mounted, dragging the index down roughly 1.6 per cent on Thursday, while Microsoft was rewarded earlier in the week for converting AI investment into cash. Apple slipped 1.23 per cent and, at US$5.03 trillion, passed NVIDIA as the most valuable company, while NVIDIA fell 4.2 per cent to US$204.64, leaving it worth US$4.94 trillion.

Joe Tigay, a portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the market was moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the show me phase. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said the company still expected 2026 cash capital expenditures of approximately US$220 billion. On Intel's call, management said data center demand exceeds supply but guided fourth-quarter gross margin to 38 per cent, compared with 44.1 per cent in the third quarter, and warned of a PC slowdown linked to memory prices. The Business Times reported that the index had slipped below its 20-day, 50-day and 100-day simple moving averages, at 30,050, 29,812 and 29,559, while remaining above a rising 200-day average at 27,912.

This was the third time in 2026 that the index fell more than 10 per cent below a record, after closes of 23,132.77 on March 27 and 27,192 on July 29, and both times it later set new records. The Business Times said the immediate task for bulls was to reclaim the 29,559 to 30,050 band, with 30,500 and 31,200 as hurdles above, and the late-October low near 28,800 as first support, with a break exposing the 28,000 region and then the 200-day average. stories.Headline: Expert discusses AI’s role in modern warfare
stories.Summary:
Paul Scharre, an expert on artificial intelligence and autonomous systems in war, spoke on Thursday at the University Theatre at Cameron University in Lawton, Oklahoma. His presentation, titled “Power in the Age of Artificial Intelligence,” was part of Cameron’s academic festival, whose theme this year is “Being Human in the Age of AI.” Scharre is executive vice president of the Washington, D.C.-based think tank the Center for a New American Security. He said the age of AI warfare is not some future thing and is happening now.

Scharre said AI systems are playing roles in military conflicts around the world, including Gaza and the wars in Ukraine. He said drones are used on a massive scale in warfare, with Ukraine producing millions of drones a year. He described first-person view drones, which stream a live video feed from an onboard camera to a human pilot, letting the pilot fly as if sitting inside the drone. He said autonomy is built into these drones, so when a pilot sees a target and locks on, the drone can fly itself to the target.

Scharre said the growing use of AI in warfare raises the question of whether the military should use those systems to make decisions. He asked whether humans want to be making these decisions or whether machines should have such autonomy as a soldier. He said world leaders have discussed this issue at the United Nations for more than a decade without settling on a solution. He said they eventually agreed that the law of war should still apply to autonomous weapons, but beyond that there is no agreement among countries on what to do or whether there ought to be some limits.

Separately, Ecuador’s Ambassador to India, Fernando Xavier Bucheli Vargas, opened a session at the Embassy of Ecuador in New Delhi on October 29, 2026, on AI in diplomacy. The session, “AI for Ambassadors ,  From Insight to Advantage,” was attended by 16 diplomats, including 13 Heads of Mission, representing 14 countries. Technical presentations were delivered by Naveen Sharma, chairman of Anaika Global and author of “Prompt to Political Power ,  Political Leader’s AI Mastery Manual,” and Poonam Dey, an AI practitioner with academic qualifications in computer science and psychology. The programme focused on how AI-powered tools could help embassies and high commissions improve the efficiency of their operations, strengthen understanding of political and economic developments, and support more informed diplomatic decision-making, with presentations demonstrating practical applications rather than theory.

stories.Headline: Google's PageBreak AI agent finds over 500 XSS bugs
stories.Summary:
Google's AI-powered security agent, PageBreak, has found more than 500 cross-site scripting vulnerabilities in its web applications since it began full operation in January, according to a paper published by Google. The system uses Gemini models to autonomously investigate potential vulnerabilities. It reports these only after deterministic validators successfully reproduce the exploit against a running application. This process results in a near-zero false-positive rate.

With PageBreak, every vulnerability hypothesis is tested against a running environment with a real exploit, such as executing JavaScript for XSS, writing to a world-readable location for path traversal, or triggering outbound DNS for RCE. Google also retains non-deterministic findings internally to seed deeper future scans, identify gaps in its validation capabilities, and guide the development of new validators. These unverified candidates are not sent to product teams, keeping their attention focused on high-confidence vulnerabilities. In a separate article on Google Bug Hunters, Michał Bentkowski describes three technical cases found by PageBreak: an XSS vulnerability, a cache-poisoning issue caused by a service misconfiguration, and a path-traversal vulnerability.

Michał Bentkowski, an information security engineer at Google, explained that early in PageBreak's development the team made a conscious decision to prioritize deterministic validation. Rather than simply hypothesizing bugs based on code patterns, the system closes the loop by verifying potential flaws against running environments. He also noted that the validators are currently lacking in capabilities to cover all vulnerability types or complex scenarios, which comes with the risk of false negatives. Lukas Weichselbaum, a senior staff information security engineer at Google, stressed the importance of reducing false positives, noting that many AI-generated bug reports sound convincing but turn out to be wrong, and that the validators are plain code written by security engineers, not by the model, and live outside the agent loop.

Bentkowski says PageBreak benefits from Google's engineering environment, particularly its monorepo end-to-end code visibility, security signals that connect live HTTP traffic to source code, and existing scanning infrastructure that provides authenticated access to its web applications. Google is integrating PageBreak with other agentic security initiatives such as CodeMender to automatically generate fixes for the vulnerabilities it discovers. The longer-term goal is to reduce product-team involvement to validating AI-generated fixes. No independent validation of the 500+ vulnerabilities has been provided.

stories.Headline: How Can Organizations Combat the AI-Enhanced Threat Actor?
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, Dan Lohrmann moderated a session called "Combatting the Artificially Enhanced Threat Actor" at the Secure Delaware conference, which is hosted by Government Technology. The two expert panelists were Dovid Clarke, Chief Executive Officer of RedShield, and Amad Sheikh, Chief Information Security Officer at the University of Delaware. Lohrmann asked the packed audience two yes or no questions, one about whether AI-enabled attackers are already changing the cybersecurity risk their organizations face and one about whether their organizations had adjusted priorities because AI can speed up vulnerability discovery or exploitation. Most hands went up to answer yes. The panelists described growing cyber threats driven by AI, alongside growing use of AI in governments and universities worldwide, with examples ranging from Hugging Face and poorly governed AI to shadow AI and a rising number of ransomware and other AI-powered attacks from bad actors.

The panel said AI genuinely scales phishing and speeds up social engineering, which lowers the barrier for low-skill attackers, while hype exceeds reality on autonomous zero-day discovery and fully self-driving complex breaches remain rare. The real threat is volume and velocity, and total autonomous orchestration is exaggerated. AI compresses the time from vulnerability disclosure to weaponized exploitation from weeks down to hours, because attackers automate exploit generation instantly while defenders are held back by manual testing and change windows. Traditional patching cycles are too slow, turning disclosure into an immediate race against machine-speed attacks. Rigorous asset management and strict identity access controls become even more important because they prevent automated lateral movement and shrink the attack surface, and rapid patch management with continuous backup verification supports recovery when machine-speed exploits get past perimeter defenses.

On prioritization, the panel said organizations should move from static CVSS scores to threat-informed prioritization based on active exploitation data, aiming automated patching and isolation at high-risk external assets first. Combining contextual threat intelligence with continuous attack surface management lets large public-sector and university security teams outpace machine-speed scans, use limited resources efficiently and protect critical infrastructure from automated exploitation waves. Information sharing through groups like REN-ISAC and MS-ISAC lets universities and local governments pool threat intelligence instantly, and turning individual detections into automated collective blocklists and defensive playbooks helps public-sector organizations neutralize machine-speed threats together faster than any single entity could alone. On communicating with executives, the panel said leaders should ground discussions in business risk and operational impact rather than technical hype, frame AI threats as faster velocity and scale on existing vulnerabilities such as automated phishing and quicker exploit delivery rather than speculative sci-fi scenarios, and use objective threat intelligence to separate proven adversary tactics from vendor marketing. Presenting AI as a risk multiplier rather than a new paradigm keeps leadership focused on funding baseline controls like asset visibility, identity control and rapid patching.

Lohrmann wrote that what he enjoyed most were the practical stories and real-life impacts from the experts and the audience questions, most of which covered awareness and helping enterprise business leaders and government leaders understand the risks and benefits of AI. He said it was clear at the session that personal roles still have a huge impact and that the basics can never be dropped. In his view it still comes down to people, process and technology solutions, and people problems and solutions are the most important piece. The articles do not say what specific follow-up actions, deadlines or policy changes come next.

stories.Headline: Iowa State University professor gives lecture on AI’s potential to protect power grids, infrastructure
stories.Summary:
On Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, Manimaran Govindarasu, an Iowa State University professor, gave a lecture at Penn State in 108 Chambers Building in University Park, Pennsylvania. At least 20 Penn State students and faculty attended the hourlong talk, which began several minutes late because of technical difficulties. Govindarasu holds the titles Anson Marston Distinguished Professor in Engineering and Murray J. and Ruth M. Harpole Professor in Electrical and Computer Engineering. The lecture covered how cybersecurity can address AI-based threats to power grids and other energy infrastructure.

Govindarasu said AI is used by cybersecurity professionals to find vulnerabilities, including in the PHP coding language used by servers of up to 70% of all websites. He argued that because AI capabilities are growing among both defenders and attackers, more investigation is needed into how AI can help prevent attacks on power grids, including attacks improved or created by AI, and how to direct response and recovery after such incidents. He said stricter security measures such as a "zero-trust" architecture, which adds stricter authorization and access controls within a system, could also help protect energy infrastructure. He has conducted years of research on power grid cybersecurity, often with funding from academic organizations and federal agencies including the U.S. Department of Energy and Department of Defense.

Govindarasu said in an interview that cybersecurity professionals need a more "adversarial" way of thinking to use AI and other emerging technologies such as quantum computing to protect energy infrastructure. He said national and economic security center on the security and resiliency of the grid, and that hackers or terrorist groups could target critical infrastructure with AI-based adversarial models. He said defenders must first understand what adversaries can do so they can stay ahead by developing advanced security solutions. Nilanjan Chaudhuri, a Penn State College of Engineering professor whose interests include AI and energy systems, said he shares Govindarasu's views and that harnessing AI for cybersecurity will require cooperation across disciplines such as engineering and computer science.

Steve Zukley, a master's degree student in electrical engineering who was required to attend, said the intersection of AI and cybersecurity was something he had not really considered. He said much of the U.S. power grid, including its computer systems, is several decades old, so there is a growing need to keep pace with modern threats. He said the lecture showed how AI could potentially provide up-to-date protection of the country's energy infrastructure, and that if the grid goes down during a blizzard or heat wave, people will pass away. He said quantum computing is still on the horizon, but everyone, the good guys and the bad guys, has access to AI.

stories.Headline: Veterans Affairs Ridesharing Program: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence for Optimal Rideshare Requests
stories.Summary:
In 2017, Charles Franklin was working as a community employment coordinator at the VA in Boston, where rising housing costs pushed veterans to seek affordable housing outside the city. Limited public transportation made it hard for those veterans to find and keep jobs. In 2018, Franklin piloted a program that gave 10 veterans in the VA homeless program a vehicle for the first four weeks of their new jobs. All 10 veterans kept their employment and later moved into more fulfilling and higher-paying positions.

The pilot's success brought additional funding, and the effort grew into what is now the VA Rideshare Program, with a platform where veterans can request and schedule rides. The service is free, since the VA covers all expenses and handles payment, and rides can be booked through the app or the customer service center up to 30 days in advance or on demand. Customer service is available 24/7 to address safety concerns and help with rescheduling. In 2021 the program was approved for national expansion, and it now covers same-day mental health appointments, medical appointments, help reaching safe destinations when stranded, and more recently food service delivery.

The platform is driven by artificial intelligence, which analyzes each ride based on ZIP code, day of the week, hour, and cost. Using historical data, the AI calculates the most efficient rideshare company for the request, considering time and location, and then schedules the ride. The VA is working on features that use AI to adapt to market changes, including new vehicle emission regulations set by states and localities, so the algorithms can select electric vehicles or vehicles meeting required emission standards based on location. The program operates in all 50 states plus 3 U.S. territories and has provided more than 700,000 rides, and 1,270 participating veterans kept employment for at least one year.

The platform has 92 transportation company APIs built in, including taxi services for areas not served by Lyft or Uber. The average cost per ride is $31.55, or $2.39 per mile, including software development fees, and 93% of every dollar spent supports veterans in accessing transportation services. The article also notes that the General Services Administration has a blanket purchase agreement for rideshare services with Lyft and Uber, which could be a viable solution for federal sites, though the VA did not use this agreement. Rideshare services may be able to replace employee shuttle buses, reduce rental vehicle requests, or decrease fleet vehicle numbers.

stories.Headline: Auburn Engineering artificial intelligence and aquaculture research projects part of $8.1 million statewide investment
stories.Summary:
Auburn University researchers in artificial intelligence and aquaculture will receive nearly $1.3 million in research grants, Gov. Kay Ivey announced this week. The funding is part of a combined $8.1 million investment from the Alabama Research and Development Enhancement Fund, which is administered by the Alabama Department of Economic and Community Affairs (ADECA). Three Auburn projects were included among the grants, which are being issued to provide practical solutions to emerging challenges and to promote economic growth in the region. The Auburn research projects are expected to run for two years.

One project will receive $600,000 to develop an AI platform that can aid law enforcement, first responders and veterans in recognizing post-traumatic stress disorder. That project is led by Xiao Qin, a professor in the Department of Computer Science and Software Engineering. A second project will receive $277,240 to enhance AI technology and make AI easier to use for the public and organizations, and its lead investigator is Jiaqi Wang, an assistant professor in the same department. A third project will receive $387,658 to study the use of microalgae to convert aquaculture wastewater and paper mill emissions into protein-rich fish feed, with Jin Wang, a professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering, as principal investigator.

Steve Taylor, senior vice president for research and economic development, said the investment confirms Auburn's position as a trusted partner in improving quality of life for the citizens of Alabama. He said the funds will be used to leverage Auburn researchers' expertise in AI technology development and chemical engineering processes. According to Taylor, the work aims to make AI tools easier to use, to enhance community safety and to help farmers ensure a cost-effective agricultural supply chain. The projects align with Auburn's Strategic Plan 2035 goals for doubling its research activity through impactful scholarly work that enhances economic prosperity and solves problems through collaborative team science.

stories.Headline: AI Infrastructure on DOE Lands Request for Information
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Energy released a Request for Information on October 29, 2026, through its Office of Policy. The request asks data center developers, energy developers, and the broader public for input on using DOE land for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The department said the goal is to help America lead the world in AI while helping to lower energy costs. It wants to co-locate data centers and new energy infrastructure on DOE lands.

DOE has identified 16 potential sites that it says are uniquely positioned for rapid data center construction. These sites have in-place energy infrastructure and the ability to fast-track permitting for new energy generation such as nuclear. The information collected will be used to inform development, encourage private-public partnerships, and enable construction at select DOE sites. The department set a target of commencing operation by the end of 2027. Publicly available information about each site, including location and available acreage, is provided in appendices to the RFI.

The RFI also aims to gather information on potential development approaches, technology solutions, operational models, and economic considerations for establishing AI infrastructure. The sites offer industry a chance to partner with DOE's world-class research facilities co-located there. DOE said such partnerships could further advancements in power systems design needed to run the centers and in developing next-generation data center hardware. The department framed the effort as helping ensure America leads the world in AI while helping to lower energy costs.

stories.Headline: UNESCO and Chile’s Supreme Court Explore Artificial Intelligence Training for Judges

UNESCO representatives met with the President of Chile's Supreme Court, Gloria Ana Chevesich, on 26 October to discuss artificial intelligence and its growing presence in the judicial sphere. The meeting let the two sides exchange experiences and explore possible cooperation on how the technology relates to the work of courts. Discussions covered training, knowledge sharing and the opportunities artificial intelligence could offer for justice. Esther Kuisch Laroche, Director of the UNESCO Regional Office in Santiago, attended alongside Guilherme Canela, Director of UNESCO's Division for Digital Inclusion and Policies and Digital Transformation in Paris.

The UNESCO representatives shared the experience of UNESCO's Global Initiative for Judges, which has supported judicial professionals across different regions since 2013. The initiative has helped strengthen the capacities of more than 39,000 judicial actors in over 160 countries. The conversation builds on a relationship between UNESCO and the Chilean judiciary that began in 2014. Both institutions discussed possible areas of collaboration based on their respective experience, areas of work and shared interest in examining artificial intelligence's role in justice.

Kuisch Laroche said UNESCO greatly values the chance for dialogue with the Supreme Court of Chile, which allows the two sides to share experiences and explore new possibilities for collaboration in an area of growing importance. She said UNESCO hopes to keep strengthening the exchange, making its international experience available while also learning from the perspectives and progress of the Chilean judiciary. She described cooperation as a mutual exchange and stressed the value of learning from Chilean judicial perspectives and developments. The conversation established areas for further consideration without announcing a new training programme or formal agreement.

Cooperation between UNESCO and the Chilean judiciary dates to Chile's hosting of the 17th Ibero-American Judicial Summit in Santiago from 2 to 4 April 2014. The relationship also included a meeting hosted by the Supreme Court during the 2024 World Press Freedom Day Conference. That discussion focused on crimes against the environment and the role of judicial systems in protecting journalists and other critical voices. stories.Headline: Indian News Publishers Challenge Privacy Law in Supreme Court
stories.Summary:
A group of 21 Indian news publishers filed a lawsuit in the Supreme Court on October 6, 2026, challenging India's privacy law. The group includes companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, such as Network18 and NDTV, along with the Indian Express and Times Internet. The Digital News Publishers Association filed the 698-page petition, which was reported for the first time by Reuters. The case is due to be heard on Tuesday and is the most high-profile challenge to the law so far.

The law was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government last year to protect the digital personal data of users. Its contentious provisions take effect in May 2027, and the publishers want most of them quashed. They argue the law could force a journalist to get prior consent from a person they want to investigate and could force publishers to erase stories. The publishers also say the law's powers to demand information could expose reporters' sources.

The DNPA said in its filing that the law would make investigative journalism a "benign and neutered recorder of events" and called the provisions pre-censorship. The group said media companies received verbal assurances in an August meeting that press freedom would be protected, but there was no written carve-out for journalists as in the European Union, Singapore and Britain. The law lets people withdraw consent at any time and demand their data be erased, which the DNPA says could force members to unpublish or heavily redact factual reports. The DNPA, the media groups and India's information technology ministry did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.

The lawsuit comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Modi took office in 2014. India fell to 157th out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index this year, down from 140th in 2014, though the government rejects the rankings. The government says it respects press freedom and that India's vibrant press ecosystem does not need validation from foreign bodies. The challenge is unusual because it comes from businesses headed by Ambani and Adani, whom opposition parties allege are close to Modi, charges the businesses and government deny.

stories.Headline: OpenAI slashes funding target by $10 billion
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has cut the target for its latest funding round by $10 billion, the Financial Times reported on Friday, October 31, 2026, citing people with knowledge of the matter. The ChatGPT maker is now seeking about $20 billion, down from its earlier goal. The report said the move came amid a selloff in tech stocks driven by worries about artificial intelligence spending. OpenAI set a Friday deadline for investors to commit to the round. The report said OpenAI's desired valuation has dropped to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion.

The first close is expected to raise less than $20 billion after some investors reduced their allocations. A group of UAE investors that includes the state-backed technology fund MGX is expected to be the largest participant, and the deal would give OpenAI the option to lease newly developed computing capacity in the region. Venture capital firms including Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to take part, and wealthy individuals will have the option to invest in a later retail offering at the $1.25 trillion valuation. The articles do not name any OpenAI executive or other official as speaking about the change, and they give no direct statements from the company or its investors. The information comes from people with knowledge of the matter, as cited by the Financial Times.

Reuters has reported that OpenAI, which is pursuing a listing in 2027, has been keen to close the round partly to get ahead of an imminent listing by Anthropic, since the two are tapping a similar investor base. The articles do not say what OpenAI itself has said about the report. US tech stocks have suffered a rout amid growing worries over massive spending on AI, according to the report. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index dropped 2.9 percent on Friday and is down 7.8 percent from its all-time closing high reached on October 6. The articles say the first close is expected to raise less than $20 billion, and they do not say what happens after that beyond the planned 2027 listing and the possible later retail offering.

Articles.Title: OpenAI slashes funding target by $10 billion

stories.Headline: AI data centers could be raising your electric bill — even if there's not one in your town
stories.Summary:
The articles describe how the growth of AI data centers is affecting electricity bills and local politics in the United States. Data centers consumed about 4.4% of all U.S. electricity in 2023, up from 58 terawatt-hours in 2014 to 176 terawatt-hours in 2023, according to the Yahoo article. The Department of Energy's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects that share could reach between 6.7% and 12% of the country's total electricity consumption by 2028. The NPR article reports that this midterm election, voters in more than 40 cities and towns across eight states will decide ballot measures on data center bans, moratoriums and requirements that residents get a vote before one is built.

The Yahoo article says utilities may need to build new power plants, substations and transmission lines when a large data center connects to the grid, and depending on local regulations some of that expense can be passed to everyone who pays an electric bill. PJM Interconnection, which manages the grid for 67 million people across 13 states and Washington, D.C., saw auction prices rise roughly 1,000% in two years, reaching a record $333.44 per megawatt-day in December 2025, with its July 2026 auction slightly lower at $325. PJM's independent market monitor estimated that data center demand contributed $29.4 billion to capacity auction costs across four auctions. In Maryland, households are estimated to be paying an extra $168 to $216 a year, primarily because of growing data center demand, and a 2026 study from NC State, Carnegie Mellon and other universities projected wholesale electricity prices could rise between 6% and 29% nationally by 2030, with some regions seeing increases as high as 57%.

Ari Peskoe, director of Harvard's Electricity Law Initiative, told NPR that those costs can be spread across businesses and households throughout the region. Ohio approved rules in July 2025 requiring large data centers to pay for most of the electricity capacity they reserve, even if they don't use it all, and Virginia has considered a similar approach. In June 2026, New Jersey passed a law requiring large data centers to pay for the infrastructure they need instead of passing those costs on to residents, and Wisconsin regulators ruled that people who already pay electric bills shouldn't have to help cover the cost of new data centers. Several tech companies have signed a federal pledge to cover their own power needs, and Anthropic, the company behind Claude, has said it will cover any electricity price increases caused by its data centers, but consumer advocates are skeptical. Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, discussed the backlash with NPR's Fresh Air, and the article notes that in Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown, who is challenging Republican Senator Jon Husted, accuses Husted of aggressively courting data centers and backing corporate tax breaks while residents face rising electricity bills.

A Consumer Reports survey of more than 2,000 adults released in October 2026 found that 81% of people who had stayed in the same home for at least three years had seen their electricity bills rise, with 28% reporting increases of 20% to 49%, and 84% said they would support their utility creating a separate rate category for large users like data centers. A Gallup survey earlier in the year found that seven in 10 Americans oppose building AI data centers in their area. Most major data center projects go through a state's public utility commission, where regulators decide who pays, and residents in Wisconsin and Kentucky have already submitted thousands of comments about proposed data center rates. The Yahoo article says AI data centers aren't going away anytime soon, but who ends up paying for all that power is still being worked out, and in many cases homeowners can weigh in before the decision is made.

stories.Headline: Meet Factory Droid 1.0: A Model-Independent Coding Agent Harness Built on Script Mode
stories.Summary:
Factory released Droid 1.0, the largest update yet to its Droid agent harness, on October 31, 2026. The main change is programmatic tool calling, which is now on by default. In this mode the model writes a program that runs its tools, so one model request can drive hundreds of tool calls. The base prompt is 13,055 input tokens, down 37% from 20,887, and only 2 tool definitions ship up front, down from 11.

Droid 1.0 runs on a macOS and Windows desktop app, a terminal UI, and the Node SDK @factory/droid-sdk. It works with any supported model, including users' own API keys, and users can pick a model or let Factory Router choose a cost-efficient mix. Factory reports a best result of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4 with Claude Opus 5.5, at $4.73 per passed task. With GPT-6.1 Sol, Droid takes 10% longer per passed task than Codex.

Factory defines a harness as everything around the model, meaning the prompts, the tools, how tool results return, and the loop. In Script mode the model writes JavaScript that runs in a sandbox with no file, network, or system access of its own. Raw files, search results, and logs stay inside the program, and only printed output returns to the model. Factory says Script mode cuts Droid's cost by 15% versus direct tool calling on Claude Opus 5.5, and it is on by default for 10 models, including GPT-6.1 Sol and Kimi K3.

Factory ran each harness against Droid on the same model, with 3 trials per task from October 23 to 28, 2026. On Claude Opus 5.5, Droid scores 65.2%, while Cursor and OpenCode score 62.1%, Devin 59.6%, and Claude Code 57.6%, and Droid costs up to 24% less. On GPT-6.1 Sol, Droid scores 57.6% at $0.79 per passed task, against Codex at 54.0%, OpenCode at 51.0%, and Devin at 45.0%. Most changes came from an internal Agent Factory loop in which agents read failures and propose changes that engineers review and merge.

Articles.Title: Meet Factory Droid 1.0: A Model-Independent Coding Agent Harness Built on Script Mode

stories.Headline: Anthropic proposes court review for high-risk AI models
stories.Summary:
Anthropic sent a letter to California Governor Gavin Newsom on October 15, 2026, proposing that courts be able to block high-risk artificial intelligence models. The company suggested that when a review finds a model poses a serious risk, the government should be able to ask a court to block it. Under the proposal, independent verification organizations would report risks to California's attorney general. The attorney general could then seek a court order to suspend a model's deployment, internal use, or further development if it presents a near-term risk of catastrophic harm. Reuters reported the letter on October 28, 2026, and the story spread across several outlets.

The proposal is a policy recommendation, not a law, and no court has acted on it. Anthropic also said large frontier AI developers should publish risk reports at least every six months. Evaluators should have access comparable to a company's own risk staff, subject to limits protecting customer data and sensitive details, and they should be free to publish their findings. Anthropic discussed a kill switch for AI models, saying it should be part of safety measures but not the sole focus, and instead proposed a circuit breaker approach that detects problems through monitoring and responds where they occur, including at the agent or customer level. The company said taking an entire model offline only makes sense in extreme situations.

Anthropic argued that a law focused only on model shutdown could provide a false sense of reassurance. The letter was sent in response to ideas raised in Newsom's recent executive order. OpenAI also sent suggestions to Governor Newsom on October 20, reportedly supporting shutdown controls and embedded auditors, though it did not match Anthropic's court-blocking proposal. The reporting reviewed does not say how Newsom's office responded, and it does not describe procedures such as hearings, emergency relief, or appeals for the court process.

The proposal comes as California considers stronger AI safety rules and US lawmakers debate controls on high-risk models. California has wrestled with frontier-AI safety for years, and Newsom vetoed SB 1047 in September 2024, arguing it was too broad and could discourage innovation. Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, 2026, and Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, 2026, showing the release pace a court process would have to match. The reporting offers no signal on whether Newsom finds the proposal more palatable, and whether the reading of a rarely used remedy holds will depend on bill text, not the letter.

Articles.Title: Anthropic proposes court review for high-risk AI models - TechGig

stories.Headline: Right Law Group Founder Alexis Austin Litle Speaks on AI Security and Vendor Risks at MaxLawCon 2026
stories.Summary:
Alexis Austin Litle, founder of the Colorado criminal defense firm Right Law Group and the legal technology company LexAxiom, spoke at MaxLawCon 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia, on October 8 and 9. Her presentation was titled "How to Read the Matrix: A Framework to Help You Evaluate Legal Tech AI Companies." She gave law firm owners a practical way to assess AI products before bringing them into their firms. The session focused on what happens to confidential client information, how secure the software is, and whether vendors can back up their claims.

Litle introduced a framework meant to help attorneys evaluate legal AI companies without needing an extensive technical background. Rather than relying on product demonstrations or sales materials, it encourages law firms to ask specific questions about how a vendor handles information, what security measures are in place, and whether its claims can be independently assessed. She has published supporting materials on her personal website, including an AI Vendor Evaluation Scorecard with 12 questions attorneys can use when reviewing legal technology products. Her resources also include a guide to assessing vendor security claims and an explanation of common AI marketing terminology.

Litle said lawyers are being flooded with AI products and every vendor claims its technology is secure and will save lawyers time. She said being secure is not the same as protecting client confidentiality. She said lawyers have an obligation to ensure AI models are not trained on clients' confidential data and that the data is not stored on LLM servers or accessible by third parties. She said that in criminal defense this opens clients' data up to possibly being subpoenaed and used against them, and that under rules of professional responsibility lawyers must understand how these tools work, where the data goes, and who may have access to it.

Litle founded Right Law Group in 2018 after working as a Colorado prosecutor, including as Chief of the Domestic Violence Unit in the state's 10th Judicial District. Earlier in 2026 she presented "Ethics and AI in Law: From Deepfakes to Defense Strategy Memos" for the El Paso County Bar Association. At Right Law Group, every attorney is a former prosecutor, and the firm has offices in Colorado Springs, Castle Rock, Highlands Ranch, and Denver. The firm handles DUI, domestic violence, assault, drug offenses, and other misdemeanor and felony cases, and offers free initial consultations and 24/7 availability.
