stories.Headline: A Senate draft could let Medicare test paying for AI that performs clinical tasks without real-time physician review
stories.Summary:
Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican who chairs the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, released a discussion draft on Oct. 29 called the PATIENT AI Act. The draft would direct the CMS Innovation Center to run a five-year payment model for artificial intelligence applications that can perform a clinical function on their own. The proposal has not been introduced or voted on, and Cassidy is asking for public comments by Dec. 1. The draft does not define “autonomously,” set payment rates, list covered conditions or tasks, or say how much patients would pay out of pocket.

Under the draft, the model would start no later than 24 months after the law is enacted and run for five years. Medicare would choose which AI applications and providers take part using published criteria, including clinical promise, patient safety, evidence gaps, and potential benefit to Medicare patients. Participants would need to give patients informed beneficiary notice when an AI tool is part of their care, and participation could not reduce existing Medicare appeal rights. The evaluation would measure effects on patient outcomes, safety, access, and patient experience, not only cost.

Cassidy's office said the goal is to create regulatory predictability while prioritizing patient safety, and Cassidy said AI in health care must be done responsibly and to the benefit of patients, innovators, and consumers. Dr. John Whyte, CEO of the American Medical Association, told the Times that models built to independently provide patient care are not ready for widespread use. HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison said the department was taking a responsible, evidence-based approach to AI and expanding its use as evidence demonstrates value. The draft also says it does not alter liability under federal or state law, and it sends the question of who is liable when autonomous AI causes harm to further study through a nonprofit review.

In September, the administration was weighing how Medicare could pay for AI tools that provide care or diagnoses, and officials discussed paying AI “physicians” 60% to 80% of what human doctors earn for the same service, according to a person involved who spoke to The New York Times, Becker's reported. That was described as a discussion, not a decision. The FDA has authorized more than 1,500 medical devices that include AI for narrow tasks, such as flagging tumors on scans, but has no rules designed for chatbots or AI agents that could prescribe medications, according to Becker's. Nothing changes for Medicare patients today, and Cassidy lost his Republican primary in May, with his term ending in early January, so any formal bill would likely need a new sponsor or reintroduction in the next Congress.

Articles.Title: A Senate draft could let Medicare test paying for AI that performs clinical tasks without real-time physician review - Medical Daily

stories.Headline: United Parcel Service (UPS) Sees $15 Billion AI Data Centre Logistics Market
stories.Summary:
United Parcel Service flagged AI data centre logistics as a major focus area in comments from its CEO in 2026, according to an article published on 31 October 2026. Management referenced a roughly US$15 billion annual revenue opportunity tied to logistics services for AI-related infrastructure projects. UPS plans to support AI data centre buildouts across air, ocean, warehousing, and last mile delivery operations. The article describes UPS as a US-based logistics group with a US$91.3 billion market cap that moves parcels and freight across air, sea, warehousing, and ground delivery.

The article says the US$15 billion opportunity lines up with UPS's shift toward higher-yield business-to-business and healthcare-like contracts, where complexity justifies better pricing. It notes that rivals such as FedEx and DHL are active in this kind of project work. The article also says analysts have flagged debt levels and dividend cover as minor pressure points. It adds that scaling AI data centre logistics without straining cash or service quality is what the company's story will depend on, alongside building closures, automation rollouts and a high dividend payout.

The article attributes the comments to the CEO but does not name the person. It paraphrases the company's position as being that the main factor needing to go right is continued execution on automation, RFID and AI projects, so that a lower-cost, higher-yield network offsets labor, fuel and contract risks over the coming years. The article frames the question for readers as whether this new focus truly deepens the premium mix or just adds another complex project stream. It also says readers need a clear view of where UPS is trying to steer its mix and margins over several years.

The article is general commentary based on historical data and analyst forecasts, and it states it is not financial advice or a recommendation to buy or sell stock. It says its analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material. It notes that Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned. The article does not say what happens next beyond the company's stated plans to support AI data centre buildouts.

Articles.Title: United Parcel Service (UPS) Sees $15 Billion AI Data Centre Logistics Market

stories.Headline: AI adoption could add AUD $93 billion, report finds
stories.Summary:
The Tech Council of Australia released research on artificial intelligence adoption by small and medium-sized businesses, finding that wider use could add up to AUD $93 billion in annual economic value. The report was prepared by Delwood Advisory with support from Employment Hero, Google and Deputy, and drew on data from Deputy, Xero and LinkedIn. It found that only one in four SMEs is using AI, while just 5% have adopted it broadly across their operations. The research was released on 29 October 2026.

The report estimates that an average SME moving from no AI use to broad adoption could achieve annual productivity gains worth AUD $136,000. It cites research showing that 94% of SMEs using AI reported productivity improvements, while 54% of SME employees using AI reported improved job satisfaction. It identifies a gap in adoption between regional and metropolitan businesses, and notes that construction, hospitality and retail are among the industries with the largest differences in uptake between SMEs and larger companies. Barriers to adoption include limited understanding of AI, workforce skills gaps, uncertainty about return on investment, and concerns about security and reliability. The report recommends wider access to affordable training, practical advice and industry-specific examples.

Dr Kate Cornick, Chief Executive Officer of the Tech Council of Australia, said small businesses employ almost two-thirds of Australia's private-sector workforce, so improving their productivity matters to the whole economy. She said most SMEs are not yet using AI and there is a significant gap between what the technology could deliver and what small businesses currently get from it. She said that for owners dealing with rising costs and staffing pressures, even reducing time spent on routine administration can make a difference, and many need practical advice on which applications will be useful and how to introduce them. She said support needs to be better targeted because regional businesses remain behind their metropolitan counterparts and some industries face much greater adoption gaps, and that government and industry can build on existing programs.

Ben Thompson, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Employment Hero, said payroll, super, awards and compliance consume a small business owner's week and that AI takes real weight off that pile. He said his own company's product teams use AI to move through the roadmap faster, its marketing team tests and refines campaigns in days rather than weeks, and AI agents now handle 95% of routine HR support questions. He said many owners do not know where to start and regional businesses are still behind cities, and that owners need practical training, guidance and tools that work, especially in the regions and sectors furthest behind. The report adds to the wider debate over how quickly small businesses can adopt AI as larger companies move faster and absorb more of the early benefits, and its focus on regional and sector-based gaps suggests policymakers and industry groups may need to target support more narrowly rather than rely on broad national programs.

Articles.Title: AI adoption could add AUD $93 billion, report finds - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: In Pursuit of Practicality: 52 real use cases for AI in wholesale distribution today - National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors
stories.Summary:
The National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors published a white paper on November 1, 2026, titled In Pursuit of Practicality: 52 real use cases for AI in wholesale distribution today. The association said it set out to create a structured resource because many distributors still lack clear guidance on implementing artificial intelligence practically, despite widespread enthusiasm. The research effort lasted multiple months and included surveys, interviews, extensive publication scanning, and deep synthesis. It ultimately surfaced more than 50 use cases of AI for distribution.

The white paper is offered free with registration through a form on the NAW website. The form asks for a name, email, country, state or province, company name, and primary sector, and it requires consent to the terms and conditions and the privacy policy. The primary sector list includes Building Materials/Construction Supplies, Electrical, Fasteners, Food & Beverage, Healthcare/Pharmaceuticals, HVACR/Plumbing/PVF, Industrial MRO/Automation/Hose, Jan-San, Machinery, Metals, Office/Paper & Packaging, Plastics, Power Transmission/Fluid Power, Safety, and Wholesale Other. By submitting the form, users agree to receive communications from NAW/MDM about this and other related products and services, and they can unsubscribe at any time through the Manage Preferences link in any email.

The association is responsible for the research and the white paper, and it describes the work as its own multi-month effort. The form states that consent to the use of personal information can be withdrawn at any time, and it points users to the privacy policy for more information. The page also notes that the country and state fields are required by privacy laws. The white paper is sponsored, though the page does not name the sponsor beyond a sponsored by label.

The page lists other white papers from NAW, including an executive summary on making field sales performance repeatable from October 29, 2026, a guide on preparing an industrial distributor for exit from October 1, 2026, and a security paper titled Think Like a Criminal. Defend Like a Pro. from September 11, 2026. The page does not say what happens after registration beyond the offer of the free white paper. It also does not give a publication date for the white paper beyond the November 1, 2026 timestamp on the article.

Articles.Title: In Pursuit of Practicality: 52 real use cases for AI in wholesale distribution today - National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors

stories.Headline: Mass. ‘Future Booth’ gives residents a direct line to lawmakers as state debates AI safeguards
stories.Summary:
Ari Rosenthal, a local educator and activist, set up a phone booth called the “Future Booth” in communities around Boston, Boston 25 News reported on November 1, 2026. Visitors can plug in their phones and call state legislators to share their views on artificial intelligence. The booth includes phone numbers for six legislators involved in deciding the fate of the bill. Rosenthal is a teacher and co-founder of the Massachusetts AI Action Network.

The booth is meant to draw calls about Senate Bill 3228, which includes AI safety and transparency provisions aimed at large AI developers. Rosenthal says the booth has hosted well over 1,000 conversations about AI. The bill went into conference committee in September, and its final outcome depends on negotiations between House and Senate lawmakers. Lawmakers are debating legislation that would put safeguards in place for AI developers.

Rosenthal said the effort is not anti-AI but focused on safe AI, and he compared it to wanting airbags in a car you love. He said the lack of federal regulation has put more attention on states to address public safety, mandatory reporting, third-party audits and transparency. He said people’s opinions matter and that AI is so technical that many people feel frozen, but it does impact their lives. Critics argue additional regulation could slow innovation, increase costs and make Massachusetts less attractive to AI businesses.

Articles.Title: Mass. ‘Future Booth’ gives residents a direct line to lawmakers as state debates AI safeguards

stories.Headline: Billionaire Howard Marks’ AI Warning and Top 5 Non-AI Stock Picks
stories.Summary:
Billionaire investor Howard Marks, co-founder of Oaktree Capital Management, warned in an interview with investor and author William Green earlier in October 2026 that the artificial intelligence investment boom could repeat the dot-com bubble. Marks said AI could transform the world without necessarily making investors wealthy. He acknowledged his earlier warning that most companies investors were betting on to profit from AI could eventually become worthless. Marks made his name partly by questioning internet and technology stock valuations in a January 2000 memo titled bubble.com, months before the dot-com bubble burst.

Marks said change the world and investors making money are not the same thing. He questioned who will capture AI's profits, noting that aggressive competition could force companies to cut prices and reduce margins, and that businesses using AI could pass savings to consumers instead of earning higher profits. He warned investors should not assume today's leaders are certain to be the leaders of tomorrow, and he described chasing smaller, speculative AI companies as a lottery-ticket mentality. He also said nobody can say exactly how AI's labor-saving tool will turn into profits, and that companies are spending enormous sums on computing infrastructure with unclear revenue and profit to come.

Marks is responsible for the warning, which comes from his long study of markets, risk and speculative bubbles. Oaktree, founded in 1995, manages more than $200 billion in assets. The article also lists five non-AI stocks in Oaktree's second-quarter 2026 13F filing, ranked by stake value, after excluding TORM, whose shares Brookfield took control of in July 2026. They are Viper Energy, Telephone and Data Systems, AngloGold Ashanti, Garrett Motion and Expand Energy.

The article gives no further context on what happens next beyond the stock details. It says Oaktree raised its TDS stake by 24% in the second quarter to $196 million, trimmed AngloGold Ashanti by 2%, cut Garrett Motion by 48%, and held Viper Energy and Expand Energy unchanged. TDS dropped its Array offer in September and plans to restart buybacks. AngloGold kept its full-year guidance and expects most output in the second half.

Articles.Title: Billionaire Howard Marks’ AI Warning and Top 5 Non-AI Stock Picks

stories.Headline: AI Labs Pay Lawyers $400 an Hour to Train Models
stories.Summary:
AI labs are paying lawyers, doctors and engineers to help train artificial intelligence models, Bloomberg reported. A civil rights attorney can be offered up to $400 an hour for the work, with no client involved. Platforms such as Mercor recruit and place these specialists with AI labs, while Handshake AI connects students, graduates and professionals with technical training projects. Data annotator now ranks fourth on LinkedIn's list of the fastest-growing U.S. jobs, and experts make up 30% of participants on the British data-work platform Prolific.

Recruiters advertise $400 an hour for attorneys, $170 an hour for condensed matter physics experts and up to $120 for software engineers, all to help train next-generation AI systems. Mercor told Bloomberg its workers average $110 an hour, though it said it did not have data on what share of tasks pay that rate. Mercor's legal listing pays $60 to $150 an hour and asks experts to write a problem from a matter they handled, with the facts, forum and governing law, plus a reference answer that a model's attempt is graded against. Handshake's physician posting lists up to $200 an hour and asks for a medical license and direct patient care experience, while its lawyer posting seeks a law degree, a license and practice experience at $90 to $110 an hour. Fellows are paid by Handshake, not the AI labs, and hourly projects pay for time spent revising and resubmitting work.

Mercor describes the job as applying professional judgment to how a model reasons and responds. Jack Weis, a Princeton chemical engineering Ph.D. who graduated in 2024 and applied to more than 2,300 jobs, took a $70-an-hour Mercor gig in January, The Wall Street Journal reported. He wrote chemical engineering questions for a language model in a program called the Studio, evaluated its answers and tried to improve them, working four to 20 hours a week while the software recorded his screen. Researchers at Scale AI, a rival data vendor, found that checklist-style rubrics built from reference answers written by experts and stronger models produced significantly better models than rubrics generated by AI alone. The work does not always last: Weis received less work over time, and in mid-March Mercor cut his contract, which he learned from a Slack message sent to a group of 810 people.

Mercor was hit with at least seven class action lawsuits in April after a data breach, PYMNTS reported. The suits say the breach exposed contractors' interview recordings, facial biometric data and screenshots of their computers, and allege Mercor monitored those computers, shared the data with clients and used recorded interviews to train AI models. Mercor has said it disputes what it called speculative claims in the suits, and in July it said only a limited subset of experts had sensitive information leaked, Staffing Industry Analysts reported. Mercor announced July 9 that it was buying Deeptune, a startup that builds simulated software environments for training AI agents, and in August Nvidia discussed joining a funding round that would value Mercor at $20 billion, double its valuation from October 2025.

Articles.Title: AI Labs Pay Lawyers $400 an Hour to Train Models - PYMNTS.com

stories.Headline: Nuclear reactors under construction rise to 79 globally on AI demand
stories.Summary:
The number of nuclear reactors under construction worldwide has risen to 79, the highest figure in 40 years. Nikkei Asia reported the figure on November 2, 2026, in a story dated November 1. The report says the total is the largest since 1986. It links the rise to high fossil fuel prices and the growing use of energy-hungry artificial intelligence.

The articles give few further details on the projects. They name Egypt, which is building its first nuclear power plant with help from Russia. They do not list the other countries building reactors or give a breakdown by country. They also do not give a start date for the 79 figure or say how many reactors were under construction before.

The articles do not say who is responsible for the global total or quote officials on it. They do not name any company, agency or government as leading the build-out. No statements from officials or executives appear in the text provided. The only named project is Egypt's first plant, built with Russian assistance.

The context given is rising energy costs and the spread of AI, which the report says are speeding up plans for new plants. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that. They do not give a timeline for completing the 79 reactors or say whether more are expected. They also do not say how the count will be tracked.

Articles.Title: Nuclear reactors under construction rise to 79 globally on AI demand

stories.Headline: Will AI Provide a Boost for XRP? The XRP Blockchain Ledger Just Hit 14 Million in AI Agent Transactions.
stories.Summary:
By October 27, 2026, artificial intelligence agents had made 14.6 million payments on the XRP Ledger, according to a Motley Fool article published October 31, 2026. Those payments were worth just $33,506 in total, or around a fifth of a penny per transaction. One service, the Heurist Inference Router, accounted for 10.4 million of the payments, or 71%, billed in Ripple's Ripple USD stablecoin. The article says this activity has not done much for XRP holders so far.

RippleX's engineering lead, J. Ayo Akinyele, aims for 100 million payments made by AI agents, though the article says he gave no time frame. He also claims that around 25% of transactions on the ledger are made by agents today, a claim the article says cannot be verified because public data is not comprehensive enough. As of October 27, 195.2 million payments totaling $42.2 million were settled on other blockchains, which the article says makes XRPL's market share quite small. The article adds that AI agent developers tend to go where users, tooling and dollars already are, and in crypto that means Ethereum is far more attractive.

The article says XRP holders would need a mechanism to get upside, and the only one they have, fee burns, is negligible. Agents paying in RLUSD need XRP only for fees, which the article describes as practically nonexistent. All 14.6 million agent payments on the XRP Ledger have destroyed only about 146 XRP, or $193, while the coin's market cap is $83.3 billion, far too large to be moved by this level of activity. The article says it is faintly possible that AI agents could force XRP's price higher a few years from now, but that would require much more activity to depend on holding or burning XRP itself.

The article's context is that AI use in finance could keep growing, and if it does, the current sum might be just the start. It notes that at least a few AI agents are sending money and making payments on the XRP Ledger today. The article does not say what happens next beyond Akinyele's target and the possibility of more agent activity. It advises against loading up on the coin expecting a benefit.

Articles.Title: Will AI Provide a Boost for XRP? The XRP Blockchain Ledger Just Hit 14 Million in AI Agent Transactions.

stories.Headline: Can AI crack the Cup? The bots are all in on Point Of Law
stories.Summary:
Five leading AI models, Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Perplexity and Gemini, were each given the same form and data pack on all 24 Melbourne Cup runners. The pack included barriers, weights and penalties, jockeys and trainers, career histories, track and distance records, sectional data and ratings, a speed map and the current market. Each model was asked to build its own model from scratch, price the field to a 100 per cent market and give a top pick, a best value bet, a lay and a probability-based top four. The exercise followed the Cox Plate, where Cosmic Crusader was the top pick for ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini and every model had him and Birdman somewhere in its top four.

Point Of Law is the top pick for ChatGPT, Perplexity, Grok and Gemini, and appears in every top four. ChatGPT rates him $12.05 against a market price of $6.50 and says he is its most likely winner but not worth that price. Claude goes its own way with Shockletz, rated $8.20 against $11, noting she drops 7kg to the minimum 51kg. Soul Of Spain is the value pick for ChatGPT and Grok at $41, while Claude and Gemini land on Zakouma at $27. James J Braddock is the lay for Claude, ChatGPT and Perplexity at $14, and Gemini lays Knight's Choice at $31.

The models agree James J Braddock is too short at $14, citing his seven starts, his failure to race beyond 2420m, his 24-length defeat in the Irish Derby and barrier 24. ChatGPT says Point Of Law has three wins from five starts and arrives off a Geelong Cup victory with 53kg after a two-kilo penalty, but has yet to race beyond 2846m. Perplexity says Soul Of Spain was beaten just 0.26 lengths in the Sydney Cup over 3200m and has the best last-600m figure at the distance range in the field. Grok calls Point Of Law the only runner combining a recent strong win, ideal weight and the right settling profile for the trip.

The bots found more common ground in the Cup than in the Cox Plate, with Point Of Law on top for three of the four and in every top four. Juja Kibo and Shockletz each feature in three of the four top fours, while Hopewell Rock, second favourite at $9.50, makes only two. The value picks split down the middle, with two models on Soul Of Spain and two on Zakouma. The race is on Tuesday.

Articles.Title: Can AI crack the Cup? The bots are all in on Point Of Law

stories.Headline: Adopt AI technology to boost legal efficiency, Ugandan lawyers urged
stories.Summary:
Justice Geoffrey Kiryabwire of Uganda's Court of Appeal warned on Friday, October 30, 2026, that lawyers who fail to adopt modern information technology and Artificial Intelligence risk being pushed out of the profession. He spoke in Kampala at the launch of the PM Law AI tool. He urged legal practitioners to identify their technological needs and craft strategies to keep pace with digital developments. He said computers will not replace lawyers, but lawyers who use computers effectively will replace those who do not.

The new platform is an AI chatbot accessible through WhatsApp, designed and curated for Uganda's legal landscape. It was developed by Agentic AI, a company based in France and the United States that has been fully incorporated in Uganda. The tool answers complex questions rooted in local jurisprudence that general global AI systems often misinterpret. Dr. Paul Mukiibi, team leader of the PM Law Digital Hub, said internal studies showed WhatsApp is already the primary communication platform for Ugandan lawyers.

He said the chatbot is built on Uganda's legal jurisprudence and avoids hallucinations, giving answers based on the country's statutory framework and court decisions and updating users whenever there is a change. Mr. Anthony Asiimwe, Vice President of the Uganda Law Society, welcomed the innovation and expressed optimism that integrating AI tools into daily practice will streamline research, enhance operational efficiency, and improve access to justice across the country. Justice Kiryabwire said embracing digital transformation is no longer optional and noted that a chatbot on a widely used app like WhatsApp offers an accessible entry point for practitioners. Dr. Mukiibi said technology has moved legal research away from the days of running to the library for a book, and that research can now be done anywhere with the right gadget, internet, and data.

He said the tool is timely for research not only for lawyers but also for members of the bench, academia, and the entire legal fraternity. The launch comes as Uganda's Judiciary increasingly digitizes its operations. Courts across the country are progressively moving away from physical paper filings to electronic court management systems. These systems let practitioners and the public upload documents, track case progression, and monitor schedules online.

Articles.Title: Adopt AI technology to boost legal efficiency, Ugandan lawyers urged

stories.Headline: July House launches ‘CLYNK(CLYNK)’, an AI advertising platform using actors’ digital likenesses
stories.Summary:
July House, an AI IP and platform company led by CEO Jeong Ui-seok, launched an AI advertising production platform called CLYNK, according to a report by Son Bong-Seok published on November 2, 2026. The platform connects advertisers, IP rightsholders such as actors, and AI creators in one place. Advertisers can choose an actor, get approval from the actor's side, and produce ads based on digital likenesses through AI creators. Model fees for each actor are listed publicly on the platform, so advertisers can request production immediately.

The whole process, from the actor's approval and use rights to creation by AI creators, review of deliverables, and settlement, takes place within the single platform. An actor's digital likeness is used only within the scope the actor has consented to, and all production goes through the rightsholder's approval process. To mark the launch, July House is preparing a production-cost support program, and the first 50 advertisers who apply for launch notifications will receive up to $750, or 1,000,000 KRW. Applications can be made on the official CLYNK website.

In November, July House will also introduce a program called Starring, in which actors directly choose the advertisers they will work with. Jeong said consent should be certain, creation should be free, and transactions should be transparent, and he said CLYNK operates by this principle. He added that the company will build a market where actors, advertisers, and AI creators can all work with peace of mind. July House Group protects existing intellectual property rights while expanding business opportunities using AI technology, and its affiliates include ARKAIN, ASTRX, and the Korea Digital DNA Center, and it also holds a stake in BA Entertainment.

Articles.Title: July House launches ‘CLYNK(CLYNK)’, an AI advertising platform using actors’ digital likenesses

stories.Headline: AI Nuclear Push: $4.6B Raised, 2 Reactors Building [2026]
stories.Summary:
US nuclear startups have raised $4.6 billion so far in 2026, up from $3.8 billion in all of 2025, according to a Bloomberg report carried by EnergyNow.com. The money is driven by tech companies that want carbon-free power around the clock for their AI data centers. The hardware does not exist yet, though. The same report says only two new commercial reactors are under construction in the US and Canada, and no other project has won approval from regulators. Bloomberg first published the piece on Sept. 25, and it was still circulating through energy and finance outlets as of Oct. 31, 2026.

The gap between cash and kilowatts is the core of the story. Bloomberg Intelligence senior analyst Scott Levine does not expect widespread commercialization until around 2035. A Carnegie Endowment study by John Pendleton and Mackenzie Schuessler, dated June 2, says hyperscalers spent $443 billion on data centers in 2025 and are on track for more than $700 billion in 2026. An Energy Transitions Commission report dated Oct. 6 puts early US small modular reactor cost estimates at roughly $140 to $270 per megawatt-hour, while large reactors fall in a range of $40 to $190 per megawatt-hour. The same summary says US SMR capital cost estimates have climbed from $3,000 to $10,000 per kilowatt to $12,000 to $15,000 per kilowatt.

Carnegie counts about 13 gigawatts of potential nuclear capacity tied to hyperscaler commitments by the mid-2030s, roughly 6.9 GW from power purchase agreements and roughly 6.1 GW from direct partnerships with reactor developers. The deals that deliver soonest involve existing plants, including Microsoft with Constellation Energy on an 835 MW Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart in 2027 and Amazon with Talen Energy on 1.9 GW at Susquehanna by 2032. New-reactor deals cluster in the 2030 to 2039 window. Carnegie estimates projected hyperscaler nuclear output at 102 terawatt-hours a year against mid-range 2035 data center demand of 560 terawatt-hours a year, which works out to about 18% coverage.

Washington has tried to speed things up. Executive Order 14300, signed in May 2025, told the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to decide new reactor applications within 18 months and renewals within 12 months. Carnegie reports the commission completed more than 700 licensing actions in 2025, 90% of them ahead of schedule, and in March 2026 the NRC finalized Part 53, a risk-informed framework written for advanced reactors. Bloomberg frames regulators as only one of three bottlenecks, alongside cost and supply chain. Capital can accelerate paperwork and fund engineering teams, but it cannot compress the time needed to pour concrete, forge pressure vessels, and fuel a core.

Articles.Title: AI Nuclear Push: $4.6B Raised, 2 Reactors Building [2026] - shattered.io

stories.Headline: KB Kookmin Bank to lead $9.45 bil. AI infrastructure financing - The Korea Times
stories.Summary:
KB Kookmin Bank said on Sunday that it had secured the lead arranger role in a 12.6 trillion won project, worth about $9.45 billion, to build AI computing infrastructure in Korea. The project is led by Brookfield, one of the world’s largest alternative asset managers. It involves buying high-performance computing equipment, including GPUs, and supplying the infrastructure to Naver Cloud. The bank announced the deal on Nov. 1, 2026, according to The Korea Times.

Of the 12.6 trillion won in total costs, roughly 10.7 trillion won will be raised through loans. The deal is the largest syndicated loan arrangement in Korea’s history and the country’s first GPU financing deal. Unlike conventional project financing, which has centered on assets like real estate or power plants, the structure relies on anticipated long-term revenue from supplying AI computing capacity to support the upfront investment. Hana Bank, Shinhan Bank, Woori Bank and NH Investment & Securities are also reportedly taking part.

As lead arranger, KB Kookmin Bank is overseeing the financing structure, assembling the lending syndicate and coordinating loan terms. A bank official said the transaction is significant because it opens up a new area of financing. The official said the bank will keep expanding support for industries driving growth and help strengthen the competitiveness of domestic industries through productive finance. KB Kookmin Bank also said it plans to expand support for strategic high-tech industries after the deal.

Articles.Title:
KB Kookmin Bank to lead
$9.45 bil. AI infrastructure financing - The Korea Times

stories.Headline: EU DMA [2026]: 10% Revenue Fines Hit Big Tech Cloud, AI
stories.Summary:
The European Commission is pushing on three fronts at once to rein in U.S. tech giants as of November 1, 2026. It is weighing a cloud gatekeeper decision that would pull Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure under the Digital Markets Act. It has a draft AI Office rulebook open for feedback. It also just finished a Digital Markets Act review that left the law mostly intact. Bloomberg reported on October 2 that the Commission plans to name AWS and Azure as gatekeepers as soon as November, though the decision is still a draft and could slip.

On June 25, 2026 the Commission told Amazon and Microsoft it had reached a preliminary view that their cloud services should be designated under the Digital Markets Act. It called AWS the largest and Azure the second largest cloud computing service in the EU. Its reasoning rested on lock-in effects, high switching costs, large ecosystems and entrenched positions that have lasted for years. It also said AI tools and partnerships have become a decisive factor when companies buy cloud services. The cloud designation decision is due in November 2026, and the cloud investigation that could add interoperability and data portability duties runs to May 2027.

If the designation goes through, both companies get six months to bring the designated cloud services into line with the Digital Markets Act. The Register reported that the penalty ceiling for non-compliance is 10 percent of worldwide annual turnover. The obligations reporters described include interoperability, data access, rules against favoring a provider's own services, and limits on lock-in tactics. The AI Office feedback window closes on November 9, 2026, and adoption of the AI Office rules is planned for the fourth quarter of 2026. The draft AI Office rules would take effect 20 days after publication in the Official Journal.

Microsoft told reporters it was in a productive dialogue with regulators, while according to The Register it also argued that ignoring the growing power of Google Cloud and Gemini would tilt the market in a harmful way. AWS said European customers already enjoy an unusually wide choice of cloud options and, per The Register, argued the findings disregard the breadth of services on offer and could deter investment. Neither company confirmed the designation was coming. The Commission said the assessments were ongoing and no final decision had been taken, and it had already shared its preliminary assessments with both companies in June.

Articles.Title: EU DMA [2026]: 10% Revenue Fines Hit Big Tech Cloud, AI - shattered.io

stories.Headline: EXPLAINED | Why Are Neighbours Taking Elon Musk’s AI Power Plant to Court?
stories.Summary:
In Southaven, Mississippi, gas turbines that supply electricity to xAI’s Colossus 2 data centre have become the centre of a clean-air lawsuit. On October 30, US District Judge Debra M. Brown allowed claims brought by the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, or NAACP, and its Mississippi branch against xAI and subsidiary MZX Tech to proceed. The centre sits across the state line in Memphis, Tennessee, and supports Grok, xAI’s chatbot. The plaintiffs allege the companies built and operated the turbines without required air permits, and the judge rejected the companies’ dismissal arguments. The ruling does not settle liability or award damages.

The company had argued that the turbines’ portability and limited intended use placed them outside the permit requirements at issue. Mississippi’s environmental regulator had accepted an exemption for turbines remaining attached to portable units and staying on site for no more than a year, and the company relied on that interpretation. The federal judge rejected the mobile-source defence, finding the turbines did not qualify for the claimed exemption under the applicable rules. In a July 30 site update, the company listed 69 temporary turbines and said it had agreed a removal timetable with Mississippi’s regulator. The regulator’s agreement records a separate March permit authorising construction of 41 permanent turbines, which should not be confused with authorisation for the disputed temporary equipment.

The NAACP says pollution threatens its members and surrounding communities, including predominantly Black neighbourhoods, and its argument concerns who bears the local costs of infrastructure serving a much wider customer base. The Clean Air Act allows qualifying citizens and organisations to bring certain enforcement cases, and xAI challenged the NAACP’s right to proceed and the constitutionality of that mechanism. The judge rejected those arguments at this stage. The company says it is investing in emissions controls, reducing noise and replacing temporary generation with a permitted permanent power plant, and it said local air-quality monitoring met or exceeded federal standards. That is the company’s assessment, and the update does not independently establish residents’ exposure.

The lawsuit can proceed, and the plaintiffs are also seeking an injunction, a court order restricting operations. Their lawyers’ October 30 update said that request remained undecided, and the dismissal ruling itself did not order a shutdown. The next questions concern what the court orders, which turbines remain operational, and how the transition to permanent power changes emissions. Evidence from permits, operating records and independent monitoring will be crucial to establishing what the plant actually releases and what nearby residents breathe.

Articles.Title: EXPLAINED | Why Are Neighbours Taking Elon Musk’s AI Power Plant to Court?

stories.Headline: Cloudflare AI Search billing separates retrieval costs from model charges
stories.Summary:
Cloudflare set November 1, 2026 as the start of usage billing for AI Search, according to an October 1 release note. The change follows October's general availability announcement for the product. The note separates retrieval costs from model charges. Managed Workers AI embeddings and reranking are included in AI Search pricing.

The pricing counts ingestion on the final indexed chunks after parsing and chunking. Overlapping text counts in every chunk where it appears, so the original file's length is not a one-to-one proxy for the ingestion meter. For scanned documents, OCR-extracted text also counts as image-processing tokens in addition to base ingestion. Generation, query rewriting and external model providers continue to use the customer's account and gateway. Their usage is billed and logged through the applicable service.

Cloudflare's release history identifies generation, query rewriting and external model providers as separate from retrieval. The pricing page confirms that their usage is billed and logged through the applicable service. An absent embedding entry in Gateway does not establish that a retrieval workload was unused or free. The articles do not name an individual spokesperson or give direct comments.

Articles.Title: Cloudflare AI Search billing separates retrieval costs from model charges

stories.Headline: Case Study: AI Redefines Next-Gen Drilling Vibration Compliance
stories.Summary:
Tomax, a Norwegian specialist company, used artificial intelligence to analyze high-fidelity data from the full drilling process, according to a case study. Ole Andre Høiland, an artificial intelligence adviser to Tomax, monitored the company's 4,000-Hz parallel data pipeline from the driller's cabin as it streamed uninterrupted data to storage. The company targeted an active, modern 150-ton automated drilling rig that was built in late 2025. The rig was equipped with a unique strain and torsion measurement unit, or sub, integrated as an extension to the derrick drilling machine.

The sub unit came from an industry leader in control and diagnostics of rotating machinery, and it was accurately calibrated. Traditional analysis of drilling dynamics often uses data from downhole accelerometers, but those systems typically capture a mix of effects rather than the underlying coupling of forces that cause resonances. On most rigs, surface input and reactive loads are recorded at sparse intervals, typically every 10 seconds or longer. Capturing critical information at a high-fidelity level in this environment presents two challenges, signal integrity and the data pipeline. Modern sensor assemblies can export structural acoustics and stress waves at extreme sample rates, but the bottleneck is the data pipeline and the need for a continuous stream of megabytes of time-stamped data every second into a usable database.

The case study describes a successful solution for data harvesting on a level that is both new and found to meet the requirement for applying AI and machine learning solutions. The study concludes with examples from analysis that reveal the potential from a true image of everything going on in a drillstring. The fundamentals of these resonances reside in the transfer of torsional and axial forces from surface to the bit. The problem of downhole vibrations remains a significant barrier for the drilling industry, and an emerging technology based on direct interception of disturbing resonances is now being used to address the issue. Such solutions rely on a new level of understanding of the true bottomhole assembly dynamics, and AI and machine learning techniques are now helping deliver the full picture.

Articles.Title: Case Study: AI Redefines Next-Gen Drilling Vibration Compliance

stories.Headline: Runway AI YouTube Scraping Class Action Survives Dismissal
stories.Summary:
On October 30, 2026, Judge Lewis A. Kaplan of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York denied Runway AI's motion to dismiss a consolidated class action, Ace Cam, Inc. v. Runway AI, Inc., No. 1:26-cv-01362. The ruling lets the case move forward and is not a finding that Runway broke the law. The lawsuit claims Runway violated the anti-circumvention provision of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. § 1201, by getting around YouTube's measures against bulk downloading to copy creators' videos and train its Gen-3 model. Runway argued the law does not apply because anyone can watch YouTube videos for free, and it asked the court to dismiss the case with prejudice.

The creators allege YouTube uses five technical measures to stop anyone from pulling out the underlying video files, including a rolling cipher, IP blocking and rate limits, session-bound links, CAPTCHA challenges and proof-of-origin tokens. They say Runway used the open-source downloader yt-dlp to defeat the rolling cipher, kept retrieving files after session authorizations had lapsed, and rotated through IP addresses with virtual machines and proxy services. Much of the factual basis comes from a July 2024 report by 404 Media, which the complaint cites, describing an internal spreadsheet listing about 3,968 YouTube channels and more than 100,000 videos. The complaint asks for statutory damages, an injunction against further circumvention and attorneys' fees, and under 17 U.S.C. § 1203 a court may award statutory damages of $200 to $2,500 per act of circumvention.

Judge Kaplan rejected each of Runway's three main arguments for now, writing that scrambling and encryption are examples of access controls, not an exhaustive list, and that the public nature of YouTube content does not leave it unprotected. The court found the creators had plausibly alleged the measures control access, and said the law does not require creators to put the measures in place themselves. Runway's briefs point out that Yout v. Recording Industry Association of America, a 2022 Connecticut decision the judge relied on, is on appeal at the Second Circuit.

The first complaint was filed on February 18, 2026, and a second creator suit followed on February 27, 2026. Judge Kaplan consolidated the cases on March 27, 2026, and appointed Tom Kherkher of Ellzey Kherkher Sanford Montgomery LLP and Gary Klinger of Milberg, PLLC as interim co-lead class counsel. The plaintiffs filed a consolidated complaint on April 27, 2026, Runway moved to dismiss on May 27, 2026, and a third related case was consolidated on June 9, 2026. With the motion denied, the case moves toward Runway's answer and discovery, then the plaintiffs would have to ask the court to certify the class. There is no settlement, no claim form and no deadline for creators to act on.

Articles.Title: Runway AI YouTube Scraping Class Action Survives Dismissal

stories.Headline: CJI, Law Minister stress on human oversight in AI use - The Sunday Guardian
stories.Summary:
Chief Justice of India Justice Surya Kant and Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal spoke about artificial intelligence at the Legally Speaking: 4th Law and Constitution Dialogue 2026, organised by the ITV Network in New Delhi. The event also featured senior advocate Mahesh Jethmalani and Rajya Sabha MPs Dr Abhishek Manu Singhvi and Sasmit Patra. The speakers focused on responsible regulation of AI, accountability for autonomous systems and protection of constitutional rights. The Chief Justice said AI was becoming an important subject for judiciaries worldwide, especially in legal research, translation and case management.

The Chief Justice called for international cooperation among courts rather than isolated experimentation, saying that since all courts are learning at the same time it makes little sense for each to learn alone. He highlighted the proposed Judicial Innovation Lab as a platform for judicial institutions to jointly examine emerging technologies. He said technological advancement would not necessarily threaten the justice system as long as human beings remain responsible for judicial decisions. Meghwal discussed agentic AI and asked whether AI could recommend arguments for petitioners and respondents or suggest judicial outcomes. He said technology should assist rather than replace human beings.

Jethmalani said tools such as ChatGPT and Claude are increasingly used by lawyers, and he cautioned against exaggerated fears, arguing that responsible use and an appropriate legal framework could address risks. He said technology must remain the servant of justice and never its master, and he raised concerns about privacy violations, deepfakes and misuse of generated content, referring to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and 2026 rules on synthetically generated information. Singhvi called for a comprehensive global legal framework for accountability, warning that the autonomy of machines must never become the anonymity of responsibility. He warned that AI trained on flawed historical data could reproduce discrimination, turning yesterday's injustice into tomorrow's automated precedent.

Patra called on lawmakers to understand AI, its algorithms and emerging technologies before framing legislation, and expressed concern over the gap between AI's growing influence and legislators' technological understanding. He said AI could strengthen legislative processes through research and analysis, but decisions on public interest, citizens' rights and social priorities must remain guided by human judgement. He stressed that technological progress must operate within constitutional boundaries, particularly Articles 14, 19 and 21, and recalled Dr Ambedkar's address to the Constituent Assembly on November 4, 1948, on constitutional morality. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: CJI, Law Minister stress on human oversight in AI use - The Sunday Guardian

stories.Headline: Chipmakers' $5 Billion Meta Stake Exposes the Circular Deals Propping Up the AI Trade
stories.Summary:
Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom agreed to buy $5 billion of Meta Platforms stock in the company's $25 billion equity sale, a deal reported on November 1, 2026. The commitment landed as AI stocks sold off on worries about the scale of infrastructure financing. All three chipmakers gave back their gains for the week on Friday as the broader tech market slid. Meta enlarged its initial stock offering after strong demand and sold other types of shares alongside it.

The deal tightens financial links among companies that build and buy AI infrastructure, because the chipmakers are investing in a major customer that buys their chips. Most of the risk sits on the debt side, where chipmakers and hyperscalers back weaker data-center operators. Nvidia is the second-largest shareholder in CoreWeave, whose 2031 bonds trade more than 10 points over Treasurys, up from just over 4 points in June. Nvidia has also provided a $105 billion backstop for an Ohio data center that SoftBank's SB Energy is building for OpenAI.

S&P Global cut its outlook on Meta to negative from stable late Friday, keeping its AA- rating. The agency projected capital spending of $140 billion this year, negative free cash flow through 2028, and leverage that could exceed 1.0x as soon as 2027. A Meta spokesperson said the company disagrees with the assessment and pointed to significant product and business opportunities ahead. Kasim Kutay, chief executive of Denmark's Novo Holdings, said what is scary is the circularity in both fixed income and the equity world should there be a correction.

OpenAI has cut the target for its latest fundraising round to $20 billion from $30 billion and lowered its expected valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion, according to the Financial Times. Anthropic filed an S-1 on Monday ahead of a public listing next month, showing sharply higher revenue and positive cash flow in the first half of the year. Alphabet shares fell about 12% on Thursday, their worst day on record, after its cash flow sank deeper into negative territory. Market veteran Ed Yardeni said the AI boom faces financial, physical and political constraints, but he views them as healthy for its durability and argued that further AI jitters could set up buying opportunities.

Articles.Title: Chipmakers' $5 Billion Meta Stake Exposes the Circular Deals Propping Up the AI Trade

stories.Headline: Chamath Palihapitiya Sounds The Alarm On AI's $400 Billion Debt Problem — And Why Treasury Investors Should Care
stories.Summary:
Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya warned on a recent episode of the All-In podcast that the artificial intelligence boom is becoming a debt-fueled spending spree. He said the companies at the center of the boom were previously among the most profitable and cash-generative businesses in the world. Now, he said, they are spending so aggressively that they are burning through cash accumulated over the years. That is forcing them to increasingly tap debt markets to fund their AI ambitions, he added.

Palihapitiya said the AI complex now carries roughly $340 billion to $400 billion in debt, a figure that could climb significantly as companies keep investing through 2027. He estimated that what AI companies need to raise through the end of 2027 could equal about 30% of all the debt the U.S. Treasury is expected to issue in the same period. According to IO Fund, AI-related debt issuance reached $466 billion through September, up from $101 billion in the same period of 2025. Goldman Sachs puts the figure at $489 billion as of July 22, already above the $322 billion raised throughout 2025.

Palihapitiya said the biggest technology companies are pouring money into data centers, GPUs, networking equipment and other infrastructure, and have decided to put the foot down on spending because they believe it will generate significant growth in the years ahead. He said that as they do so, they deplete their cash and have to raise debt. His bigger concern, he said, is that AI borrowing needs could collide with the U.S. government's own financing needs, with AI companies competing with the Treasury for the same pool of investor capital. He said the most important part of the capital market this starts to crowd out is the appetite for government Treasuries.

At the time of writing, the 10-year Treasury yield hovered around 4.933%, down by nearly a basis point on Friday. The iShares 7-10 Year Treasury Bond ETF edged lower by 0.02% in Friday's after-hours session, while the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF declined 0.23%. In the same session, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF declined 1.77%, the Invesco QQQ Trust fell 3.47%, and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust closed lower by 1.07%. Palihapitiya's warning is that the AI spending boom could have consequences far beyond the technology sector if companies continue turning to debt markets at this pace.

Articles.Title: Chamath Palihapitiya Sounds The Alarm On AI's $400 Billion Debt Problem — And Why Treasury Investors Should Care

stories.Headline: GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio on peaceful mode
stories.Summary:
GPT-5.6 Sol, running in Codex with a low thinking level, completed a peaceful Factorio run with no biters in 13.5 hours of game time, according to a post by ryanmadden.net published on October 31, 2026. The run used a game manager and a Python library that let the model play the game programmatically while enforcing the same restrictions human players face in the GUI, such as player reach and fog of war. The author recorded the entire run and posted a timelapse on YouTube, and the run manager also captured production statistics throughout the game. The author had planned to stop the run after blue science research but kept it going because Sol was surprisingly effective. The rocket launch was only achieved through significant manual effort by Sol, which repeatedly ferried supplies between areas of the factory to paper over late-game failures to connect certain production systems.

The post says Sol exceeded expectations in some areas while showing clear weaknesses in others. The scaling issues the author expected at the blue science stage appeared later and slowed Sol's relative progress significantly. The author was pleased with the improvement over previous attempts with GPT-5.5, which suffered from failures to use transport belts at all. The post also links earlier work, including Claude Code playing Factorio, work towards beating Factorio autonomously, and Faketorio, an agent testbed.

The author, who writes the ryanmadden.net post, said he is working on a more detailed highlights and commentary post and video, and that people can subscribe at the bottom of the post or on YouTube for more details. He said he is optimistic about autonomous Factorio play as a medium for building intuition about the nature of model capabilities. He said playing Factorio is in many ways analogous to programming but is much more legible to casual observers, which makes it convenient for grounding discussion of model behaviors. He said he looks forward to testing other models and thinking levels, as well as non-peaceful runs.

Articles.Title: GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio on peaceful mode

stories.Headline: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent for Auditing Privacy Leakage in LLM Jailbreak Responses
stories.Summary:
A paper posted on arXiv on November 1, 2026 describes a new tool for checking whether responses from large language models leak personal information when users try to jailbreak them. The authors are Krishna Kanth Nakka, Yujun Wang, Shijie Zhou, Tu Nguyen, Gabriele Gelardi and Xuebing Zhou. They first studied existing privacy evaluators and found that these tools often disagree, especially on ambiguous cases that need more evidence or targeted analysis. The paper is titled PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent for Auditing Privacy Leakage in LLM Jailbreak Responses.

The authors introduce PrivacyEvalClaw, which they describe as a training-free deliberative agent for evaluating privacy leakage in jailbreak responses. Instead of relying on isolated single-pass judgments, it treats evaluators and analysis modules as tools, gathers evidence adaptively, investigates uncertain disclosures and reconciles conflicting signals before giving a final judgment. The primary experiments use pairwise LLM-as-Judge evaluation of complete trajectories. According to the abstract, PrivacyEvalClaw achieves favorable win rates against competing baselines across outcome, process and overall quality, and it produces explicit reasoning traces that make the evaluation process more transparent and auditable.

The paper attributes the work to the six named authors and presents the findings as their own study and experiments. It says existing approaches increasingly rely on guard models and LLM-as-Judges, and that these evaluators may interpret the same response differently. The authors state that their systematic study found substantial disagreement among privacy evaluators, particularly in ambiguous cases. They present PrivacyEvalClaw as a response to those findings, with the aim of making privacy evaluation of jailbreak responses more reliable and auditable.

The articles give no information beyond the paper's abstract and listing page, so no further context or next steps are reported. The page notes that arXivLabs is a framework for collaborators to develop and share features on the site, and that partners in it accept values including openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. It also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community. More to follow.

Articles.Title: PrivacyEvalClaw: A Tool-Augmented Deliberative Agent for Auditing Privacy Leakage in LLM Jailbreak Responses

stories.Headline: Is the "End of SaaS" Really True? Characteristics of SaaS Growing Rapidly in the AI Era, as Seen in Stripe Data
stories.Summary:
Stripe released data showing that new platform sign-ups on its system in the last three months of 2026 surpassed the total for the whole second half of 2025, and the number of new platform businesses rose more than 180% year on year. The company said platforms that started operating in the last three months were confirmed to be real businesses with customers. Platforms that began operating in January 2026 reached $1 million in payment volume within that period at a higher rate than any earlier group. Stripe published the figures in a press release dated November 1, 2026.

The data also showed that more than 55% of new platforms on Stripe as of August 2026 used AI in some way, and self-serve platforms with full integrations were up about 360% year on year. Stripe said the growth contrasted with pessimistic market forecasts earlier in the year, when about $1 trillion in software company market value disappeared in the 30 days from late January 2026 and major media called the drop the end of SaaS. Stripe said share prices later recovered to pre-crash levels, and its own research found weekly transaction counts at 100 large non-AI SaaS companies on Stripe dipped briefly, then rebounded and kept growing. Stripe said platforms that are deeply embedded in customers' core operations keep a strong advantage, and that tying together money management and payments adds further differentiation.

Eric Noeth, a partner at the private equity firm Advent, said the clear test of a platform's advantage is what happens on the day a customer stops using it. If business continues without disruption after cancellation, the product can easily be swapped for another, he said, but if insurance payouts stop, cars cannot be sold, or payments cannot be made, the product has a strong advantage and is hard to replace. Stripe said fast-growing platforms often focus on the needs of a specific industry, citing Aesthetic Record, which serves aesthetic medical clinics with records, workflows, patient engagement and compliance, and Bloomerang, which builds donor management, event check-in and tax receipt issuance for nonprofits into its CRM. Stripe listed three shared traits of strong platforms, namely handling core work such as bookings or inventory, holding valuable business data such as customer history and pricing logic, and closely linking daily operations with money movement.

Stripe said AI has lowered the cost and barrier to building software, so a good product idea alone is no longer enough and building for a specific industry's needs has become a new way for founders to stand out. It said AI is also helping platforms improve their own workflows, from sign-up and onboarding automation to scheduling, prioritization of unpaid invoices, credit and fraud risk reduction, and AI agents that act for customer businesses. Stripe said the debate over the end of SaaS was an important warning for the software industry, and that some single-function products will be easy to build and copy and hard to keep charging for by account. It said platforms that support core operations and play a central role in moving and managing money are more deeply rooted in customers' business ecosystems, and will become harder to replace as they help customers raise and manage funds and take card payments.

Articles.Title: Is the "End of SaaS" Really True? Characteristics of SaaS Growing Rapidly in the AI Era, as Seen in Stripe Data

stories.Headline: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
stories.Summary:
Zhen Yang, Wen Wang, Xander Xu and Ying-Cong Chen posted a paper on arXiv on November 1, 2026, asking whether large language models can uncover hidden physical laws through free exploration. The authors introduce LongChang, an automated framework that builds simulated worlds in which one or more physical laws differ from ordinary physics. In these worlds the tested models act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to pursue their own questions, with no research tasks and no hints about the altered laws. Separate model agents generate and review scenes, check tool designs, and judge reports for correctness and experimental support.

The framework uses the altered laws and the exploration records to judge each report, and those records then guide how scenes evolve for further exploration. This lets the full cycle run without human intervention. The authors tested 12 models, and GPT-6-Astra reached a discovery rate of 16.7% while the other 11 models scored 0%. The exploration records show anomalies that were never investigated and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.

The paper is credited to the four authors, and the work is listed under Computation and Language, Artificial Intelligence and Multiagent Systems. The abstract presents the framework and the results without stating a separate conclusion or next step. It says the records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered laws. The paper is available as a PDF and in experimental HTML form, with its TeX source also posted.

Articles.Title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?

stories.Headline: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization
stories.Summary:
Ning Yang, Bohan Cui, Zhuowen Liu and Yuting Wang posted a paper on arXiv on November 1, 2026 describing a method called ResCom. The work addresses low-bit weight and activation quantization, which cuts the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models. The authors note that activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration, because reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot tell activations within the same quantization bin apart. Their proposal is a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error.

The method relies on an output-aware calibration procedure that picks residual directions by how much they contribute to output reconstruction. It computes the correction in closed form, with no gradient training and no updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections lowered WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147. The same setting improved MMLU by 2.89 percentage points and raised five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. The authors also evaluated models from 1B to 70B parameters and a held-out C4 set to test the method beyond this setting.

The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time, according to the abstract. A separate compact-storage implementation keeps a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16. The paper is listed on arXiv with a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and the page also describes arXivLabs, a framework for collaborators to develop and share features on the site. The abstract does not say what happens next beyond the reported evaluations.

Articles.Title: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization

stories.Headline: Security Flaws Found in Five Popular AI Coding Tools, Including OpenAI Codex
stories.Summary:
Security vulnerabilities have been found in five popular AI development tools, according to a report by The Register on Oct. 29 local time. The cybersecurity startup Forever Security identified the flaws in SpaceXAI's Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Anthropic's Claude Desktop, Microsoft's Visual Studio Code and OpenAI's Codex. The tools give their embedded browsers capabilities and system access that ordinary web browsers do not allow. Forever Security called this class of vulnerabilities Embrace, short for EMbedded BRowser.

The flaws could allow remote code execution in Cursor, data theft in Claude Desktop, Codex and VS Code, and address bar spoofing in GitHub Copilot. Forever Security reported the Cursor flaw on Sept. 10, and Cursor applied a patch on Oct. 1. GitHub fixed its Copilot flaw on its own through the v1.1.29 patch released on Oct. 13. The Codex and VS Code flaws remained unpatched at the time of publication.

Anthropic first rejected the Claude Desktop report submitted on July 23, saying the issue did not involve a security boundary protected by Workspace Trust. The next day another company, Noma Security, reported the same flaw, and Anthropic then recognized it as valid. OpenAI received the Codex report on July 27 but did not respond to the researchers, though it told The Register it was aware of the issue and working on a fix. Microsoft classified the VS Code report from Sept. 10 as invalid, citing the same Workspace Trust argument.

Workspace Trust is a VS Code feature that decides whether an opened project or folder can be trusted and limits what functions and permissions are available inside it. Forever Security found that restrictions on local page access in Claude Desktop and VS Code could be bypassed using Web Workers, a browser feature that runs JavaScript in background threads. Codex had no mechanism limiting local HTML file access to the project folder in the first place, so files across the system could be read directly. The report says the Codex and VS Code flaws were still unpatched when it was published.

Articles.Title: Security Flaws Found in Five Popular AI Coding Tools, Including OpenAI Codex

stories.Headline: Mississippi Judge Lets NAACP Clean Air Act Case Against X.AI Proceed
stories.Summary:
A federal judge in Mississippi has allowed a Clean Air Act lawsuit by two NAACP groups to move forward against X.AI Corp. and MZX Tech LLC. The opinion was released on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. The judge rejected the companies' bid to dismiss the case. The ruling lets the claims proceed but does not establish that the companies broke the law. The NAACP and the Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP filed the case on April 14, 2026.

They allege the companies installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, from August to December 2025 without an air permit. The plaintiffs say the turbines powered AI data centers in the Greater Memphis area. They also say the turbines emitted smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter that could pose health risks and cause unpleasant odors. The judge found the plaintiffs have standing under the Clean Air Act. The judge also ruled that the turbines do not qualify as mobile sources under Mississippi's state implementation plan.

The judge rejected arguments that the law's citizen-suit provision violates Article II or the private nondelegation doctrine. In a June motion to dismiss, the companies had argued the turbines were mobile sources exempt from permitting, challenged the plaintiffs' right to sue, and argued that citizen suits by community groups are unconstitutional. The decision follows an Oct. 19 order that allowed the federal government to join the case while denying its request to end it. The claims against X.AI Corp. and MZX Tech LLC will now proceed in federal court.

Articles.Title: Mississippi Judge Lets NAACP Clean Air Act Case Against X.AI Proceed - TOKENPOST

stories.Headline: AI's Flaws Demand Real Human Oversight, Not Token Review
stories.Summary:
The article describes an episode in which the president released an answer from Google's Gemini model during a dispute over whether the heads of the new prosecution office and the serious crimes investigation agency should attend Cabinet meetings. The release was meant to support the president's position. Opposition figures then obtained an answer from the same AI supporting the opposite view and presented it. The AI gave different answers on the same issue, which the article says raises the question of how much AI answers should be trusted and how they should be verified.

The article says the vulnerabilities of large language models are hallucination, inconsistency, sycophancy and bias, which concern factuality, consistency, independence and fairness. It says these stem from models calculating the probability of the next word and aiming for a plausible sentence rather than a true one. It cites a 2025 joint study by the European Broadcasting Union and Britain's BBC in which 45% of AI news answers contained significant problems, including with sourcing. It names retrieval-augmented generation and comparison against original texts as remedies, while saying these too have limits.

The article says human oversight, or human-in-the-loop, is offered as a solution but that human involvement does not immediately mean substantive control. It says people fall into automation bias and confirmation bias, and that when AI's sycophancy meets human confirmation bias, errors are reinforced. It says overseers need a high level of expertise different from what exists now, and that limited oversight capacity must be allocated according to risk. It says work affecting rights, safety or property should be reviewed before execution, while work that is easy to correct needs only sample checks.

The article says institutions adopting high-risk AI should be required to guarantee expertise training for overseers, an appropriate workload and the authority to halt or modify, and that developers should provide the grounds and execution records needed for verification. It says judgments on important matters should be made independently before seeing the AI's answer, and that some tasks should be performed without AI. It says errors missed during oversight should be examined for their causes so the same mistakes are not repeated. It concludes that as AI's capabilities are built up, effort must also go into human judgment and control.

stories.Headline: Tech leaders voice concerns on AI impact on coding education
stories.Summary:
Several tech leaders raised concerns about coding education and the unintended effects of AI in software development, TechGig reported on November 1, 2026. Thomas Dohmke, co-founder and CEO of Entire, spoke at WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San Jose. He said he worries people may believe they no longer need to learn coding because of AI. He stressed that understanding the basics of computer science remains fundamental for all children. Entire recently launched a GitHub alternative that uses AI agents for code review through a system called Trails.

Josh Bentley, senior director of community advocacy at SAP, warned that the speed of AI-driven building could lead to a lack of understanding of what is being created. Darko Mesaroš, distinguished developer advocate at AWS, raised concerns about what he called AI slop and the need for more intentional software building. Mark Cavage, president and chief operating officer at Docker, said the industry needs to quickly establish safeguards and efficiencies around AI agents. Cassidy Williams, senior director of developer advocacy at GitHub, raised issues about safety guardrails and the cost of accessing AI tools. She advocated for accessible tools to prevent people from being priced out of the future.

Matt Hobbs, head of Cloud, Engineering, Data, and AI at PwC, found the pace of change exciting and noted the ability to rebuild and improve software faster and safer. Frederic Branczyk, vice president of data engineering at Dash0, kept a cautiously optimistic outlook and acknowledged the uncertainties ahead despite AI's benefits for his company and customers. The article gives no further details on what the concerns require or change. It also does not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: AI-Driven Attacks Target Factories, Pushing Layered Defense
stories.Summary:
In August, five U.S. government agencies, including the National Security Agency and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, warned of attacks on internet-exposed Siemens industrial control devices. The attackers used attack tools built with artificial intelligence and a program disguised as a legitimate equipment-monitoring tool. That program could reach the memory and configuration data of control devices. The case raised concern because it showed AI can produce attack tools that exploit known vulnerabilities without the need to find new ones.

The U.S. government recommended blocking direct internet exposure of such devices, applying security patches and tightening access controls. Siemens said it applies a security by design principle that builds security in from the earliest stages of product development. The company is also strengthening AI-assisted security testing, including penetration testing and AI red-team testing on its AI products and solutions. Siemens has joined Anthropic's Project Glasswing, an effort to harden critical software and improve the cyber resilience of major infrastructure.

Fortinet pointed to microsegmentation, which separates information technology networks from operational technology networks and breaks internal access rights into finer units, as a central countermeasure. An industrial demilitarized zone between the two networks can limit direct paths to production equipment, and remote access for outside maintenance contractors should be confined to what is strictly needed. For aging control devices that are hard to update, virtual patching uses an industrial intrusion prevention system to block attacks on known vulnerabilities at the network level. AhnLab said companies should map the OT assets inside their plants and pair regular vulnerability checks and security updates with controls on external access and detection of abnormal behavior. An AhnLab official said that concentrating security in only one area of an OT environment can open gaps elsewhere, and that firms need a layered security framework covering the entire industrial control system.

ESTsecurity emphasized protecting manufacturers' core technical data and building recovery systems for use after a breach. It said access to product data management systems, network-attached storage and source code servers should be kept to a minimum, and large outbound data transfers should be monitored. It recommended security patches and multi-factor authentication for external access services such as virtual private networks and remote desktops. Backup data should be stored separately from the network, and recovery procedures for production systems should be rehearsed periodically.
