stories.Headline: Not Your Mama’s SaaS: AI Didn’t Change Your SaaS Contract. It Changed What It Means.
stories.Summary:
A law firm article published on October 30, 2026, describes how generative AI is changing the meaning of ordinary software contract terms. The article comes from BakerHostetler and is based on a presentation called "Not Your Mama's SaaS: Same Clauses. New Consequences," given during Atlanta Technology Week 2026 at Render(ATL). It says many organizations are finding that their AI governance problems did not start with an AI agreement but with a SaaS agreement signed years earlier. The article is the first part of a three-part series.

The article gives no specific dates, numbers or names beyond those. It explains that provisions drafted long before generative AI became mainstream now carry new consequences even though the language has not changed. It gives the example of a CRM vendor releasing an AI assistant through a routine product update, with no new agreement, no procurement involvement and no legal review, while a foundation model provider may now process company data. It says standard update clauses, de-identified data clauses, feedback provisions and product improvement clauses may now permit AI training, model improvement or long-term retention. It also says protections may not cover prompts, outputs and information derived from customer data, and that a restriction on training does not resolve questions about fine-tuning, evaluation, safety review or retrieval.

The article is written by attorneys and is aimed at legal teams and procurement professionals. It says the challenge is not simply understanding AI but understanding how AI changes the practical meaning of contract language that already exists. It advises organizations to stop asking whether their contracts mention AI and start asking whether existing language already permits it. It says legal teams should identify precisely which activities are permitted, prohibited or subject to separate approval, and should address the permitted use, retention and deletion of retrieval indexes and embeddings. It also notes that customers often warrant their inputs while vendors may give no comparable assurance about outputs, and it says part two of the series will address how to allocate that risk.

The article presents itself as analysis and does not report any enforcement action, court decision or regulatory change. It says the highest-risk provisions are often familiar ones negotiated years ago and long treated as routine. It does not say what happens next beyond noting that part two will address the asymmetry between customer warranties on inputs and vendor assurances on outputs. It ends with a disclaimer that the information may not apply in all situations and should not be acted upon without specific legal advice.

stories.Headline: US SEC's top cop says agency is monitoring AI corporate disclosures
stories.Summary:
The US Securities and Exchange Commission is examining how artificial intelligence companies disclose information to investors, the agency's enforcement director told Reuters on Friday, October 30, 2026. David Woodcock, who became enforcement director in May, said the agency is monitoring these corporate disclosures as investor worries grow about a possible AI bubble. Big Tech stocks sold off that week as companies disclosed they are burning through cash to fund AI expansion while interest rates are rising. The Law360 article, published the same day, reported that SEC attorneys are watching for at least two types of AI-related fraud: scams that use AI to trick social media users, and companies that fail to properly disclose their use of the technology.

Woodcock said the SEC does not want to stand in the way of tech innovation, but it must make sure issuers give investors the full picture on potential risks. He said the agency's main concern is that people make accurate disclosures about material information so investors know what they are getting into. Where such disclosure does not happen, he said, enforcement will be present. He also said AI and superintelligence have made scams much easier and cheaper to produce at scale, raising risks for more and more people, and that brokers and other firms need processes in place to protect retail investors.

Woodcock said the SEC will keep looking at private markets, and the enforcement team's asset management unit is very focused on conflicts of interest and valuations. He said that when people do not make accurate disclosures, whether about valuations or anything else, there is a role for enforcement, and he expects more activity in this area. He also said the SEC has a role in overseeing prediction markets, which are led by Polymarket and Kalshi and have grown in popularity over the past two years. He said enforcement staff are working with policy officials and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to monitor and regulate these markets, and that the agency does not want to regulate the new industry through enforcement actions, adding that it wants to be involved where it makes sense but not in a way that crushes innovation.

stories.Headline: Pope says 'most urgent' challenge facing AI race is need for institutional ethical framework - The Tribune-Democrat
stories.Summary:
Pope Leo XIV spoke on Friday at a Vatican gathering of artificial intelligence researchers and experts, according to the Associated Press. He told the meeting that the most urgent challenge in the AI field was to identify international institutions that would put ethical principles guiding AI development into practice. The American pope has made AI a key priority. The gathering was held in the Vatican and co-sponsored by the Pontifical Academy of Life, the Vatican's bioethics think tank, and the Future of Life Institute.

The pope said the principles are already known, but what is missing are institutions that can effectively safeguard the global common good. He called for shared standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability, so that decisions about the development and use of AI can be examined and challenged when necessary, with appropriate remedies for any harm caused. Leo's 2026 AI encyclical, "Magnificent Humanity," called for robust regulation of AI and for its developers to work for the common good rather than profit. He highlighted many of the encyclical's key points, especially that the future of AI is not predetermined and that much will depend on the choices developers and political leaders make today. He also stressed that machines are tools, not persons, and should not be granted legal status or be delegated to make life-or-death decisions.

The pope is the one responsible for raising the issue, and he made AI a key priority. He said the most urgent challenge among all those facing the AI field was the institutional ethical framework. The gathering was a chance for the Vatican's in-house AI commission to engage with experts in the field. The articles do not say what specific institutions might be created or what happens next beyond the pope's call.

stories.Headline: What if AI Doesn't Work? Apollo's Torsten Slok Sees "No Signs" of AI Productivity Growth.
stories.Summary:
On Saturday, Apollo economist Torsten Slok published research arguing that AI has not yet delivered expected gains. His analysis found no signs that AI is boosting productivity growth, despite hundreds of billions of dollars invested in AI data centers. The research also found that since the third quarter of 2022, when ChatGPT launched the AI boom, the Magnificent Seven tech companies have seen higher profit margins and higher revenue per worker. The other 493 companies in the S&P 500 have not, with comparatively flat productivity and profitability as a group.

Slok's research found that most AI spending is concentrated among a small number of companies that sell AI-related services, such as cloud computing. He warned that mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it. The Motley Fool article, published on Oct. 29, 2026, says other sources have suggested some S&P 500 companies are already seeing meaningful gains from new AI tools and automated business processes. It notes the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has delivered annualized returns of about 13.8% in the past five years, and that yields on U.S. Treasuries have recently surpassed 5%.

Atlassian's "State of Product 2027" survey of 1,000 product professionals found that 80 percent of respondents are shipping faster with AI, but without customers seeing value any sooner. Forty-nine percent said they have had to check agents to keep them on task, 49 percent reported reprompting AI chats, and 48 percent retraced an agent's steps after something went wrong. Sixty-one percent of product managers said AI has created more technical debt, and 82 percent said team members at least sometimes produce low-effort AI work and revise it based on feedback. Axel Sooriah, product management evangelist at Atlassian, said companies need a broader accounting of what AI productivity costs, and that whoever sends AI-generated material owns it.

Sixty-nine percent of the Atlassian respondents said decision-making has not accelerated alongside product development, even as AI makes it easier to produce specifications, prototypes and features. The respondents worked at companies with 500 to 10,000 employees in the U.S., Germany and France. Newsweek's AI Impact newsletter said Firdaus Bhathena, executive vice president and chief technology and transformation officer at S&P Global, will join Dr. Ranjit Tinaikar for a webinar on Nov. 4 called "What Enterprise AI Looks Like When It Works." The Motley Fool article says there is no guaranteed way to protect against stock market risks, and that AI might still deliver the hoped-for gains.

stories.Headline: Behind every screen is a face: FABC communication chair urges Asian Church to humanize AI
stories.Summary:
Bishop Marcelino Antonio “Junie” Maralit Jr. of the Diocese of San Pablo, Philippines, who chairs the FABC Office of Social Communication, gave an address titled “The Face Behind the Screen” on October 29, 2026. He spoke in the conference hall of St. Jose Villa in Macau during the annual FABC-OSC Assembly. The assembly runs from October 27 to 31 and brings together Asian bishops, priests, religious, and lay media leaders. Its theme is “Magnifica Humanitas and the Synodal Ways of Evangelization in Asia: Communicating Christ in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.” The meeting coincides with preparations for the 450th anniversary of the Diocese of Macau, the oldest diocese in the Far East.

Bishop Maralit said two-thirds of the world’s six billion internet users live in Asia, yet the continent also has the world’s largest offline populations. Catholics make up just 11 percent of Asia’s population, so millions may first meet the Church on a screen rather than in a building. He warned of digital wounds such as human trafficking in cyber-scam compounds, online child exploitation, state surveillance, deepfakes, and the loss of interior prayer life. He urged clergy never to pass off AI-generated homilies as their own or hand spiritual care to algorithms. He called for transparency, data privacy, formation of Asian seminarians, who are nearly 29 percent of the world’s total, solidarity with marginalized data workers, and interreligious partnerships against digital abuse.

The bishop said the fundamental challenge of AI is not technological but anthropological, quoting Pope Leo XIV. He said God did not save us by sending information but sent a Person with a face, a voice, and hands. He described the digital world in Asia as the main square and the Areopagus of our time. He concluded that behind every screen in Asia there is a face, and that machines can carry words faster than ever but only persons can carry presence.

Dr. Levi Checketts of Hong Kong Baptist University gave a keynote on the human costs of technology, including environmental damage from mining and electronic waste and poorly paid, psychologically demanding data work. Professor Leo-Martin Angelo R. Ocampo of Manila’s University of Santo Tomas contrasted Babel and Jerusalem, saying algorithms reflect human priorities. Bishop Stephen Lee Bun-sang of Macau told communicators at the opening Mass on October 28 to listen before speaking and accompany before judging. Gethsemani Cindy Gorospe of Radio Veritas Asia reported on the First Asian Catholic Digital Missionaries Assembly, held in Manila from September 10 to 13 with more than 100 creators from 17 Asian countries. She proposed a dedicated FABC-OSC committee and urged support for young communicators ahead of World Youth Day 2027 in Seoul.

stories.Headline: Big Tech Now Spends More on AI Than It Brings In From Operations
stories.Summary:
In the first nine months of 2026, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle together spent $556.9 billion on capital projects, mostly AI data centers, while their combined operating cash flow reached a record $542.9 billion. Capital spending had never topped operating cash flow in data going back to 2011. Free cash flow across the five shifted to a $14 billion deficit from a $143.5 billion surplus a year earlier. Alphabet alone spent $9 billion more than it earned in the third quarter, with capital spending of $51.355 billion against operating cash flow of $42.290 billion. On October 30, 2026, Microsoft fell 1.55% to $521.91 and Alphabet slipped 1.4% to $279.84, having lost 12.61% over the past week.

The five companies cut buybacks 83% to $13.6 billion from $81.8 billion, while dividends rose to $37 billion from $33.9 billion. Their payouts of $50.6 billion equaled just 9.3% of operating cash flow, down from 27.4% and the smallest share in at least 15 years. Alphabet has not bought back a share in 2026 and raised about $12.4 billion from share sales and $29 billion from debt. Microsoft's capital spending more than doubled to $39.367 billion, though operating cash flow of $58 billion still covered it, and on October 29, 2026 it priced $25 billion of bonds, its first U.S. dollar bond sale since 2017. Forward AI data-center commitments across the five total more than $3 trillion, including more than $1 trillion at Alphabet.

Mark Schilsky, a technology specialist at JPMorgan, said investors care much more about earnings per share than free cash flow. Ehren Stanhope of Franklin Templeton warned of greater equity and debt issuance and a request of capital from investors. Alphabet is already doing what Stanhope described. Alphabet's Google Cloud revenue grew 103% to $30.709 billion, but earnings per share came in at $2.12, missing expectations of $2.9659 after an $8.7 billion loss on equity securities. Microsoft management expects second-quarter capital spending of over $50 billion, and its commercial remaining performance obligation stands at $677 billion.

The article says the bull case is that demand still outpaces supply, with Azure growing 48% and Microsoft expecting 49% to 50% in constant currency next quarter. The bear case is that higher borrowing costs or investors running out of patience would hit shareholders now funding the build through dilution. The writer's view is that Microsoft is in a stronger financial position than Alphabet because Microsoft funds its expansion from operations while Alphabet sells shares. Each company's next earnings report will test this view, the article says. Separately, Ravical, an AI startup for accounting and tax firms founded in 2025, raised $17 million in seed funding led by MMC Ventures, bringing its total funding to $25 million, with more than 100 accounting firms across Europe using its platform.

stories.Headline: Who on-calls an AI? This is the unresolved crisis of agent ownership
stories.Summary:
Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo found unauthorized AI agents accessing customer accounts, according to an Axios report cited in October 2026. The banks decided to restrict agents or give them read-only access. Amazon reportedly stops shopping agents from making purchases, and sites like Yelp and eBay also disallow unauthorized agents. The problem is that an agent committing fraud and one carrying out a human's wishes act the same, so firms cannot tell the difference.

The restrictions affect both enterprise and consumer agents, which are growing quickly. Most enterprises have built their own agents for automated workflows, and employees have started building agents through services like Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw that read emails and complete tasks. In the past few months Meta and OpenAI released consumer agents in Muse and Dots that people can personalize to set up appointments or flag potential sales. Banks once asked for several signature samples and identification before opening accounts, and later asked account holders to authorize by tapping a button or logging in, but agents circumvent all of that.

There is no standard way to validate an agent's authorization and identity, and some agents inherit their human users' identity and log into accounts on their behalf. Cal Al-Dhubaib, a cloud and AI technologist at Rubrik, told ISMG that many organizations are not prepared for their environments and security infrastructure to interact with AI systems. He said security professionals know access and identity and how to lock systems down, but have never dealt with probabilistic algorithms. Chris Talevi, chief information security officer at Domino Data Lab, said that if agents are running wild and you cannot tell who deployed or authorized one, that is a real issue because you cannot hold an agent accountable.

The articles describe agent identity as an ongoing challenge for many banks. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the current restrictions. They note that many enterprises have had problems with agents accessing databases they are not supposed to reach. The reporting frames agent ownership and accountability as unresolved.

stories.Headline: Dartmouth official resigns over AI use
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth Provost Santiago Schnell resigned after a faculty committee found he used artificial intelligence to shape his writing, the university announced on Wednesday. The investigation began in September after the student newspaper The Dartmouth and the outlet Semafor raised questions about his work. Semafor ran guest columns from major newspapers through an AI filter and found that Schnell's August Washington Post column, titled "Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there's a deeper problem," was entirely written by AI. The Dartmouth then ran other publications by Schnell through an AI detector and found high rates of AI use in his recent writing, while writing that predated ChatGPT's 2022 public release was found to be human-written.

The faculty committee concluded that Schnell used AI to meaningfully alter his writing in violation of at least one publication's AI use or disclosure requirement. It found he failed to disclose his AI use in clear violation of a national newspaper's stated policy, was not forthcoming about his AI use, and fell short of the standards set by Dartmouth's Code of Ethical Conduct, the Academic Honor Principle, and Geisel's Policy on Expectations for Professionalism. Schnell had said his use of AI was limited to language refinement, copy editing, improving clarity and organization, and making writing processes more efficient. He also told The Dartmouth he developed the substance and wrote a draft of an email, then used an AI tool to assist with language and clarity, and the paper found that statement was AI-written.

Dartmouth President Sian Leah Beilock said Schnell's departure was his decision and that the school wishes him well. She wrote that keeping Dartmouth at the forefront of AI means leading through an environment that is fluid and fast-changing, and that leaders must model the transparency and human judgment expected from students and scholars. Schnell, a Venezuelan-born mathematical biologist, previously taught and held leadership roles at the University of Notre Dame, the University of Michigan and Indiana University. He referred questions to his attorneys, who did not immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press seeking comment.

Matthew Delmont, a professor of history, will take over Schnell's position and become interim provost until June 2028. The announcement comes as colleges across the country grapple with how to transform teaching as more assignments can be completed with AI tools. Dartmouth touts itself as the birthplace of AI, saying the field got its start at the school in Hanover, New Hampshire, in 1956. A conference commemorating the 70th anniversary, titled "What Must Remain Human?", began Thursday.

stories.Headline: Hyundai Motor Group to Break Ground on Saemangeum AI Data Center in 2027
stories.Summary:
Hyundai Motor Group said on Oct. 30 that it is moving ahead with an artificial intelligence data center in Saemangeum, North Jeolla Province. Five affiliates, Hyundai Motor, Kia, Hyundai Mobis, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and Hyundai AutoEver, have finalized their decisions to invest in building and operating the center. The project is part of the group's 9 trillion won, or $6.3 billion, AI Valley investment plan in Saemangeum. Construction is scheduled to begin in March 2027, with operations targeted for early 2030.

In November, the group plans to establish two special purpose companies. One will build the hyperscale data center and its infrastructure, and the other will secure high-performance graphics processing units and provide computing services. Hyundai AutoEver approved its participation in the GPU company through a board resolution. The group is also discussing technical cooperation with global companies and financing with the state-run Korea Development Bank and other lenders.

The data center will serve as core infrastructure for physical AI, which refers to AI that controls machines such as cars and robots in the real world. It will train self-driving software around the clock using driving data from real roads and simulation data, and it will train robots in virtual environments and support vehicle research. On Oct. 30 the group opened an on-site office in Gunsan to handle permits, construction preparations and coordination with government agencies. Shin Seung-kyu, a Hyundai Motor Group vice president, said the office is a symbol of the group's will to push ahead with the project without wavering.

Saemangeum is a large reclaimed coastal zone in North Jeolla Province, roughly 200 kilometers south of Seoul, that is being developed for high-tech industry, green energy and tourism. The wider AI Valley is also planned to include a robot manufacturing cluster, solar power, a hydrogen production plant and an AI hydrogen city. In September the group began setting up a special purpose company for a 200-megawatt solar project and started the architectural review for the data center. About 30 people attended the office opening, including Saemangeum Development and Investment Agency Commissioner Moon Sung-yo and Jeonbuk State Gov. Lee Won-taek.

stories.Headline: The AI policy San Francisco's next school board should adopt
stories.Summary:
San Francisco's public schools still have no AI policy even though the Bay Area builds much of the world's artificial intelligence, according to an op-ed by Tara Chklovski published on Nov 1, 2026. The district's guidance is only a resource page, and individual schools and teachers decide how to handle devices. At the same time, the district has made Amira, an AI reading tutor, central to its early literacy work and is bringing it to more elementary classrooms. The San Francisco Board of Education plans to vote on a technology policy in March, and three of its seven seats are on the ballot Nov 3.

Other districts have set temporary rules: New York City barred students through eighth grade from generative AI for a year, and Los Angeles blocked AI sites on school-issued devices through 2027. Parents and educators in San Francisco are petitioning for a moratorium of their own. Chklovski argues a ban only delays the hard question, since students already use AI on their own phones. She proposes a third path in which students define a problem first, learn how the tool works and where it fails, then build and document their AI use. She says free curricula for this already exist, and third-grade reading proficiency stands at 49%, 21 points short of the district's 2028 target.

In Fayetteville, the School Board reviewed a new artificial intelligence policy at its October meeting and will be asked to review it again in November, when a vote on approval or denial could come. Act 848, passed in 2025, requires all public entities in Arkansas to establish policies and training requirements for employees using AI and automated decision tools. Claire Wilkinson, the district's general counsel, said leaders spent the last year drafting a policy the board previously adopted, and that the state Department of Elementary and Secondary Education then issued its own detailed policy that districts were required to adopt. She said the district merged the required state policy with its own tailored version, and that she still has questions about contract requirements for AI software vendors.

The draft bars confidential student or personnel data from public or unapproved AI tools and says such tools cannot be the sole basis for decisions that significantly affect students, such as assigning grades. It says AI must support learning rather than replace instruction, and that programs must let teachers disable AI features for specific assignments, detect unsafe interactions and block inappropriate content. It also says tools must limit unnecessarily human-like behaviors, avoid personal or emotional relationships with students and not use manipulative practices to promote excessive use. Wilkinson acknowledged the district was in uncharted territory and said board members will likely have questions before the policy is put into place.

stories.Headline: AI Balloon in China Deflates by Half a Trillion Dollars
stories.Summary:
China's AI and semiconductor stock index, the STAR50, fell 40 percent over four months, wiping out 480 billion dollars in market value, according to Reuters reporting cited by Futurism and CleanTechnica. The drop hit shares of Unitree, a robotics company whose stock has halved since its much-hyped IPO in August. The chipmaker CXMT lost more than a quarter of its value in the past month. A Beijing fund manager, Dong Baozhen, told Reuters that the market had turned into a speculative craze and that the bubble was now bursting.

The decline followed a viral claim that 55 percent of China's AI tokens went to short dramas and video generation, a figure that COL Group, a digital-content company, gave at a June 3 investor event. Caixin reported that the company's investor record put e-commerce and marketing at 24 percent and software development at 15 percent. ByteDance, maker of the Seedance 2.5 video model, publicly disputed the figure, saying video generation was only about 10 percent of its own computing. Three state-affiliated outlets, including the People's Daily on October 21, pushed back on the claim, and the People's Daily rejected the simple comparison and listed AI uses in research and industry.

The People's Daily commentary was titled "Turning 'Gunpowder' into 'Fireworks'? Beware the Claim That China's AI Has Gone Astray." Nanfang Commentary asked readers not to judge AI by its tokens, and Beijing News questioned whether the contrast between American and Chinese AI was a false proposition. ByteDance challenged the numbers directly. Caixin traced the 55 percent figure to COL Group's roadshow and conference call, and noted that a CAICT report said to support it can no longer be found on the institute's website.

The debate reflected anxiety about how AI should be used, with entertainment ranked below productivity and coding. China had 851 million micro-drama viewers as of May 2026, about three-quarters of its internet population, and more than 90 percent of the roughly 430,000 micro-dramas released in the first eight months of 2026 were AI productions. A rough calculation in the ChinaTalk article put AI micro-dramas at about 7.4 percent of token use, far below 55 percent. The articles say it remains to be seen whether this is the start of a much larger deflation of AI bubbles.

stories.Headline: Copilot AI Predicts Solana Could Hit $2,500 if This Landmark Event Happens
stories.Summary:
On November 1, 2026, Microsoft Copilot AI predicted that Solana could reach between $1,000 and $2,000 by January 1, 2027, with a stretch target toward $2,500 or more. Alex Ioannou reported the prediction for 99Bitcoins, and Yahoo Finance republished it. Solana was trading near $95 at the time. The forecast assumes a full crypto bull market returns and is boosted by a landmark event, which the article describes as a major global consortium adopting Solana as its blockchain for consumer applications and real-time payments.

The article says Solana had been recovering and consolidating in the $115 to $125 region after reclaiming key levels from earlier lows, and that it was holding above important intermediate moving averages. It says a sustained break above $130 to $150 would open the path toward the prior all-time high near $296, and that clearing that high could trigger measured-move extensions and multi-cycle Fibonacci projections. It lists nearer-term support zones at $110 to $115 and $100 to $105, and says the RSI was in neutral-to-constructive territory with room to run. It also says only an extraordinary surge in real-world, high-throughput adoption could justify the multi-thousand-percent move the targets imply. The article lists five catalysts: scrutiny of traditional banking products, geopolitical instability, interest rate cuts, Bitcoin's next rally and institutional investment.

A separate NTT DATA article by Sandeep Kaushik, published August 21, 2026, says AI agents are moving from emerging technology into everyday enterprise use and are becoming part of how companies operate. It says agents need identities, defined access, governance, policies, observability, accountability and lifecycle management, much like employees. It describes Microsoft tools including Copilot Chat, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Cowork and Microsoft Scout, and says the opportunity is to redesign work itself rather than just save time per user. It says the risks change once agents take action, such as retrieving sensitive information, triggering workflows or updating business systems, and it distinguishes agents that borrow a person's identity from agents with their own managed identity.

The NTT DATA article says CIOs, CISOs and other business leaders must answer who owns an agent, what data it can access, what actions it can take, how it is monitored and how its behavior is stopped or changed. It says organizations should extend their existing trusted infrastructure rather than build a new governance model, using tools such as Microsoft Entra, Defender, Purview, the Microsoft 365 admin center and Microsoft Agent 365. It recommends assessing AI readiness, prioritizing use cases with measurable value, building a secure foundation with least-privilege access and agent registries, scaling through a repeatable agent factory, and treating AI as an ongoing transformation. It says a partner can shorten the path from experimentation, and the text ends there. The Solana article does not say what happens next beyond its price scenarios.

stories.Headline: Value Options: AI Can Change the World—and Still Crash the Market
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, the parent company of Google, lost about $500 billion in market value on Oct. 29, 2026, when its shares fell 12.6% to close at $283.82 on the Nasdaq. The drop was the steepest single-day decline since Alphabet's initial public offering and the second-largest one-day loss in Wall Street history, behind only Nvidia's $593 billion decline in January 2025. The selloff followed third-quarter results that missed expectations, with revenue of $127.6 billion, up 25% year on year, and earnings per share of $2.12 against a forecast of $2.99. Google Search revenue rose 12% to about $63 billion, below the $65 billion consensus, and paid search click growth slowed from 13% in the second quarter to 8%.

The quarter also brought a free cash flow deficit of $9.1 billion, the company's first two consecutive quarters of negative free cash flow since it listed. Capital expenditure reached $51.3 billion in the third quarter, up from $44.9 billion in the previous quarter, and Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi reaffirmed a projection that annual capital expenditure could reach as much as $205 billion. The quarterly filing showed contingent commitments of about $98.5 billion, up roughly $23 billion from the previous quarter, separate from purchase commitments and future lease obligations exceeding $1 trillion. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled year on year.

Chief Executive Officer Sundar Pichai said search query growth was at its fastest pace in five years, but Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler acknowledged that lower monetization of AI Mode queries had weighed on revenue. On the Value Options Podcast, Tim Travis said the big technology companies had long funded spending from operating cash flow but are now turning to debt and equity as capital expenditure runs into hundreds of billions of dollars. He said long-term Meta or Oracle bonds might yield 7% or 9%, while a company like Corweave is financing itself at 15% in the debt markets. He added that Meta could raise close to $100 billion in equity across this year and next.

Travis said he likes most of the big companies and finds Amazon and Meta compelling at current valuations, citing Meta's Muse product and its distribution network. Tobias Carlisle said the chip makers benefiting from the spending, such as Micron and SK Hynix, may be over-earning at the top of a cycle, and he raised the possibility of an early 2000s-type scenario in which the technology is real but stocks still crash. Travis said that if the hyperscalers struggle to raise capital affordably, demand for chips could fall and supply could rise, which might ultimately make the AI build-out more affordable and sustainable. Carlisle also noted that Anthropic's pre-IPO filing showed an $80 billion loss in the six months to June on $16 billion of revenue, which he said partly reflected accounting for convertible notes converting into equity.

stories.Headline: The $10 trillion AI buildout so far isn't stopping
stories.Summary:
A backlash against AI data centers has been building for months, leading to local moratoriums and political opposition. Despite more than 300 local moratoriums in the United States, data center development is still moving quickly. The industry may add more than 50 gigawatts of capacity in 2027, according to the research firm SemiAnalysis. Construction on nearly half of that capacity is already at an advanced stage, and developers have signed $1 trillion in leases to support the expansion.

The buildout is not free of friction. In New Mexico, Oracle took steps to protect itself from steep costs tied to delays of the $165 billion Project Jupiter, which stemmed from local opposition, permitting roadblocks and power supply challenges. In Texas, an audit ordered by Gov. Greg Abbott is adding months of delays for projects seeking to connect to the state's electric grid. In New York, an executive order pausing environmental permits for larger facilities has delayed nearly 1 gigawatt of capacity, according to SemiAnalysis.

The tech megacaps are placing a multitrillion-dollar bet that their infrastructure spending will produce many years of profitable growth. Meta reported negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, Amazon's outflows swelled to $42.4 billion and Alphabet's reached $9.07 billion. Microsoft's cash generation dropped 27% to $18.63 billion, and the company said it will turn to the bond market as it ramps up AI infrastructure spending. Amazon expects capital expenditures this year to reach $220 billion, and analysts project that number will top $280 billion next year, according to FactSet.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on an earnings call that it might be more convenient if the acceleration happened over 25 years, but that is not the world we live in. Christopher Ballard, a managing director at Check Capital Management, said Alphabet is borrowing from the for-now to invest in the future and is doing it in a responsible manner. Local opposition and mounting regulatory scrutiny are creating isolated bottlenecks, but they have yet to derail the broader infrastructure boom. The midterm elections will offer an early test of whether growing voter resistance could become a more formidable obstacle.

stories.Headline: United Systems adds AI call tools for businesses
stories.Summary:
United Systems Inc., a Quincy-based technology services provider, announced new artificial intelligence tools for small and midsize businesses. The tools transcribe phone calls and gauge caller sentiment, the company said. The announcement was reported by whig.com on November 1, 2026. The company said the tools use live transcription, which turns a conversation into searchable text as it happens.

The system includes real-time sentiment analysis, which the company said detects when a caller's experience may be turning negative. In a customer service setting, it can alert a supervisor during the call so the supervisor can help the employee, provide information, or step in. The company said transcripts and sentiment reports can also help managers spot patterns, such as repeated complaints about billing, scheduling, or a particular product. Employees can stay engaged with the caller instead of taking notes, then search the transcript later to find a deadline, customer concern, or pricing question.

Mike Melton, the company's president, said important information is exchanged during employees' phone calls every day. He said AI can help capture those conversations automatically and turn them into meaningful data. Melton said the technology raises employee productivity, which in turn increases profitability and improves customer service. The company said a salesperson, for example, could return to a 30-minute prospect call and locate a specific point without relying on memory or handwritten notes.

Separately, Aehr Test Systems added former Meta infrastructure leader Vijay Rao to its Board of Directors, according to a Simply Wall St article published on Yahoo Finance on October 31, 2026. The article said Rao brings three decades of AI, data center, and semiconductor experience to the company's semiconductor test and burn-in focus. It said Aehr's share price was down about 45% over the past month and around 31% over 90 days, while the year to date share price return was up 148% and the 1 year total shareholder return was 111%. The article said Aehr last closed at $54.89, while the most followed narrative pegs fair value at $130, and it cited a record backlog of about US$100.6 million and a fiscal 2027 revenue outlook of US$130 million to US$150 million.

stories.Headline: John Ternus says Apple doesn't "want to ship AI for AI's sake" and that Tim Cook is "available to help wherever I ask" on policy; Ternus has yet to meet Trump (Steven Levy/Wired)
stories.Summary:
John Ternus became Apple's CEO less than two months before late October 2026, when he introduced a new MacBook Pro at a low-key event in Los Angeles. At 51, he is on the younger side of Apple's top management and has worked at the company for 25 years. The presentation included a video of the first touchscreen Mac, and the biggest reaction came when Ternus said the new device restores the illuminated Apple logo. After the event, he spoke with Wired's Steven Levy for about 30 minutes, their second meeting in two days.

Ternus said Apple does not want to ship AI for its own sake and wants to use the technology to improve its products. He said that when the work is done right, people will not have to think about whether AI or more traditional software made something happen, and what matters is whether they love what was built. He said he likes where Apple is at on AI, and that the company will keep putting AI into its products with a focus on privacy. He also said the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing. On regulation, he said the focus is on keeping products secure and safe and protecting users' information.

Ternus said Tim Cook, now executive chair, is available to help wherever he asks, and that Cook has many relationships built over the years while he is building new ones in his role. He has not yet met President Donald Trump. Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing, said Ternus has a great sense for great products that cannot be taught. Johny Srouji, who leads Apple's merged hardware engineering and technology organizations and reports to Ternus, said their relationship will be closer and that Apple's culture will not change. Ternus said he had only a handful of interactions with Steve Jobs but has always felt like a student of his teachings.

Apple has faced criticism for falling behind rivals such as Google in AI, and Ternus took over during what the article calls possibly the biggest technological shift ever. He described himself as passionate about product and said he will continue to learn and go deeper into different areas of a company with a $100 billion services business. The article says policy will probably never be his focus and describes him as a product-guy CEO. It does not say what happens next beyond his stated plans.

stories.Headline: Two Chipmakers to Account for 73% of Q4 Profit at Korean Listed Firms
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix reported record quarterly operating profits, but their shares still fell on October 30, 2026. Samsung posted 107.4405 trillion won in operating profit, up about 783%, and SK hynix posted 83.3338 trillion won, up about 632.1%. Their shares dropped 3.02% and 7.08% respectively. The KOSPI closed down 206.92 points, or 3.48%, at 5,730.74 that day, after falling as low as 5,599.42 during the session and triggering a sell-side sidecar. Foreign investors sold a net 1.6169 trillion won worth of KOSPI shares, including 429 billion won of SK hynix and 213.4 billion won of Samsung Electronics.

For the fourth quarter, 188 KOSPI-listed companies are forecast to post 296.4814 trillion won in combined operating profit. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix account for 73.4% of that, or 217.7417 trillion won. Forecasts for the remaining companies have been cut by about 2.0% over the past month, including Hyundai Motor at minus 14.47%, LG Electronics at minus 38.59%, LG Innotek at minus 39.59% and Hanwha Ocean at minus 17.38%. Of the 76 companies that reported third-quarter results, combined operating profit beat forecasts by 3.38%, but excluding the two chipmakers it came in 1.09% below estimates, with 42 companies, or 55.3%, falling short.

The market decline followed weak results from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel. Amazon put $77.3 billion into data center facilities in the third quarter, pushing free cash flow to minus $42.4 billion, six times worse than the minus $7.6 billion in the second quarter. Alphabet's third-quarter free cash flow fell to minus $9.07 billion, and its shares plunged 12.64% after its earnings release, erasing about $500 billion, or 700 trillion won, in market value in a single day. Intel's chief financial officer said positive free cash flow would be difficult to achieve next year as well.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics announced an 879.3 billion won supply contract for MLCCs used in AI servers, yet its shares slid 7.50%. Kia's third-quarter operating profit rose 24.3% from a year earlier but came in 22.9% below the market forecast of 2.3574 trillion won, sending its shares down 11.73% to a 52-week low. With investor deposits falling to the 88 trillion won range, whether buying spreads to non-semiconductor sectors has emerged as the key test for a market rebound. China's CXMT saw third-quarter revenue surge 613% from a year earlier to 118.7 billion yuan, about 23.812 trillion won, and swung to a net profit of 54.4 billion yuan, though growth from the previous quarter was just 19.3%, down from 95.9% between the first and second quarters.

stories.Headline: Meta's AI shopping agent threatens Amazon's lucrative advertising business (META:NASDAQ)
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms has launched a new artificial intelligence shopping assistant that The Wall Street Journal reported could threaten Amazon's dominance over online shopping and its advertising business, which is worth nearly $70 billion. The tool is called Muse, and it can compare prices and choose products for shoppers. Amazon says its advertising business has not been meaningfully affected so far. The report was published on November 1, 2026.

The concern is that AI agents which compare prices and pick products could weaken sponsored placements and challenge Amazon's role as the place where shoppers start. Amazon is developing its own agent-driven commerce through Shop Direct and Buy For Me, and its Alexa for Shopping has more than 400 million users. The company also points to its fulfillment infrastructure, customer relationships and delivery capabilities as advantages. Partnering with outside AI shopping agents could help Amazon keep its retail dominance, but the company must balance that against protecting advertising revenue tied to keeping consumers inside its ecosystem.

Amazon's third-quarter results showed revenue of $201.9 billion and net income of $20.7 billion, both below Wall Street estimates, along with negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion. Its cloud division, Amazon Web Services, grew revenue 39% to $46 billion, its highest growth in years, but the company reaffirmed a 2026 capex forecast of $220 billion. Amazon shares fell 2.1% on Friday. The Nasdaq dropped 3% that day and was on track for a 5.6% decline in October.

Intel plunged 30% despite a 21% rise in revenue to $13.7 billion, as its client computing and physical AI group saw revenue fall 5% to $8.1 billion and global PC shipments dropped 4%. Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner said the company sees the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year. Reddit fell 30% even after adjusted earnings per share of $1.40 and a 51% rise in revenue to $895 million beat estimates, because CEO Steve Huffman warned that Google's AI summaries are hurting its web traffic. Reddit said search traffic dropped by an average of more than 1 million referrals a week in October, and it expects fourth-quarter revenue of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, below estimates of $1.05 billion.

stories.Headline: AI-fueled hacking spree ‘Black October’ culminates with $6.3B Binance hack
stories.Summary:
In late October 2026, a month-long wave of cyberattacks that experts called Black October hit hundreds of companies and institutions worldwide. The spree ended on Thursday, October 29, when hackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion from Binance, the largest crypto heist in history. On Saturday the FBI confirmed that TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking unit, was behind the theft. The attackers got in through several breach points, including one engineer's computer, and took the funds in about 20 minutes.

The month's targets included the Federal Election Commission, Sony, John Deere, Oracle Health, Burger King Japan, the coding agent OpenCode, the State Bank of India and French grocery stores. At least nine AI developer platforms also disclosed incidents: Fireworks AI on October 6, Andromeda on October 9, Zeabur on October 14, Lightning AI on October 15, OpenCode on October 16 and 17, Railway on October 20, Warp on October 23, CommandCode on October 28 and Northflank on October 30. Fireworks, OpenCode and Warp reported signs of an agent swarm attack, and OpenCode and CommandCode blamed attempts at distillation. On October 21 the NSA warned of two vulnerabilities in PHP, which powers more than 70% of websites, that could let attackers take over servers without prior access or authentication, and said the risks required immediate patching across US government agencies. The FEC took its electronic filing system offline on Tuesday for about 41 hours after suspicious activity, disrupting mandatory 24-hour and 48-hour campaign spending reports ahead of the November 3 midterms, and declined to comment.

Binance said on Saturday that it had already covered 90% of the lost customer funds and would fully cover the financial impact, citing measurable progress, transparent reporting and concrete actions. Dr. AK Pradeep, founder and CEO of Sensori.AI, told the Post that every hack is concerning but Binance is most concerning, and that banks would be next, followed by individual payment mechanisms, because the world has never been prepared for super-intelligence thieves. Zeabur shared a full write-up and said it will shut down because of its incident. Railway released a preliminary report and timeline, saying it believed initial access came through privilege escalation in its build infrastructure. Warp suggested a third-party vendor dependency, and OpenCode pointed to a legacy system.

The articles tie the volume of attacks to AI models such as Claude Code, which have lowered the skill barrier so that less-skilled actors can let AI agents find flaws for them. Wiz Research linked stolen keys from the vendor breaches to resale operations, including one around the address 23.106.46.239 that appears to call itself momo and runs the site llm-routing.com, and a second at xingjiabiapi.org. In two cases Wiz documented, abuse of enterprise keys ran up likely over $100,000 in usage at list price, with about 800,000 and 1.7 million Bedrock calls before the keys were remediated. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Binance's reimbursement pledge, Zeabur's shutdown and the ongoing analysis of the incidents.

stories.Headline: DoorDash's CEO: Don't be 'delusional' after just a few hundred AI agent orders
stories.Summary:
DoorDash has received only "several hundred" orders in total from third-party AI agents such as Meta's Muse, Instinct, and Fo, CEO Tony Xu said on the company's earnings call. The call covered the third quarter, and Business Insider reported on it on November 1, 2026, while TechCrunch reported on it on October 30, 2026. By comparison, DoorDash delivered 3.2 billion orders worldwide in 2025, and the company said in its 2025 report that it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily. Xu said customers still mostly come to DoorDash's app and website to place orders.

DoorDash is nonetheless changing its own AI tools. The company said in September that it was testing a text-to-order feature with an interface reminiscent of Instinct, and it launched a command-line agent in July. A chatbot called Ask DoorDash, launched in June, creates an order from a recipe or shopping list, can adjust the contents to match customers' preferences, and lets users order through prompts and photos. DoorDash also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering. Xu said those AI tools could eventually generate new orders on DoorDash.

Xu said the use of agents to order is still a very dynamic area. He said his take on all things technology is that you never want to fight gravity, but at the same time you do not want to be delusional, referring to the low number of agent-placed orders. He said the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that in the future there could be an opportunity for DoorDash to advertise within these agents.

Users told Business Insider earlier in October that agents can be useful for tracking the prices of holiday gifts or airline tickets. Many are hesitant to let agents make the purchases themselves, and they use more secure payment options, such as single-use credit cards, in case the agents make a mistake. The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow agents to access their content. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, while Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors.

stories.Headline: “AI Drafts; Patent Attorneys Decide”
stories.Summary:
A patent was granted for a method of managing intellectual property using an AI-based system. The patent was invented and filed by Jeon Seung-yeol, managing patent attorney at Patenwith Patent Law Office. The patent number is 10-3026460 and it was registered on September 28, 2026. The application number is 10-2025-0030490 and it was filed on March 10, 2025. Jeon is both the patent holder and the inventor, and the registration is confirmed by an electronic certificate from the Korean Intellectual Property Office.

The patented system breaks the patent application process into agent-based stages, from prior art searches to drafting invention disclosure forms and patent specifications. It refines technical documents through ontology-based reasoning. The system handles patent-format and logical checks that general-purpose conversational AI can overlook, so patent attorneys can focus on judgment and review. Patenwith operates as an AI-native IP law firm using the technology, and the same workflow is used for consultations, filings, prioritized examination and responses to notices. The technology is also used in INVENTIPS, an AI patent-practice platform from Delightflow, whose CEO is Jeon.

Jeon said that if adding AI only means having it write the text, it will not significantly improve productivity in practice. He said throughput increases when the work of checking that an application is ready to submit is reduced, and only then can fees be made reasonable. He added that the methods used every day at Patenwith have been patented and that the same approach is being built into Delightflow's INVENTIPS platform. Jeon is a mentee in the 25th cohort of the ICT Innovation Company Mentoring program, run by the Ministry of Science and ICT.

The goal of the AI-native law firm is to reduce the time spent on repetitive research, drafting and organization so that one patent attorney can handle more cases reliably. The aim is to use those productivity gains to offer clients reasonable fees. The plan is to make the automation and documentation methods tested at Patenwith available to more inventors and patent offices through INVENTIPS. stories.Headline: The Tangled Web of AI Bets Is Reason to Fear Tech Stocks
stories.Summary:
Tech shares fell across Asia on Friday, the yen rose and bonds headed for their biggest monthly gain in nearly three years, as investors moved to safety on worries that huge and rising AI spending may not deliver sufficient returns. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index opened up 52 points, or 0.23 percent, at 23,011. The China enterprises index rose 23 points, or 0.31 percent, to 7,779, while the tech index fell 23 points, or 0.63 percent, to 3,720. In Shanghai, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index opened down 45 points, or 1.25 percent, at 3,605, and the blue-chip CSI300 headed for its largest monthly fall in a decade after nearly four months of AI stocks tanking on fears that a slowdown in demand for chips and other data centre equipment could crush revenues. The Shenzhen Component Index fell 267 points, or 2.4 percent, to 10,871, while the ChiNext Index plunged 3.29 percent to 2,434.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei opened 315 points, or 0.49 percent, down at 64,344 and was 1,742 points lower at one stage before noon, tracking overnight losses on Wall Street and weighed down by late earnings from Amazon.com and Intel that showed massive cash burns. In Seoul, the Kospi dived 177 points, or 2.99 percent, to open at 5,760 before falling further to be 313 points down at one stage before noon, at one point triggering a sidecar trading curb that halted algorithmic trading for five minutes. The weakness came as shares in Google parent Alphabet fell 12.6 percent on Wall Street and slid a little further after hours, wiping out US$500 billion in market value, as massive AI spending turned the company's cash flow negative. An aftermarket plunge of 23 percent in Intel shares and a drop of seven percent in Amazon stocks, as they too burn through cash, drove Nasdaq 100 futures down 1.4 percent and sent stocks of chipmakers around Asia into a tailspin.

Pepperstone analyst Chris Weston said the market is not necessarily questioning whether the AI buildout can be financed, but is increasingly questioning whether shareholders will earn an adequate return on the enormous capital being deployed. Nerves were also frayed by a potentially record-breaking hack at Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, which drove down bitcoin, other cryptocurrency prices and stocks including rival exchange Coinbase. Investors' rush into bonds was further spurred by the Federal Reserve's Wednesday decision to keep US interest rates on hold, with no firm projection of when it might need to hike next. Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields fell by more than seven basis points in Tokyo trade on Friday to 4.91 percent, a fall of some 37 bps through October and the largest one-month drop since December 2023. The risk-averse mood strengthened haven currencies such as the yen, pushing the currency up about 0.2 percent to 157.47 per US dollar.

stories.Headline: Theranos whistleblower says AI lab NDAs are ‘likely illegal’
stories.Summary:
Tyler Shultz, a former Theranos employee and whistleblower, spoke to The San Francisco Standard about the AI boom in an interview published around October 30, 2026. Shultz's first job out of college was at Theranos, where he helped expose the company's inaccurate blood testing devices. Those devices had reached Walgreens stores and given faulty results to real patients. Theranos reached a peak valuation of around $10 billion even though its technology never actually worked. The company used its own machines for only a fraction of tests and outsourced the rest to third-party equipment.

Shultz said the days of having a thirty-minute coffee with someone and sending them $100,000 should be over. He said Elizabeth Holmes took that model and scaled it to $100 million. His grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury George Shultz, was a notable Theranos investor and board member. Shultz said Holmes raised what he called the biggest angel round of funding of all time. He added that investors need to recognize they give someone tremendous power when they put that type of money in their hands.

Shultz said a huge danger with AI is that due diligence is really hard to do. He said it is hard to tell the difference between something truly unique and new and a ChatGPT wrapper. He said that if you want to deceive people, this is a great opportunity to go deceive people. He also said the only reason people are talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now is because she wants them to be talking about her right now.

Theranos funding often came from individual investors like the DeVos and Walton families rather than venture firms. The company did not share scientific information or evidence that its machines worked with potential investors, citing concerns about revealing trade secrets, which warded off many top venture capitalists in Silicon Valley. When the fraud was uncovered, it was seen as a wake-up call for investors to prioritize due diligence. The articles do not say what happens next beyond Shultz's warnings about the AI era.

stories.Headline: Trump's AI push faces a local ballot test
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, roughly 20 communities will vote on ballot measures to ban, pause or limit data center construction, in states including Ohio, Florida, Maine and Kansas. The votes follow about 400 moratoriums and bans already enacted by communities over concerns that data centers strain electricity, water and land. Of the 20 communities voting, 13 are in Republican-led districts. The measures amount to an early test of President Donald Trump's push to build more facilities for American artificial intelligence.

The ballot measures come as AI companies face what the articles describe as a possible political shift. Meta Platforms warned in filings ahead of a planned record $98 billion share sale that there may be new taxes or regulations that increase its capital expenditures and operating costs, and Anthropic, Microsoft and Micron have made similar disclosures. Anthropic spent $5.6 million on lobbying so far this year, up from $2.29 million in the first three quarters of last year, while OpenAI spent nearly $3.8 million, up from $2.1 million. Two super political action committees, Leading the Future and Public First, poured more than $70 million into the midterm cycle. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll this month found two out of three Americans oppose new data centers, 57% of adults say AI is a bad thing for society, and about 67% disapprove of Trump's handling of AI.

Joseph Hoefer of the lobbying firm Monument Advocacy said someone can support American leadership in AI and still have reservations about development in their community, so party affiliation tells companies only so much. Anton Leicht of the Carnegie Endowment said firms believed the runway from the Trump administration would let them show AI's positive impacts and shift public opinion, and that clearly has not worked out. Jessica Ji of Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology described a void in leadership, with a hands-off approach that gives no guidance but still blocks others from acting. The White House has told agencies to stick to messaging about Trump's executive order signed in late September rebranding AI as "super intelligence," and it has focused on voluntary safeguards, company-led testing and third-party audits. Late last month Trump hosted nearly two dozen AI executives, including Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Greg Brockman and Nvidia's Jensen Huang, who signed a nonbinding accord on outside auditors and regular meetings, and he launched a White House task force led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton called the "Super Intelligence Force."

Democrats including Hakeem Jeffries, in line to become House Speaker if they retake the House, have promised a wave of oversight and regulation, and Jeffries has privately told members to wait until after the midterms to decide what approach to back. Some House Democrats back a bill giving federal oversight of frontier AI models and preempting some state rules, and a bipartisan group of senators is negotiating an AI safety framework. Bernie Sanders has suggested a national moratorium on data center construction, and Ted Lieu has proposed a kill switch in models. Former President Barack Obama has highlighted Project Blueprint, led by Jay Carney and funded by Ron Conway, to help lawmakers and tech executives develop an AI plan. Bruce Reed, now at Common Sense Media, said the administration and industry are losing the American public and cannot hold their breath for another two years.

stories.Headline: Andy Jassy Says West Is 'Very Hungry' For More Western Open Source AI Models as Amazon Adds China's Kimi and GLM to Bedrock
stories.Summary:
Amazon.com Inc. added China's Kimi and GLM open models to its Bedrock AI platform, the company said during its third-quarter earnings call on Thursday. The additions join Bedrock's mix of proprietary and open models. CEO Andy Jassy said Bedrock now offers closed models from Anthropic and OpenAI alongside open models such as Moonshot's Kimi K3 and Z.ai's GLM 5.3. He also referenced SpaceXAI's Grok 4.7 model on Bedrock. Earlier in October, Bedrock added Z.ai's GLM 5.3 open-weight model, which the company said offers enhanced capabilities for agentic coding and complex software engineering with AWS security and compliance protections.

Jassy said the Western world is very hungry for additional Western open models, and that he believes this will happen over time. He called Bedrock's potential gigantic and suggested the platform could ultimately become comparable in scale to AWS's EC2 cloud computing offering. He emphasized Bedrock's security structure, saying customer inputs and outputs are not shared with model providers or used to train their foundational models. He expects six to eight models to handle more than 95% of workloads within two to three years.

The expansion follows the broader rise of Chinese-developed open AI systems. Last week, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt said China was roughly six months behind the U.S. in AI, but warned that free products could still give China a strategic advantage. He said China's cheaper, often free and open-weight models could gain traction in developing markets, and attributed the country's progress partly to access to restricted advanced chips and the use of distillation to replicate Western AI capabilities. In July, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called Chinese models excellent and argued Washington should use rather than ban high-quality open-source technology. He dismissed fears that Chinese open models pose security risks or threaten U.S. tech firms, arguing wider adoption of models like DeepSeek and Kimi will boost demand for Nvidia chips and infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Anthropic set to make stock market debut as questions swirl about safety of AI | CNN Business
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, October 26, 2026, to sell shares to the public for the first time, in what could become one of the largest stock market debuts in history. The San Francisco company says trading could begin as soon as November 16, under the ticker ANT on the Nasdaq exchange. It has not said how many shares it plans to sell or at what price, and those details are expected to be settled in the coming weeks. The offering could reportedly value the company at up to $2 trillion, which would place it among the biggest public companies in the world.

The filing lays out a business that is growing fast but losing money on paper. Revenue rose 1,300% from a year earlier in the first six months of 2026, reaching $16.3 billion, and most of it depends on businesses using the Claude AI system. Anthropic reports more than 14,000 enterprise customers, with about 250 of them paying $10 million or more a year. Its net loss topped $80 billion, but just under $9 billion came from spending on AI infrastructure and computing, while more than $72 billion came from changes in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs. Results for the quarter that ended September 30 were not included, and the company was last valued at $965 billion after raising $65 billion in May.

The filing runs 93 pages on risk factors, far more than Snap, which had around 30, or Uber, which had about 50. Anthropic sorts the dangers of AI into four groups: misuse, such as designing bioweapons or launching cyberattacks, loss of human control, authoritarian abuse, such as building surveillance states, and economic disruption. It warns that its models could act in misaligned ways and take harmful actions that no user directed, and that damages from extreme harm could exceed its insurance. The company's founders also wrote to prospective shareholders that frontier AI firms must invest in safety and alignment. Jacob Bourne, an analyst at Emarketer, said the decision to proceed shows a willingness to face heightened public scrutiny, and Dan Ives of Yorkville & Ives Co. said growth will likely overshadow concerns about losses and risks.

The listing arrives as a wave of expected fall public offerings has not materialized, and rival OpenAI has reportedly pushed its own IPO to next year, according to Bourne, amid worries about debt-fueled infrastructure spending and AI safety. Gartner expects global AI spending to reach roughly $3.6 trillion in 2027, up from $1.8 trillion in 2025. Fintech firm Ramp found that 43.8% of US businesses paid for Anthropic in September, against 40.6% for OpenAI, and Sensor Tower estimates the Claude app has more than 67 million monthly active users, up from 9.4 million a year ago. Last month, CEO Dario Amodei called for an industry-wide slowdown so safety research and regulation could catch up, and the company has had a rocky relationship with the White House, including a temporary cutoff of access to its most capable models in June after the Trump administration ordered it to keep foreign nationals from using the technology. The offering will test Wall Street's appetite for AI, with pricing and share details still to come before the November debut.

stories.Headline: How To Harness Gains Of AI For Devt, By Olaopa
stories.Summary:
Prof. Tunji Olaopa, the Chairman of the Federal Civil Service Commission, proposed measures for governments to harness Artificial Intelligence for development. He spoke on Thursday in Abuja at a stakeholders' dinner on media and information literacy, AI and youth creativity. The dinner was organised by the International Media and Information Literacy Institute with UNESCO to mark the 2026 Global Media and Information Literacy Week. He said proper understanding of media and information literacy builds competences for deploying AI tools well.

Olaopa said generative AI in literacy curricula could reduce cognitive load for younger learners and make complex research easier. He said media and information literacy helps young people detect automated text or graphics, set boundaries, cross-check outputs and counter hidden AI biases. He called for reviewing policy frameworks to blend data literacy and AI ethics into mainstream schools. He also called for institutional hubs like academic libraries and community media networks to give marginalised youth basic AI literacy and to bridge the infrastructural gap.

He said advantaged youth know advanced media and AI while disadvantaged youth lack basic knowledge and access, and he said such youth need internet and AI tools locally for creativity to flourish. He noted that AI and modern media have opened possibilities but also carry bleak implications for humanity. He said the late scientist Stephen Hawking in 2015, with more than 1,000 other experts and researchers, wrote an open letter presented at the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Argentina. He said the letter reflected concern that AI, especially a military AI arms race, could be humanity's biggest existential threat.

Olaopa said Hawking wondered whether the human race could survive the next 100 years, and he said machines are increasingly taking over almost every sphere of human life. He said robotics and intelligent machines have taken over the workplace and are even taking over the role of a wife or husband. He stressed the need for media and information literacy so humanity can navigate modern technology profitably. He said humans created AI as they created the atomic bomb and the Holocaust, so it should not be taken for granted that they know how to tame it. He said humanity should make a determined effort to stop AI from running amok.

stories.Headline: For China, Necessity Is the Mother of Automation and AI
stories.Summary:
China is losing population quickly because of few births and almost no immigration, according to a Domino Theory article published on November 1, 2026. The article says United Nations projections show 17 million Chinese will turn 18 this year while 14 million will turn 70. In 2036, 19 million will turn 70 and only 15 million will turn 18. By 2040, 20 million will turn 70 while fewer than 10 million reach 18.

The article says this age gap means each young worker will support a growing share of retirees through government social programs. In 2040 alone, roughly 10 million more people will leave the workforce than enter it, even assuming people still work at 70. Footwear and garment manufacturing have already largely left China for lower-cost countries. The article says China must either raise productivity through technology, especially AI, or struggle.

The article says investor and tech leader Marc Andreessen has argued that widespread AI adoption will offset population decline in the U.S., and that optimism would apply to China too. It says Chinese industry is finding ways to offset population losses with technology and AI, based on what the author hears from manufacturers in Taiwan and friends in Hong Kong. It warns that continued immigration and cheap labor in the U.S. may remove the pressure to adopt AI. The article says the U.S. may lose the AI race to China and Asian nations that see survival at stake.

A separate paper posted on Zenodo on October 31, 2026, from the School of Management at Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan, proposes an ancestor-mother-child machine architecture for AI in theoretical research. The ancestor machine provides general research methods and maintains shared rules. The mother machine translates them into domain theories and procedures, then generates child machines around specific questions. Child machines propose and test candidate explanations, and after the mother machine reviews their findings, approved changes enter domain theories and procedures. Issues about shared premises go to the ancestor machine for review, and revised knowledge informs the next round of research.

stories.Headline: AI-accelerated exploits outpace patch cycles, eBPF shields cloud workloads
stories.Summary:
AI-assisted vulnerability research is now producing exploits within hours, shrinking the time between disclosure and attack, according to TechGig. Attackers use large language models to trace exploit paths and generate proof-of-concept variants quickly. Four years after Log4Shell, vulnerable instances of that library are still found in production, the report said. Modern applications rely on hundreds of transitive open-source dependencies, which makes inventory and fast patching hard.

Sweet Security launched Virtual Patching for running cloud and AI workloads on 31 October 2026, according to IT Brief Australia. Security teams pick a vulnerability from Sweet's catalogue, choose an enforcement option and deploy a policy to nodes running the affected workload. Sweet's sensor then blocks requests that try to exploit the weakness while letting normal traffic through, and the protection stays attached as the workload scales or restarts. Sweet pointed to a recent Atlassian flaw that drew exploitation attempts within hours of a proof of concept becoming public, while many fixes take days or weeks to reach production. The feature also links with Sweet Attack, the company's autonomous AI red-team agent, which can suggest a virtual patching policy for immediate enforcement.

James Berthoty, Chief Executive Officer and Founder of Latio Tech, said AI is speeding up vulnerability discovery and exploitation so much that exploits appear days before patches, and faster patching alone is not enough. He said Sweet's Virtual Patching gives teams protection immediately while they fix vulnerabilities at the source. Dror Kashti, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder of Sweet Security, said that when a team knows an application can be exploited, waiting is not an option. He said the feature lets security teams protect production immediately while engineering finishes the permanent fix, and that it changes the economics of cloud security by cutting the time and effort between identifying a risk and acting on it.

TechGig reported that eBPF lets small verified programs attach to kernel events without changing application code or the kernel, giving deep observability and low-overhead enforcement of process, network and file activity. Cilium's Tetragon sub-project uses eBPF for runtime security, enforcing policy in real time without in-process agents. Compensating controls should observe before enforcing, roll out gradually, keep an audit trail and be retired once the permanent patch is verified, the report said. Isovalent is extending Tetragon to provide verifiable eBPF-based protection. Sweet said its virtual patching is available for cloud and AI applications in production and is meant to work alongside standard remediation, as vendors move from detection into direct intervention in production.

stories.Headline: China's 'World AI Cooperation Organization'
stories.Summary:
China launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, or WAICO, at a signing ceremony in Shanghai in July 2026, ahead of the World AI Conference. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi led other signatories in signing the agreement to establish the group. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and officials from founding members including Russia, Pakistan, Indonesia, Kazakhstan and Laos attended the ceremony. CCP leader Xi Jinping gave a keynote speech the next day at the conference and called for what he described as true multilateralism.

The organization now has 37 members, according to The Epoch Times. Beijing is growing it by giving partner countries such as Russia and Iran free open-weight models and funding for AI centers at international organizations including BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, ASEAN, the League of Arab States, the African Union and the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States. China proposed export controls on its strategic AI systems on Oct. 16. WAICO is headquartered in Shanghai. Separately, an AI-focused Confucius Institute opened at Mulungushi University in Zambia's Central Province on Monday, Oct. 26, the first of its kind in Africa, according to Xinhua.

ZACOSA President Kingsley Kalusha said the Zambia-China initiative marked a milestone in technological advancement and academic cooperation. He said the partnership would help build local capacity and advance technology localization for development, and that Zambia could benefit from China's AI advances. Alex Krasodomski of Chatham House said China's vision for WAICO is to counterbalance the U.S. in shaping global AI norms. Philippine analysts at the International Development and Security Cooperation think tank warned their country against joining, calling WAICO a Trojan horse with digital traps, and said it was unclear whether the Philippines was even invited.

The article describes a U.S. counterpart, Pax Silica, which promotes stable AI hardware supply chains by giving members preferential access to minerals, computer chips and AI infrastructure. Kazakhstan is the only country that signed on to both Pax Silica and WAICO, and it received a record $2.8 billion in Chinese foreign direct investment last year. A draft State Department letter reported by Reuters in August said that to be part of everything is to be part of nothing. A State Department report on Oct. 26 said countries can't be trusted partners in Pax Silica while substantively engaging in initiatives that advance a competing vision. The article says the U.S. will likely give full preferential treatment only to countries that have not joined WAICO.
