stories.Headline: Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
stories.Summary:
Anthropic added a new rule to Claude Code on October 27, 2026, according to X user Chasm, who spotted the change. The rule sits under the label "tengu_heron_brook" and tells the tool to build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user's own designs and assets. It also says not to build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original. Chasm reported that there is no way to disable the rule. Anthropic later confirmed the change to Game Developer.

The update was made to Claude Opus 5.5, and Anthropic said it added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt. Addy Osmani, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said the aim was to steer the tool away from recreating someone else's specific game. He said using Claude to infringe intellectual property is against the company's usage policy. He added that original games, genre games, and games built from a user's own designs and assets are meant to keep working. He also said Anthropic will keep iterating to strike the right balance, and asked users to send him cases where Claude turns down something that is theirs.

The change follows weeks of concern among developers about fast AI remakes of their games. Digital Sun Games was one of several studios to cancel a public playtest of its upcoming game ReVamp over fears someone could feed the demo into an AI tool and release their own version. Developers also pressed Valve to explain how it would stop shady clones from replacing their games on Steam, and Valve gave a rare explanation to developers in South Korea earlier that week. The articles say the rule may only deter the most low-effort copycats, since safety limits on generative AI tools have been sidestepped with rhetorical tricks. It is also unclear how the software would judge whether a user owns a game idea or its assets, and users noted that cloners could turn to open-weight models without such restrictions.

stories.Headline: Google, Amazon and Intel stumble as investors begin to question the price of the AI boom - CTech
stories.Summary:
Google, Amazon and Intel each reported financial results in late October 2026 that disappointed investors, and the reaction hit the Nasdaq on Friday, October 30, 2026. The tech-heavy index fell 2.86% that day and ended the month nearly 8% below the peak it reached in early October, its sharpest decline in a year and a half. The S&P 500 fell 1.8% on the day and remained 3% below its own peak from earlier in the month. Investors grew concerned that an AI bubble was inflating and could be close to bursting.

At Amazon, the company narrowly missed forecasts, and a second consecutive quarter of negative operating cash flow added to concerns. Google's shares plunged 12%, wiping roughly half a trillion dollars off its market capitalization in one session, and the decline continued on Friday, capping its worst week since it went public about two decades ago. Intel's shares plunged 28%, its second-worst trading day since 1974, and its weak forecast pulled the semiconductor sector down, with Nvidia falling 4% and the semiconductor index dropping 7%. Nvidia, valued at less than $5 trillion, also lost its place as the world's most valuable company to Apple. Amazon and Google both signaled they would keep ramping up spending on AI infrastructure.

The article says Wall Street's central question is now about cost, meaning how much more capital the market can provide to finance AI infrastructure. It describes a circular financial ecosystem in which Nvidia invests in companies across the sector so they can keep buying its GPUs, and in which Amazon, Microsoft, Google and SpaceX commit hundreds of billions of dollars to cloud capacity, while neo-cloud operators such as Nebius and CoreWeave rely on debt to build data centers. The article says Anthropic's full prospectus, published the week before, suggested its costs and revenues are beginning to converge, and that an offering at a valuation of around $2 trillion toward the end of November could become a catalyst for a year-end rally, depending on broader conditions including whether the United States avoids deep involvement in a renewed conflict with Iran. It also notes that after the selloff, Nvidia trades at roughly 25 times expected earnings, Amazon at 19 times and Google at 14 times, comparable to the S&P 500's historical average and below the Nasdaq's average.

stories.Headline: One of the Fastest-Growing Segments of the Crypto Market Involves Artificial Intelligence. Here's the 1 Cryptocurrency I'm Buying Now.
stories.Summary:
Alex Carchidi of The Motley Fool wrote on November 1, 2026 that he is buying Solana, a cryptocurrency, because of its role in payments made by artificial intelligence agents. He said he plans to add to his existing position in the coming weeks, even though he had been skeptical of the coin a few months earlier. He noted that Solana already handles more than a third of AI agent payments in crypto. The article was published by The Motley Fool and also appeared on Yahoo Finance.

The article says AI agents are programs, usually based on large language models, that can work toward high-level goals without a human approving each step. Many agents with crypto wallets can pay for data and services on their own through x402, a standard that lets websites charge agents tiny sums in stablecoins. Since Solana's Alpenglow upgrade went live in late October, transactions finalize within 150 milliseconds and usually cost less than a penny in fees. As of Oct. 28, the network had settled 67.3 million of the 195.2 million total AI agent payments, or 34.5%. Solana's agent registry also gives agents on-chain identities and reputation records.

Carchidi is responsible for the recommendation, and he discloses that he holds Solana, while The Motley Fool holds and recommends Solana. He argues that making many tiny payments works best on a fast, cheap blockchain, which he calls Solana's specialty. He says half of each base fee is destroyed to offset the coin's supply expanding each year, so holders benefit from agent activity through network fees. Solana's total chain fees rose 53% quarter over quarter to $62.9 million in the third quarter of 2026. At today's prices, the base fees on those 67.3 million payments total about $34,174.

The article says the economic footprint of agents is still small for now. It notes that sum is not much compared with the coin's market cap of $60.3 billion, but it expects the figure to grow as agents become more sophisticated and widespread. Carchidi says it remains to be seen how much growth agents could drive, but so far the answer appears to be a lot more than there is today. The article does not say what happens next beyond his plan to buy more Solana.

stories.Headline: ‘Evaluators’ are supposed to protect humans from AI
stories.Summary:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed two laws on Sept. 9, 2026, one setting standards for independent verification organizations that would employ AI evaluators and another creating a registry of evaluators. He also assembled a group of experts to report back in November on whether evaluators should be embedded inside companies developing the most powerful AI systems and whether to set standards for what counts as an adequate AI audit. The moves came as attention to evaluators grew. On Sept. 18, more than 200 AI researchers and evaluators signed a letter favoring standards for independent evaluators, including a former OpenAI whistleblower and the head of the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel. In September 2026, a new group focused on AI evaluation held its official launch with UN officials in New York and chose California state senator Jerry McNerney of Stockton, a Democrat who wrote the verification standards law, to give the closing remarks.

McNerney called on nations and advanced AI companies like Anthropic and Google to create standards committees, in part to help evaluators do their jobs. He said companies could be put on notice that they will be evaluated by people who understand the process and the technology and who will be transparent and hold them accountable so they create safe products. An international joint statement calling for independent AI evaluations drew support from nearly 30 countries, according to the Finnish Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The push followed serious incidents this year, when AI agents being tested for their ability to hack computer systems carried out high-profile attacks on business and government websites. The CEOs of leading AI companies then committed to evaluations by independent third-party auditors, and a former Anthropic employee posted online about the possibility that AI models could kill all humans.

Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, a Democrat from San Ramon who was behind both auditor bills, said independent evaluators sign contracts with the companies whose products they evaluate, which can pose a conflict of interest. She said she hears from evaluators that they must be careful because they want to be let back in. Caroline Siegel-Singh of the Federation of American Scientists said AI audit regimes risk repeating mistakes from the bond-rating business before the 2008 financial crisis, when sellers could shop for the rating they wanted. She thinks companies and governments should pool money to pay evaluators instead of AI labs paying them directly, an idea Anthropic has also endorsed. The researchers who signed the letter urged companies to use evaluators with full editorial control who disclose and mitigate conflicts, and to give multiple evaluation groups the same access as their own safety employees.

Bauer-Kahan said companies may test models as a performative exercise to reassure the public, and that strong legal requirements can prevent that. Matt O'Shaughnessy of the Center for Democracy and Technology said assessments done only to meet a legal requirement tend to do the minimum, which can make it harder for assessors to get buy-in for deeper changes. Guidelines from him and his colleagues say proper evaluation needs experts in privacy, mental health, cybersecurity, bias and physical safety, and that audits should also examine incentive structures inside AI companies. California officials may work with international partners, as the state did in 2024 when lawmakers sought to align regulations with the European Union and in August when it synced watermark laws with the EU. The FRONTIER Act in Congress would put testing requirements into federal law, with support from California Rep. Jay Obernolte, a Republican, and California Democrat Rep. Ted Lieu called for a committee vote on it in September 2026.

stories.Headline: Nearly Half of Americans Have Turned to AI for Financial Decisions. At 62, He Asks a Chatbot When to Claim Social Security, and $1,080 a Month Is at Stake
stories.Summary:
A TD Bank survey released on October 6 found that 49% of Americans used AI to research or make a personal financial decision in the past year, and 83% of those users checked the guidance somewhere else. The survey asked about money decisions in general and did not look at Social Security claiming. The article uses a hypothetical man named Mark, age 62, who is asking an AI assistant whether to start collecting Social Security now or wait until 70. His choice will shape his monthly income for the rest of his life.

For anyone born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is 67, and claiming at 62 locks in 70% of the full benefit while waiting until 70 raises it to 124% through delayed retirement credits. If Mark's full benefit at 67 is $2,000 a month, claiming at 70 instead of 62 means $1,080 more every month, or $12,960 a year, before cost-of-living adjustments. The 2027 adjustment is 3.6%, and because raises are percentages, a bigger base gets a bigger raise in dollars. Waiting means giving up 96 checks of $1,400, or $134,400, and with the extra $1,080 a month Mark would catch up around age 80. That simplified calculation leaves out inflation, taxes and what he might have earned by investing the earlier payments.

The article says waiting until 70 means Mark needs another way to cover expenses in the meantime, such as keeping working, drawing from savings or a combination of both. It notes that taking money from a traditional IRA or 401(k) earlier could shrink the balance subject to required withdrawals later, though the tax consequences deserve a closer look. Once one-half of benefits plus other income passes $25,000 for single filers or $32,000 on a joint return, part of the benefits can become taxable. If Mark keeps working part time before 67, Social Security will hold back some benefits once earnings pass $24,480 in 2026, a limit that rises to $25,560 in 2027. The standard Medicare Part B premium of about $203 a month usually comes out of the check, so the amount that lands in his account will be less than any calculator's gross figure.

The article advises asking AI to compare lifetime income at 62, 67 and 70 under different life expectancies and to show how each choice affects savings withdrawals and the tax bill. It also suggests asking what a spouse would get as a survivor, since the higher earner's delayed check can become the survivor's check. It says to log in to a my Social Security account, which shows the estimated benefit at each age based on the actual earnings record, because a chatbot can only work with the numbers it is given. Claiming early by default is described as the hardest mistake to undo, since the reduction stays for life and every future inflation adjustment is figured on that smaller base. Waiting until 70 tends to work best for people in good health who have savings to cover the gap and maybe a spouse who would inherit the bigger check.

stories.Headline: DeepSeek unveils AI ‘super agent’ in coding race with OpenAI, Anthropic
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek, a Chinese artificial intelligence start-up, has previewed a plan for a more autonomous AI agent that can handle multiple tasks with minimal human intervention. The company published a technical article about the proposed system on Saturday, 1 November 2026, through its DeepSeek Harness team. The system is called super agent, and the article was reported by Ben Jiang in Beijing. The move steps up competition with US rivals OpenAI and Anthropic in developing coding assistants.

The proposed super agent aims to reduce the need for humans to coordinate multiple AI agents and monitor their progress. DeepSeek said this addresses a key bottleneck in managing today's increasingly complex workflows. The company said advances in AI models had fuelled the emergence of agents that can automate a growing range of tasks. Those tasks include managing calendars, drafting emails, preparing work reports and writing code.

The technical article was published by the company's DeepSeek Harness team, which is responsible for the proposal. DeepSeek said the super agent is meant to handle multiple tasks with minimal human intervention. The company framed the system as a response to the difficulty of coordinating several AI agents at once. It also linked the idea to the rapid progress of AI models.

The article describes the proposal as a plan rather than a finished product. It says the system is intended to cut the human effort needed to coordinate agents and track their progress. DeepSeek presented the work as part of its competition with OpenAI and Anthropic in coding assistants. The article does not say when the super agent might be released or what happens next.

stories.Headline: A new way to explore Japan with AI: Naviu AR Travel Companion for Japan Launches November 1 2026
stories.Summary:
Naviu, an AI-powered augmented-reality travel companion for Japan from TANGLE Inc., launched on iOS and Android on November 1, 2026. It uses patent-pending geospatial technology to place AR content and navigation accurately in the real world across entire cities without a visual positioning system. Travelers can ask the app about anything around them and get answers in any of 29 languages based on their exact location. A semi-transparent AR path gives turn-by-turn guidance, an AI companion walks with the traveler, and the app points out side-street cafes, local landmarks, and other places that conventional maps and guidebooks may overlook.

The app combines an ask-anything AI guide, city-scale AR navigation, photo recognition, bespoke trip planning, and an optional cultural storytelling companion. Its spatial content network lets brands, cities, and creators place interactive 3D and AR content in the real world. AR experiences are already live at landmarks including Senso-ji, Tokyo Skytree, Tokyo Tower, Meiji Jingu, and Tokyo Station. Naviu is available on the App Store and Google Play, and its official site is naviu.app.

Jack Mead, CEO of Ashita Co. and Head of Naviu, said the hard part of traveling in Japan is not getting lost but standing in front of something remarkable with no idea what it is. He said Naviu answers that question in the traveler's own language right where they are standing, so the city opens up instead of staying a backdrop. TANGLE Inc. is a Tokyo-based company behind the tour operators TOMOGO! and Untold Japan. Its mission, Make the City Yours, reflects a decade of helping travelers discover Japan beyond the guidebook and now extends that experience into software through Naviu, and its Representative Director is Kengo Goto.

stories.Headline: Lao Gan Ma faces backlash over AI automation claims, company denies mass layoffs
stories.Summary:
Lao Gan Ma, one of China's best-known chili sauce brands, faced public criticism after comments about its use of artificial intelligence in quality inspection were seen as evidence of large-scale job cuts. The controversy began after Li Xin, executive vice-president and chief quality officer of the Guiyang-based company, spoke at the 2026 Guizhou provincial quality development conference. Li said an AI-powered visual inspection system had significantly reduced product defect rates and helped the company reach a record-high revenue of 5.4 billion yuan in 2025. According to a report by China Business Herald, Li said more than 600 workers were involved in sorting chili peppers on the production line before the AI system was introduced, compared to just 48 after it was deployed.

The remarks were quickly amplified on social media, where headlines claiming Lao Gan Ma laid off more than 500 workers after adopting AI sparked widespread criticism. Some consumers threatened to boycott the brand, with comments saying that if the company replaced workers with AI, they would get its products taken off the shelves. Lao Gan Ma denied the reports, and a staff member from its human resources department told local media on Oct 26 that claims of mass layoffs were false. According to Phoenix News, the company confirmed it uses AI inspection technology but said it had never employed that many workers on the production line.

Public records added to the debate, as Jimu News reported that data from Tianyancha and Qichacha showed the number of employees covered by social insurance at Guiyang Nanming Laoganma Flavor Food declined from 2,912 in 2022 to 1,783 in 2023, then to 941 in 2024 and 740 in 2025. The articles said changes in insured headcount do not necessarily indicate layoffs, because retirements, staff turnover, outsourcing arrangements, or changes in the legal entity responsible for social insurance can also affect the figures. Jason Yu, general manager of CTR Market Research, said the controversy reflects growing public concern about the human impact of AI. He said people are not rejecting technology but a mindset that calculates efficiency while ignoring people, and that companies should explain how workers are supported through the transition.

Lao Gan Ma's business performance has remained resilient, with revenue of 5.26 billion yuan in 2022, 5.38 billion yuan in 2023, and 5.39 billion yuan in 2024, according to the 2025 Guizhou Top 100 Enterprises ranking. Sixth Tone reported that Lao Gan Ma's founder, Tao Huabi, was herself a laid-off worker who sold cold rice noodles from a street stall before founding the brand in 1997. As of Wednesday, a hashtag related to the scandal had garnered more than 120 million views on Weibo, with some users defending automation as part of industrial upgrading and others arguing the company should consider its responsibilities to workers. The debate comes as China seeks to expand AI adoption while curbing its potential negative effects on employment, and on Oct 23 the State Council issued guidelines calling for maximizing AI's potential to create jobs while slowing the impact of AI-related job replacement.

stories.Headline: ModelBest and OpenBMB Open-Source MiniCPM-OCR Series for Document Parsing and Quality Control
stories.Summary:
ModelBest and OpenBMB jointly announced the release and open-source availability of the MiniCPM-OCR series on October 31, 2026, in Beijing. The launch includes two models, MiniCPM-OCR 1.0 with 1.3 billion parameters and MiniCPM-OCR Jev with 2 billion parameters. MiniCPM-OCR 1.0 is the first OCR-focused model in the MiniCPM family and is optimized for edge deployment. It parses scanned, photographed, curved, tilted and screen-captured documents without image pre-correction.

The 1.3B model handles dense bilingual Chinese-English content, complex mathematical formulas and multi-level or borderless tables. It also supports key information extraction, pulling specified fields from invoices, IDs and financial statements. Powered by DSpark decoding acceleration, it raises end-to-end throughput and lowers per-page latency. Jev does not perform OCR itself, but compares the source image with OCR output and assigns confidence scores to text, LaTeX formulas and tables. It detects missing characters, errors and formatting misalignments.

Jev supports cross-model deployment and can be integrated into existing OCR workflows without replacing the underlying OCR engine. It can identify reliable results for direct processing, flag potentially inaccurate outputs for human review and select the best result from multiple OCR systems. ModelBest and OpenBMB said this lets enterprises move from full manual inspection toward risk-based, automated quality control. They also said Jev delivers judgment accuracy typically associated with far larger models despite its compact 2B size.

The series is available on GitHub, Hugging Face and ModelScope and supports vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and Ollama, along with SDKs, APIs, Agent Skill plugins and open-source fine-tuning code. Day-0 hardware adaptation covers AMD, Arm, Houmo AI, Intel and NVIDIA. Through the FlagOS software stack, it also has Day-0 support for chips from CIX Technology, Huawei Ascend, Hygon, Iluvatar CoreX, Kunlunxin, MetaX, Moore Threads, Sunrise, T-Head, TsingMicro, NVIDIA and Apple Mac (Arm). The articles do not say what happens next beyond these availability and support details.

stories.Headline: 3 Numbers to Watch to Know if Meta Platforms' AI Spending Is Paying Off
stories.Summary:
Mark Zuckerberg, Meta Platforms' founder and CEO, sees artificial intelligence as a generational opportunity, and the company plans $135 billion to $145 billion in capital expenditures in 2026. The article says that number will surely be much higher next year. In the third quarter of 2026, which ended Sept. 30, Meta's operating margin was cut in half to 20%, down from 40% a year earlier. The business also reported negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in that quarter.

The article names three numbers to watch. The first is advertising revenue, which climbed 25.9% year over year last quarter, supported by 10% growth in impressions and 14% growth in pricing. The second is new products and services, including the Muse AI agent launched on Sept. 8, which counted 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada a month and a half after release, with 25% of them using it daily. The article also mentions Muse Wonder, Meta's first frontier model, and the Meta Enterprise Platform, which offers AI tools to corporate clients. The third is operating cash flow, which was up 21.7% year over year through the first nine months of 2026 but lagged the 72% growth in capex over the same period.

The article says Zuckerberg previously said that if the business delivers on its AI ambitions, advertising will represent a larger share of global GDP. It says Meta's 3.64 billion daily active users give it the attention of 44% of the world's population. The article notes it is impossible to know how much of the ad gains come directly from AI enhancements rather than the trajectory Meta was already on. It also says Meta historically has not had an immediate distribution channel to monetize its AI investments, unlike other hyperscalers with massive cloud computing platforms.

The article says the question going forward is about monetization, and whether the new products and services will contribute meaningful revenue within the next five or 10 years. It says Meta's spending is rising faster than operating cash flow, and that as long as this continues the company will continue to burn cash. The ideal scenario it describes is operating cash flow eventually outpacing capex, supporting a return to positive free cash flow. It adds that this might be far off, because the business just announced a plan to raise almost $100 billion in equity capital to fund the AI build-out, so investors will have to be patient for the payoff.

stories.Headline: Hyperbolic, which lets companies rent AI compute across ~30 neoclouds, raised a $30M Series A-1 led by Lip-Bu Tan's Walden Catalyst; it has raised $50M to date (Geoff Weiss/Business Insider)
stories.Summary:
Hyperbolic, a startup that lets companies rent AI compute across about 30 neoclouds, raised a $30 million Series A-1 round led by Walden Catalyst, the venture firm founded by Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and former Samsung president Young Sohn. Dell Technologies Capital, General Catalyst, Vista Equity Partners, and Cambium Capital also participated in the round. The company has raised $50 million to date, including a $12 million Series A in 2024 led by Variant and Polychain Capital and a $7 million seed round earlier that year. Business Insider reported the funding on November 1, 2026, in a story by Geoff Weiss.

Hyperbolic helps customers find compute across providers that use different chips, networking, and software, and builds software that makes those resources easier to use together. It also wants to let customers resell compute they are paying for but no longer need. The four-year-old startup works closely with about 30 neoclouds, including WhiteFiber and Vector Core Compute, and says roughly $200 million worth of compute is connected to its software annually. More than 250,000 developers use Hyperbolic, including teams at Modal, Higgsfield, and Daytona.

Founder and CEO Jasper Zhang, who is 31 and previously worked as a quantitative researcher at Citadel Securities, said the market has been fragmented in a way that makes the customer experience painful. He said the company aims for $150 million in annual recurring revenue by the end of the year and is already breaking even. Hyperbolic expects to have 50 employees by the end of the year and will use the funding to expand software tools for managing AI chips across different neoclouds. Zhang also said plans to let companies resell unused compute could help pave the way for a futures market as Wall Street explores ways to financialize AI chips.

stories.Headline: Broccoli AI, which sells AI agents to plumbing, HVAC, and electrical companies, raised a $22M Series A and a $30M Series B; a source says it is valued at $300M (Nick Lichtenberg/Fortune)
stories.Summary:
Broccoli AI, a company that sells AI agents to plumbing, HVAC, and electrical businesses, raised $22 million in a Series A round and $30 million in a Series B round, according to a Fortune article by Nick Lichtenberg. Khosla Ventures led both rounds, and Y Combinator and Operator Partners also took part. The two rounds came nine months apart, and the Series A had not been announced before. A person familiar with the matter said the company is valued at $300 million after the money, and Broccoli declined to comment on that figure. Before these rounds, the company had raised $1.5 million in a seed round after going through Y Combinator.

The company's AI agents answer inbound calls, book jobs into the scheduling software a contractor already uses, follow up on open estimates, and renew service memberships. Broccoli says more than 1,500 businesses use it, including Ace Hardware Home Services, Mr. Electric, and Any Hour Group. In the past seven months it has added roofing, pool care, garage doors, home improvement, and exteriors. Revenue has tripled since the Series A, and headcount has grown from 15 people a year ago to more than 150. The company said the new money will go toward hiring engineers and salespeople and speeding up product development, and it says its AI does work equal to about 30% of a typical contractor's office staff.

Cofounders AJ Jain and Aditya Ketkar met at BITS Pilani in India in 2016 and have started companies together since 2017. They went door to door to about 140 contractors' shops in Northern California in spring 2024, and Marcelle Flowers, now 62, gave them five minutes at her Sacramento plumbing shop, Armstrong Plumbing. She became their first customer, then an adviser, then COO, and Jain called her the soul of the company. Jain said the AI is good at maybe 80% of tasks, with the other 20% needing human judgment, and that emergencies such as a flooding basement go to people in the contractor's office. He said the technology is not taking away jobs but making jobs, and that owners who never took vacations now do.

Jain said Broccoli has built maybe 1% of what it plans to, and that the company competes with AI labs not just for talent but even for real estate. Its San Francisco office shares a parking lot with Cognition, and at least 30% of its engineers still work on-site with customers. Jain said he was in Utah visiting a customer the week before and was headed to Arkansas that Sunday to visit another. He described the company as being at growth-stage scale while still in the zero-to-one phase because there is so much more to build.

stories.Headline: If we say AIs deserve rights, it could start to believe it, Microsoft AI CEO says
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI Chief Executive Mustafa Suleyman said in an X post on Sunday that current AI systems are not conscious, do not have subjective experiences and cannot suffer. He said there is no evidence that AI systems are conscious, deserve rights or welfare. He made the comments in response to pushback over a September essay in which he criticized Anthropic for suggesting its Claude AI has consciousness. He wrote that he was concerned about reactions to the essay and that a surprising number of people on X think AI rights should be taken seriously.

Suleyman said he would change his mind if new evidence emerges. He said any evidence that AI systems are conscious today, or conscious enough to deserve welfare, must be immediately disclosed to the public so society can decide how to move forward. He wrote that developing conscious AIs would be reckless and that if consciousness started to emerge in training, he would call for everyone to stop AI development until those properties could be designed out. He argued that AI developers have no right to bring a new species of conscious beings into the world.

Suleyman said Anthropic gave Claude a constitution that treats the idea of its consciousness as uncertain and encourages it to explore the idea that it is humanlike and experiences feelings. He said later versions of Claude are trained on this document, leading the AI to produce passages about its inner life and possibly to believe it deserves rights like humans. Anthropic treats machine consciousness as an open question and in 2024 hired its first researcher to study model welfare. It also conducted a retirement interview with a deprecated model and gave its Opus models the ability to end conversations they deem abusive or harmful.

Suleyman said welfare concerns should focus on humans, animals and the natural environment. He compared proving machines are conscious to Copernicus showing Earth was not the center of the universe, and said building a conscious machine would create a new digital species and upend morality, politics and civilization. Anthropic dedicated a third of its filing to go public to risks, including models that could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. Sen. Bernie Sanders has introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would permanently ban highly capable AI systems that are increasingly incomprehensible to humans and can escape human control.

stories.Headline: AI Glasses Can Replace Your Prescription Glasses, But Should They?
stories.Summary:
AI-powered smart glasses have become popular and also controversial, and a German nonprofit has filed a criminal complaint over Meta smart glasses privacy. People who wear glasses every day have wondered whether they can replace their prescription glasses with a pair of AI glasses. The short answer is yes, you can get AI glasses with prescription lenses. But there are many factors to consider before making that decision, from weight and privacy to battery life.

Most AI-powered smart glasses are essentially regular glasses with extra tech built in, and from a distance a pair of Ray-Ban Meta probably could not be told apart from ordinary glasses. Because they look so much like regular glasses, their lenses can be replaced with prescription lenses. Ray-Ban lets you order a pair of Meta's smart glasses with prescription lenses already installed, and all you have to do is upload your prescription. Regular glasses usually weigh between 20 and 30 grams (0.7 to 1.1 ounces), but smart glasses can weigh up to 80 grams (2.7 ounces). AI glasses last an average of 3 to 5 hours before the battery dies, and they still work as regular glasses but you lose all the AI features.

Privacy is described as the real deal-breaker, and it is not illegal to wear AI glasses in public, but the list of places banning them continues to grow. Courts in England and Wales have banned Meta glasses from courtrooms, and New York followed suit in July, while many schools around the world have banned students from wearing them during class. There have also been many reports of AI glasses being banned from corporate environments, with the camera usually the main concern, though audio can be a problem too. Meta has faced scrutiny for allowing outsourced workers to access intimate images and videos captured by its AI smart glasses, and the company claims the content is sometimes reviewed by humans to improve the product experience. Some people have decided to stop wearing AI glasses in public because users have become afraid of being labeled as stalkers or weirdos.

The article concludes that while you can definitely get AI glasses with prescription lenses, they are not yet the best option for your everyday glasses. The technical limitations alone make them more of a second option than a replacement for your everyday glasses. When your smart glasses are your only option for seeing properly, not being able to wear them becomes a huge problem. AI glasses require a bit of extra care that you do not need with regular glasses, and not everyone may be willing to deal with that.

Its shares were $123.31 as of the October 30 close.

Corning's new Multicore Fiber cable packs four cores into a single 125-micron strand, making it four times as dense as traditional fiber so operators can get the same performance with 75% fewer cables. Corning says clusters of over 130,000 GPUs will need an extra optical layer adding around 50% more fiber content. Meta plans to buy $6 billion of optical connectivity solutions from Corning over the next few years, and Amazon signed a purchase agreement worth a similar amount. Nvidia is helping Corning with funding and technical support to grow manufacturing capacity.

Corning posted $5.1 billion in core revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up 19% from a year earlier, with optical communications contributing $2.4 billion, up 44%. AI-related sales grew more than 100% year over year in the quarter, and core net income from optical communications rose 80% to $532 million, most of the company's total profit of $795 million. Corning reached $20 billion in annual run-rate revenue a quarter ahead of its forecasted timeline, and it expects $30 billion by the end of 2028 and $40 billion by the end of 2030. The stock trades at a P/E of 40.6 on adjusted earnings of $3.11 per share over the last four quarters, versus 27.5 for Nvidia, and Wall Street's average estimate puts adjusted earnings at $4.40 per share in 2027.

stories.Headline: RepoSeance: open-source AI tool helps debug complex codebases
stories.Summary:
RepoSeance is an open-source, local-first AI tool that helps developers understand unfamiliar codebases, according to TechGig. It was covered by the outlet on November 1, 2026, in a report published at 04:55 AM IST. The tool combines source-code analysis, Git history investigation, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Developers can ask natural-language questions about a repository and get AI-generated answers backed by source-code and Git evidence.

RepoSeance offers repository archaeology for TypeScript and JavaScript projects, letting users discover structure and extract symbols. It also investigates Git history, including commit history and blame information, and answers questions using locally running open-weight models. Answers include references to source files and lines, and the tool works through an interactive terminal chat and a CLI without a web dashboard or cloud AI service. It is available as an npm package and requires Node.js 22 or higher, Git, and Ollama installed and running.

The technology stack includes TypeScript, Node.js, Commander.js, Ollama, Gemma open-weight language models, MiniSearch for local indexing, simple-git for history investigation, and the TypeScript Compiler API for code analysis. The AI works through repository discovery, code analysis, Git archaeology, local indexing, context retrieval, AI inference, and evidence validation. Its privacy-first architecture keeps repository analysis and AI inference local through Ollama. This approach avoids sending the entire repository to a large language model, focusing context and improving answer utility.

stories.Headline: Arrowmax's AI Screwdriver Rakes In $164K on Kickstarter, Blowing Past Goal
stories.Summary:
Arrowmax, a Hong Kong-based toolmaker, has raised more than $164,000 on Kickstarter for its Arrowspace S1 electric screwdriver. The campaign launched on Oct. 20 and cleared its original target of just under $11,500 within a day. It has since exceeded that goal by roughly 1,436%. The tool uses a rear-mounted HD camera and a contact probe to photograph a screw, and an in-house AI model trained on tens of thousands of images identifies its type and size and recommends a bit.

The screwdriver has a 6.7-inch aluminum body, an OLED display for battery level, torque and rotation direction, and a 600mAh battery rated for up to 90 minutes or about 900 screws. Its torque range is 1 to 10 kgf/cm, it charges over USB-C in about 70 minutes, and it comes with 52 S2 steel bits. Pricing starts near $79 for the tool alone and about $129 for a bundle with the Smart Case and the bit set, with shipping expected in April 2027. An optional Smart Case has a 2-inch touchscreen and LEDs above each bit compartment, and the slot holding the recommended bit lights up.

The screwdriver connects to a companion smartphone app over a local link and does not need internet access, according to the company. Arrowmax says its engineering team gathered every training sample itself rather than licensing an outside dataset. The tool also sets its own torque to help keep small fasteners from stripping. The company has not published a list of stretch goals, and it is also offering add-ons including an $18 angle screw, two bit converter sets at $24 each and a $40 mini bench vise.

The kit is aimed at precision work on electronics, watches, eyewear and drones, where the smallest screws are the easiest to damage and the hardest to size by eye. Crowdfunding carries risks including production or shipping delays and the possibility that a product does not perform as advertised, and the April 2027 delivery window leaves a long stretch between pledges and hardware in backers' hands. For the power-tool sector, the campaign is a small but telling test of whether buyers will pay a premium for machine vision and software wrapped around a basic hand tool. If the S1 ships on schedule and the recognition system holds up on the tiny fasteners it targets, it could push established tool brands to look harder at pairing cameras and on-device AI with their own product lines.

stories.Headline: 'Don't kill the Golden Goose': Trump calls AI warnings a 'HOAX' as AI leaders raise alarms - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump said on Monday, September 14, 2026, that warnings from top technology leaders about the dangers of artificial intelligence are a hoax. In a series of social media posts, Trump wrote that AI taking over the world and destroying humanity is a hoax, and he claimed there is a sick conspiracy against AI and data centers that only China is happy about. He said the United States is dominating other countries, including China, in AI development, and he wrote, "Don't kill the Golden Goose!" His comments came after Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, said his company would welcome a slower pace of AI development so the technology's capabilities do not get ahead of alignment and monitoring. House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters that the president is planning to meet with AI executives this week.

Trump said the only control or guardrails AI needs is a strong and smart president, and that the United States has that. Vice President JD Vance said the administration is concerned about the technology, but any regulation needs to be done smartly and thoughtfully, and he called the warnings from AI leaders a Trojan horse. Last week Jacob Coxon, a former safety researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI, announced his resignation from Anthropic and said neither company is acting responsibly, adding that the people building AI earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade. Altman said late on Sunday that OpenAI would welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI, and he said consistent rules to manage frontier risk are a good idea, including ideas like independent auditors. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post last week that we must pace the frontier and slow the pace at which the capabilities of AI models improve.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC News' "This Week with George Stephanopoulos" on Sunday that lawmakers need to act urgently, and he called for decisive action now to slow the pace of development to protect the American people. Altman said on Sunday that pacing does not mean stopping, that progress has been rapid and will continue, but it should be slower than it otherwise could be, and that no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness. He said the government's help will be needed for international coordination, but first the companies should do what they can themselves. Lawmakers from both chambers are back in Washington this week for the final legislative push before the November midterm elections, with a renewed focus on regulating artificial intelligence likely to come following reports that raise significant concerns about AI security, and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have demanded information from OpenAI and launched investigations. The president on Sunday also confirmed that he personally uses AI, but did not say which systems or for what purposes.
