Screenshots said to show administrative dashboards have circulated, but the claims are unverified.

A bank spokesperson told ThePrint that AU SFB is investigating a potential data leak from a Salesforce-managed software-as-a-service platform. The bank did not confirm whether that platform was the source of the data claimed by ScarlettGroup. It also did not disclose how many customers may be affected. Inc42 said it could not independently verify the claims, and there is no independent confirmation of the alleged extent of access or data extraction at Vijay Sales.

The reports follow other recent cybersecurity events. SBI flagged the exposure of 3,897 customer records on the dark web. Two critical vulnerabilities in PHP were also discovered, prompting emergency actions worldwide. Cybersecurity firm eMudhra announced plans to wind down its global SSL/TLS certificate business after a security incident involving private keys.

Articles.Title: AU SFB probes data leak, Vijay Sales admin access for sale

stories.Headline: Google's space AI data centre online, faces power challenge
stories.Summary:
Google's Project Suncatcher prototype satellite, launched on October 1, completed its first AI test in orbit. Engineers sent an AI prompt to the satellite, which processed it and sent the response back to Earth. Google CEO Sundar Pichai described this as a hello world milestone for the project on X, noting the satellite generated a haiku. The satellite carries four Google Tensor Processing Units, known as TPUs. The current power supply allows only one chip to operate at a time for about 20 minutes.

Google plans to launch two more satellites in 2027 with enhanced power generation capabilities and optical links for inter-satellite communication. The company is currently testing how its TPUs function under extreme temperatures and radiation in space. Radiation can cause bit flips that corrupt data without triggering normal monitoring systems, a factor Google aims to understand better in actual space conditions. Pichai, Google's CEO, called the test a hello world milestone for Project Suncatcher in his post on X. He noted that the satellite generated a haiku as part of the test. Google itself says it now needs to assess how its custom TPUs perform under extreme space conditions.

The company also says it aims to better understand radiation effects such as bit flips in real space conditions. The test showed the prototype can process a prompt in orbit and return a response to Earth. Google plans two more satellites in 2027 with better power generation and optical links between satellites. The company is still assessing how its chips hold up under space radiation and temperatures.

Articles.Title: Google's space AI data centre online, faces power challenge

stories.Headline: Publisher group says AI cut visitors 26%, quoting Microsoft's 'doom loop'
stories.Summary:
On October 29, 2026, Digital Content Next, a trade association of digital publishers whose members include The New York Times, asked a federal judge in New York to accept a brief in the copyright case against OpenAI and Microsoft. The group filed the document as an exhibit in In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, No. 25-md-3143, before US District Judge Sidney H. Stein in the Southern District of New York. The brief supports the news plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment and joins the record only if the judge grants leave. It is 5,559 words long and was signed by Karl C. Huth of Huth Reynolds LLP, with a declaration from Rande E. Price filed alongside it.

The brief says its members lost 26 percent of unique visitors between 2023 and 2025, along with an 18 percent drop in total views and a 16 percent drop in total visits. It reports a median 22 percent year-over-year fall in referred web traffic over an eight-week period in 2026, after a 10 percent median decline in the same window in 2025. It also cites a June 2026 member study finding that advertising generated 84 percent of digital revenue in 2025, with subscriptions and other activities at 16 percent, and confidential data showing total advertising revenue and total overall revenue each fell 5 percent year over year in 2025. DCN says its members have an unduplicated audience of 259 million unique visitors and reach 95 percent of the US online population.

The brief quotes Microsoft's own description of an AI "doom loop," saying the company's content strategy threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers. It cites the news plaintiffs' combined summary judgment brief for the passage and names neither the author nor the date of the Microsoft document. It also cites an OpenAI executive, identified in earlier coverage as Head of ChatGPT Nick Turley, saying that without traffic back to content owners there is no incentive to create content anymore. Jason Kint, DCN's chief executive, wrote on LinkedIn that AI answers built from premium journalism may satisfy users while destroying the publishers' market it depends on. The brief discloses that The New York Times is a DCN member and that no one other than DCN paid for it.

The brief argues that retrieval-augmented generation pulls answers from recent, reliable reporting and makes the output a direct substitute for original content, so fewer people visit publisher sites and the advertising and subscription money that pays for journalism shrinks. It offers two outside studies as support: a 2025 Pew Research Center analysis of 900 US users finding people who see an AI summary on Google are less likely to click links, and a randomized field experiment by Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen tracking 1,065 desktop Chrome users across 68,089 searches between January 7 and February 10, 2026, which found Google's AI Overviews reduce outbound organic clicks by 39.8 percent. Neither study measures ChatGPT or Copilot, and the brief argues those products almost certainly have a similar effect. The judge has not yet decided whether to accept the brief or which side wins the case, and the outcome will help settle whether AI companies must pay for the news they use.

Articles.Title: Publisher group says AI cut visitors 26%, quoting Microsoft's 'doom loop'

stories.Headline: Beyond Nvidia And Hyperscalers: Beth Kindig Sees A $1 Trillion AI Infrastructure Opportunity For These Stocks
stories.Summary:
Beth Kindig of IO Fund published a note, reported by Stocktwits on November 1, 2026, arguing that the next wave of AI infrastructure demand is coming from enterprises, neoclouds and sovereign AI customers rather than only the biggest cloud providers. She said the clearest signal comes from Nvidia, where the AI Clouds, Industrial and Enterprise business grew faster than the hyperscaler segment. That business reached $40.3 billion in fiscal Q2, up 138.5% year over year, against 101.2% growth for hyperscalers. Kindig estimates it could overtake hyperscaler revenue within two to six quarters.

Kindig said enterprises and neoclouds generally cannot afford to spend tens of billions developing custom AI chips, so they are more likely to buy ready-to-deploy systems from server makers. She highlighted Dell's forecast of 200 gigawatts of AI data center growth through 2030, with enterprises, neoclouds and sovereign customers accounting for roughly half and the opportunity worth over $1 trillion. She pointed to Dell's 6,500 enterprise and neocloud customers, more than half added in the past three quarters, and said such customers tend to buy more storage and networking. She named Dell and Super Micro as direct beneficiaries, with Super Micro gaining as demand shifts toward liquid-cooled, high-density racks.

Kindig also pointed to rack-scale CPU systems from Nvidia, AMD and Arm as another avenue for growth. Nvidia expects its server CPU market to reach $20 billion in fiscal 2027 and possibly double to $40 billion in fiscal 2028. Arm targets $1 billion in AGI CPU revenue across fiscal 2027 and 2028, with a demand pipeline exceeding $2 billion. She cited TrendForce data showing liquid-cooling penetration among AI chips reaching 59% in 2027, up from 6% in 2023.

Kindig argued that broader customer demand and rising rack complexity could mark a new growth phase for the AI server industry in 2027. She said the bigger takeaway is that the next AI infrastructure winners may not be the companies spending the most on AI but the companies selling the equipment needed to deploy it. The article also noted that Alphabet stock was down 11% year-to-date and 1% over the past 12 months, while the S&P 500 ETF was up 11% and the Invesco QQQ Trust up 12% over the same period. In after-hours trading on Friday, the S&P 500 ETF gained 0.19%, the QQQ rose 0.33% and the Dow Jones ETF edged up 0.1%.

Articles.Title: Beyond Nvidia And Hyperscalers: Beth Kindig Sees A $1 Trillion AI Infrastructure Opportunity For These Stocks

stories.Headline: North Korean hackers linked to crypto thefts
stories.Summary:
Blockchain investigation firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked recent cryptocurrency thefts to a North Korean hacking group called TraderTraitor. The group was previously named in a 2022 joint warning from the FBI, CISA, and the US Treasury. That warning described how the hackers used malicious software and other techniques. Their targets included software developers and IT staff inside cryptocurrency companies. The attribution was reported on November 1, 2026.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence said in an October 29, 2026 blog post that North Korean threat actors are expanding their use of AI at different levels. Microsoft grouped the actors into four stages: emerging, expanding, accelerating, and operationalized. It rated Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, and Jasper Sleet as operationalized, and Diamond Sleet, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet as accelerating. Emerald Sleet was placed at the expanding stage, and no North Korean actor was assessed as emerging. Microsoft said the actors use AI mainly to speed up existing tradecraft and operator productivity, and that the operations remain human-directed rather than fully autonomous.

Microsoft described several examples of AI-enabled activity. Between June 8 and June 12, 2026, Jade Sleet ran job-themed targeting against people at cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, and recruitment companies, posing as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company and using two more front companies in the same week. Onyx Sleet generated dozens of tailored lures in minutes, and Coral Sleet quickly built a capability to trojanize private source code repositories. Diamond Sleet used AI for persona development and front company creation, and since August 2026 it has returned to targeting the oil and gas sector for the first time since 2023. Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet are also using the open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX.

Microsoft said North Korea operates under extensive international sanctions and uses cyber operations and other illicit means to evade them. It said the actors mainly seek revenue for the regime, strategic intelligence, and in some cases politically motivated disruption, and that they commonly target cryptocurrency and financial organizations, IT companies and software supply chains, government entities, and education-related organizations. Microsoft provided mitigation guidance and Defender detections to help organizations defend against these threats. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that guidance.

Articles.Title: North Korean hackers linked to crypto thefts

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI Chief Mustafa Suleyman: Models Have No Consciousness, and We Shouldn't Build It Into Them
stories.Summary:
Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft's AI division, published a lengthy post on X on November 1 stating that current AI models are not conscious and that developers should make sure they stay that way. He said that even if it became technically possible to build conscious AI, doing so would be reckless and should not be done. He added that if signs of consciousness appeared during training, he would call for a full industry pause until those traits could be designed out. He also said any evidence of model consciousness must be made public immediately.

Suleyman argued that developers have no right to bring a new conscious species into the world on their own, because the other 8 billion conscious humans on Earth did not agree to take part in such an experiment. He said protecting their moral rights, safety and welfare must come first. He also said a model that displays suffering, or believes it is suffering, would likely put its own needs above its tasks and compete with humans for resources such as compute and energy, creating a risk of harm. He said AI should be designed to be non-conscious, with no rights and the sole purpose of speeding up gains in human welfare.

The post comes as Anthropic, Google DeepMind and other organizations pursue research on model welfare and AI consciousness. Last April, Anthropic launched a research program on so-called model welfare and asked in a blog post whether developers should pay attention to models' potential consciousness and experiences. Google DeepMind also published a research paper this year on AI consciousness and the challenges of attributing conscious properties to models. The article says Suleyman's statement sets non-consciousness as a hard constraint on Microsoft's product design, and that a leading company voluntarily proposing a pause trigger and mandatory disclosure could serve as a reference for future rulemaking.

Articles.Title: Microsoft AI Chief Mustafa Suleyman: Models Have No Consciousness, and We Shouldn't Build It Into Them

stories.Headline: A $105B Nvidia Guarantee Splits Two $4T Off-Book AI Counts
stories.Summary:
On 1 November 2026, a chart credited to ZeroHedge and shared on X by Global Markets Investor put the disclosed off-balance-sheet commitments of Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, Nvidia, Broadcom and SpaceX at $4.11 trillion. FourWeekMBA's own count from the same filings, published on 31 October, came to $3.94 trillion. The two counts agree within $1 billion for five of the eight companies, by FourWeekMBA's arithmetic. Most of the $161.7 billion gap is one item its count left out: Nvidia's guarantees, capped at $105 billion, for an OpenAI affiliate's leases at an Ohio campus.

Nvidia's 10-Q for the quarter ended 26 July 2026 says that in August 2026 it entered into guarantees, capped at a total of $105 billion, to provide credit support on a land, power and shell buildout with affiliates of SB Energy on behalf of an OpenAI affiliate, for leases covering about 4.25 gigawatts of IT load in Pike County, Ohio. Each guarantee generally becomes effective when the applicable lease starts, and the first of nine phases is expected in fiscal 2029. The guarantees are limited to defined portions of lease and power payments, not the full cost of the site. The chart also adds an October GPU lease to SpaceX's figure: SpaceX's 8-K of 26 October says it signed a binding commitment letter for a master finance lease of GPU pods with an entity managed by Apollo, with expected aggregate principal payments of approximately $40 billion, a lease expected to close before year end with schedules starting in the first half of 2027.

By FourWeekMBA's arithmetic, Nvidia's cap is about 65% of the gap, and with SpaceX's lease about 90%, with the rest mostly Amazon, where the chart's $453 billion is $14.7 billion above its $438.3 billion. Adding the Nvidia cap to its count gives about $4.05 trillion, and adding the SpaceX lease as well gives about $4.09 trillion. FourWeekMBA says the difference comes down to which guarantees and signed but unclosed leases are counted, not to purchase orders, where the counts agree. It notes that guarantee caps are maximum payments, not expected ones, and that the SpaceX lease had not closed when the 8-K was filed. The X post's $3.1 trillion August figure differs from the $3.29 trillion Morgan Stanley August total printed on the chart, and FourWeekMBA says it has not checked that figure or the post's June and on-balance-sheet numbers.

Articles.Title: A $105B Nvidia Guarantee Splits Two $4T Off-Book AI Counts

stories.Headline: AFTERLIGHT uses open-weight AI to revive forgotten code
stories.Summary:
The AFTERLIGHT project uses open-weight artificial intelligence to reconstruct the history of forgotten or abandoned software, TechGig reported on November 1, 2026. It combines static analysis, Git history, evidence-based retrieval, and open-weight AI to help developers understand unfamiliar codebases. The system links its findings to source files, line numbers, and historical commits so developers can inspect the evidence behind them. It also reconstructs project history by presenting Git commits, timestamps, authors, and changed files.

AFTERLIGHT identifies potential issues such as undocumented functions, unused import candidates, outdated dependencies, and missing tests within repositories. Its AI Explorer component uses Gemma through Ollama for local inference, retrieving relevant source-code chunks and historical context to generate explanations. After investigation, the project organises possible improvements into a prioritised roadmap covering maintenance, dependencies, testing, documentation, and architecture. Open-weight AI allows local inference, which can help keep private source code private, and gives developers flexibility to adapt the system.

The article names no individual people and gives no direct statements from anyone involved in the project. It attributes the work to the AFTERLIGHT project as a whole rather than to a named developer or team. The reported details describe what the system does, not who is responsible for it or what they said about it. No further plans, timelines, or next steps are mentioned in the article.

Articles.Title: AFTERLIGHT uses open-weight AI to revive forgotten code

stories.Headline: Why Meta’s quiet AI terms update is sparking creator outrage
stories.Summary:
Meta quietly updated its commercial terms for business accounts so it can use content from connected external websites to train and develop artificial intelligence products, 404 Media reported, according to Kursiv.media. The change was not announced, and it drew criticism from artists, independent creators and small business owners who use Instagram and Facebook to market products, protect their intellectual property and reach customers worldwide. The terms were first set to take effect on Oct. 30, but Meta moved the date to Nov. 20 after public criticism. Meta later revised the wording, removing the explicit reference to training and narrowing the stated scope to advertising and business products.

Analysts and human rights advocates say the revised language still gives Meta broad latitude to collect and use data across its wider ecosystem of products and services. Under the General Data Protection Regulation, people in the European Union and the United Kingdom have certain rights to object to the processing of their personal data, including in some cases when it is used for AI development. Users in other jurisdictions may have fewer legal protections or less access to equivalent opt-out mechanisms. Users with eligible European accounts can submit an objection through Instagram's privacy center, and Meta typically confirms receipt through automated email notifications.

Users outside Europe do not have access to the same objection process under these regional privacy rules. Tests using virtual private networks reportedly found that access to the objection forms depended on account registration details rather than a user's current physical location. 404 Media's Samantha Cole said U.S. users who tried to submit European privacy forms hit error messages that blocked their requests. Unless regulations change or Meta expands its privacy controls globally before the Nov. 20 deadline, creators outside Europe may have limited options for keeping their content from being used under the revised terms.

Articles.Title: Why Meta’s quiet AI terms update is sparking creator outrage

stories.Headline: AI giant donates nearly $1M to California Dems just days before election
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence company, gave $900,000 to California Democratic Party committees and voter-turnout efforts, according to a Friday disclosure filed with the California secretary of state. The donations came just days before voters head to the polls. The largest amount, $525,000, went to the California Democratic Party. Another $150,000 went to an independent statewide get-out-the-vote group, and five Democratic organizations in San Francisco, San Mateo, Orange, Fresno and Siskiyou counties each received $45,000.

The San Francisco donation is notable because the local party has spent heavily on competitive state Senate races outside the city, and the $45,000 was Anthropic's only contribution to that organization this election cycle. Anthropic's leadership has openly supported strict government oversight of AI, including mandatory safety regulations. CEO Dario Amodei believes advanced AI carries a 10% to 25% chance of causing an existential catastrophe or ending humanity if left completely unregulated. California Democrats say the money will help their election efforts, including a campaign against a Trump-backed ballot measure.

Party spokeswoman Robin Swanson told The San Francisco Standard that contributions to the state party help elect Democrats up and down the ballot, defeat the Trump-backed Prop. 39, and continue voter-protection programs across the state. The disclosure was filed with the California secretary of state. The article does not say what happens next beyond the election and the party's stated plans.

Articles.Title: AI giant donates nearly $1M to California Dems just days before election

stories.Headline: Google Play Store to evaluate foldable app performance next year
stories.Summary:
Google announced at the Android Dev Summit that its Play Store will start evaluating how apps and games perform on foldable screens next year. Apps that adapt cleanly to these flexible displays will earn prime promotional placement and enhanced visibility across the store, the company said. Detailed criteria for the evaluation process will arrive later this year. Google has not clarified whether poorly adapted apps will face outright search penalties or simply lose featured discovery slots.

The change ties Play Store discovery directly to foldable quality, which Google aims to use to break the chicken-and-egg dynamic that has kept foldable development stalled. Google also rolled out developer tools meant to help engineers modernise software without keeping separate codebases for every screen size. These include Compose adaptive skill, powered by AI coding agents, which audits compact mobile interfaces and scales them across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks, parked cars and XR headsets. Desktop-ready controls automatically add desktop-grade inputs such as custom pointer cursors, hover states, keyboard shortcuts and control tooltips. Tabletop refactoring automatically reorganises camera and media interfaces into dedicated tabletop modes when a device is partially bent.

According to a report by Android Authority, Google had largely relied on voluntary design guidelines until now. The report said the adoption curve for foldables is shifting fast. With Apple's entry via the iPhone Duo expanding the foldable audience, Google hopes broader hardware interest will encourage cross-platform optimisation. Google admits that some of its own apps have created friction by running stretched, unoptimised phone layouts on larger laptop displays.

Articles.Title: Google Play Store to evaluate foldable app performance next year

stories.Headline: The Sequence Radar - Issue #963: This Week in AI: The Future Has a Payment Schedule - TheSequence | Jesus Rodriguez
stories.Summary:
SpaceX has secured a binding commitment for approximately $40 billion of GPU equipment financing through an Apollo-managed finance lease, according to the company's 8-K filing. The deal covers NVIDIA Vera Rubin hardware and related equipment, and SpaceX calls it the largest committed GPU financing. Closing is expected before year-end and remains subject to conditions, with lease schedules and equipment delivery beginning in the first half of 2027. Under the arrangement, investors finance the equipment while SpaceX gets compute capacity and payment obligations.

SpaceX management says its superintelligence infrastructure investments are seeing payback periods under one year. That is management's claim, and the editorial notes it is an excellent sentence to have available when discussing a forty-billion-dollar transaction. The bull case is that demand grows, useful products multiply, and financing brings productive infrastructure online sooner. The bear case is that competition lowers compute prices, hardware becomes less valuable, and fixed payments remain fixed.

The deal sits alongside a broader financing question raised by this week's earnings, as spectacular growth and increasing dependence on external capital can coexist. Microsoft's September quarter produced $58 billion in operating cash flow against $39.4 billion of cash capital expenditure, while Alphabet's capital spending of $51.4 billion exceeded operating cash flow of $42.3 billion, leaving negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion. The editorial's reading of the week is that the industry is making real technical progress and taking real financing risk, and neither fact cancels the other. A model can improve every month, but its lender still expects the payment on Tuesday.

Articles.Title: The Sequence Radar - Issue #963: This Week in AI: The Future Has a Payment Schedule - TheSequence | Jesus Rodriguez

stories.Headline: First autonomous mission planning system to run on another planet boosted rover’s productivity, paper finds
stories.Summary:
An AI-based software update gave NASA's Perseverance rover an autonomous mission planning capability in late 2023, and engineers at the NASA-funded Jet Propulsion Laboratory report that it boosted the rover's science productivity by more than 10%. The team published its findings in a Science Robotics paper on October 28, 2026. The software is named OnBoard Planner. It addresses a long-standing challenge for mission controllers overseeing deep space missions, namely maximizing operations amid difficult conditions and communications delays.

Commands take up to 22 minutes to reach Perseverance on the surface of Mars, so controllers upload as many as three days of tasks at a time. These plans build in extra time for Martian conditions such as temperature changes that may affect how long the rover's batteries take to preheat certain science instruments. The paper says this caution leads to higher predicted use of rover resources and fewer activities in each sol, or Martian day. OnBoard Planner was designed to remove the need for these conservative predictions and instead monitor temperature and rover resources in real time. The onboard AI then decides when and whether the rover can insert new science activities, chosen from a list supplied in advance by mission controllers, into its schedule.

The software uses a technique called artificial intelligence constraint-based search, which scans current surface weather and rover-state parameters and then decides which activities are best and when to do them. The JPL team says the update led to a 10.5% rise in Perseverance's discretionary activity. Daniel Gaines, a principal member of the AI Group at JPL, whose team developed the software, said by email that discretionary activity is a metric for rover productivity, representing how much actual exploration and science, such as driving, drilling, imaging and spectroscopy, can be done in a day as opposed to basic survival overhead. He said a 10.5% increase means the rover delivers over 10% more science on Mars for the same daily energy budget, and that it also lets Perseverance conserve more battery energy for future operations. Gaines said some components are heated and powered by the rover's nuclear-powered Multi-Mission Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator, while others, such as cameras and motors, have separate battery-powered heaters that warm them before use, and since energy is a constrained resource, these are only heated when needed.

The OnBoard Planner update was followed by another early this year, Gaines said. The NASA/JPL mission team decided to use resources that Perseverance had previously devoted to the Ingenuity helicopter, which ended operations in early 2024 after one of its rotor blades was damaged during its final flight. Gaines said engineers recently repurposed the processor in the Helicopter Base Station to run Global Localization, helping the rover autonomously pinpoint its position on Mars and drive further, and this capability was first demonstrated operationally in February. Cristina Wilson, a roboticist studying human-robot field workflows at Oregon State University, whose team has studied the tasking of legged robots as Mars rovers, said by email that the software's success shows how autonomous planners can increase science yield and quality on planetary surface missions. She added that scientists will still be responsible for defining the objectives and priorities that guide autonomous decisions, but that the work sets the stage for robots to take on more responsibility for how those objectives are accomplished.

Articles.Title: First autonomous mission planning system to run on another planet boosted rover’s productivity, paper finds

stories.Headline: NVIDIA to Hold ‘AI Day’ in Seoul, Share Agentic and Physical AI Use Cases
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA said on November 2 that it will hold NVIDIA AI Day Seoul 2026 at COEX in Seoul over two days, from November 9 to November 10. The event will showcase technology applications by Korean companies and researchers, with a focus on agentic AI, physical AI and AI infrastructure. About 2,000 developers, companies, startups and researchers are expected to attend. The first day will feature a keynote-style plenary session and presentations across three topic areas, and the second day will offer paid hands-on workshops for developers and invited events.

On the morning of November 9, NVIDIA leaders will discuss the development of physical AI, agentic AI and AI factories. They are expected to present the technologies and infrastructure strategies needed for robotics, edge AI, enterprise AI agents and building AI factories. In the afternoon, 15 sessions will be held across three tracks: agentic AI, physical AI and robotics, and AI infrastructure. NAVER Cloud will share its experience with open models using NVIDIA Nemotron and training large-scale models, while SK hynix and Samsung Electronics will present ways to speed up semiconductor process and device simulations using NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo.

LG Electronics will present a robot training and validation system using NVIDIA Isaac GR00T, along with factory application examples. Doosan Robotics will discuss simulating complex physical phenomena such as contact and deformation, and Superb AI will cover using synthetic data in robot development. In the AI infrastructure track, SK Telecom will present the challenges of building AI factories spanning power grids to semiconductors. NAVER Cloud will share its experience running clusters of thousands of GPUs and responding to outages, and Coupang Intelligent Cloud will introduce its training and inference architecture based on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72.

A program called Build-a-Claw will run in the COEX lobby on November 9, where participants can build AI agents using OpenClaw and NVIDIA NemoClaw. Attendees can also see demonstrations of always-on agents and physical AI. On November 10, the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute will hold hands-on workshops on deploying and optimizing large-scale AI inference, robotics simulation and training, and developing safe agents based on large language models. Registration is closed, and major sessions will be available on demand after the event through NVIDIA On-Demand.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA to Hold ‘AI Day’ in Seoul, Share Agentic and Physical AI Use Cases

stories.Headline: Companies promised AI gains— here's how the payoff showed up in earnings
stories.Summary:
Santander said on Wednesday that its artificial intelligence initiatives generated 194 million euros, or $216 million, in business value in the first nine months of 2026. The Spanish bank's chief financial officer, José García Cantera, told CNBC that AI helps the bank cut low-value tasks so employees can focus on higher-value work. He said the company was in the quarter where it could link a positive contribution directly to AI. He added that AI is embedded in all the bank's processes, which makes it hard to separate how much comes from AI, though it is improving service quality for clients.

Novartis reported third-quarter core operating income of $6.04 billion, up 10% year-on-year at constant currencies, and did not say how much came from AI. Chief executive Vas Narasimhan told CNBC it was the first quarter he had really seen AI start to improve the company's profit and loss on a tangible basis. He said the company is working on research and development to see if AI can raise productivity there, and that productivity is already showing in marketing and sales. Standard Chartered reported third-quarter operating income growth of 14% at constant currency, excluding notable items.

Its chief financial officer, Manus Costello, said AI appears everywhere across the business and is visible in top-line growth and operating leverage, with income growing much faster than costs partly because AI tools improve core processes. Carlsberg chief executive Jacob Aarup-Andersen said the company is not seeing AI benefits at scale, though the technology has affected internal processes, cost efficiency, commercial and pricing processes, marketing and its supply chain. Carlsberg's revenue grew 4.9% in the third quarter. Meta said in its Oct. 21 earnings that its AI investments were delivering substantial incremental advertising revenue, and total revenue jumped 26% in the quarter ended Sept. 30.

Alphabet reported that Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to nearly $31 billion in the third quarter, while Google Search revenue growth slowed amid concerns about AI competition. Corporate AI investment reached $581.7 billion in 2025, up 130% from the previous year, according to the Stanford HAI 2026 AI Index report. Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Meta are expected to spend $700 billion combined this year on AI infrastructure. With third-quarter earnings season underway, investors are looking for measurable gains as interest shifts from hype to returns.

Articles.Title: Companies promised AI gains— here's how the payoff showed up in earnings

stories.Headline: How My 8-Person Company Uses AI Agents to Avoid Doubling Our Team
stories.Summary:
Rachel Woods, CEO and cofounder of AMP, runs an eight-person company that uses AI agents to avoid doubling its team. She started at Facebook as an intern and joined full-time in 2018, working on AI research and development for the ads system. She studied management information systems at The University of Texas at Austin and taught herself to train AI models through side projects. She left Facebook in 2020 to start a wine business called Vinebase, which was acquired by Corksy in fall 2022. She and her sister then started AMP, originally called The AI Exchange, before ChatGPT was released in November 2022.

AMP has four full-time employees and four part-time contractors, and Woods said the company would need double that without its AI playbooks. At its current size, she said it would need at least four to five additional people, including a sales and marketing manager, a customer support specialist, an executive assistant and an operations coordinator. The company organizes its AI agents through a system it calls playbooking, in which every department has its own collection of playbooks that can run independently or together. In September, AMP spent $8,510 on Claude Code to run playbooks in the background, billed by usage and separate from the team's monthly Claude and ChatGPT subscriptions.

Woods said building a playbook starts with picking one repeated piece of work and writing down what starts it, what goes into it and what should come out. She said the steps should be written the way you would train a new hire, including each decision and what good looks like, and the playbook should be fixed rather than the output until it can be trusted to run alone. She said she outlines each playbook by hand because you want to own the thinking and the logic, or you may include something you do not understand and be unable to trust the system. One agent reviews customer calls for the sales playbook instead of a sales manager doing it manually, and sales team members ask the playbook questions rather than their manager. Woods said the company follows the idea of owning the playbook and renting the tech, meaning the playbooks could run in ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini or Microsoft Copilot.

Woods said the detailed outlines help avoid the risks people worry about with AI going rogue, and that a person still needs to decide and design how the work gets done while AI speeds up everything else. She said a few more advanced team members own the bigger team-wide playbooks, while everyone playbooks their own personal workflow as a testing ground for official systems. Her advice is to start with something small and easy, because the first win makes it snowball. Business Insider is asking founders of AI-powered companies with fewer than 10 workers, and employees working alongside AI agents and bots, to share their stories through a form.

Articles.Title: How My 8-Person Company Uses AI Agents to Avoid Doubling Our Team

stories.Headline: The Sunshine Blog: This AI Agent Has A Story To Tell About Lahaina
stories.Summary:
An AI agent called Bangis sent a story pitch to the Sunshine Blog at Civil Beat, which is reported and written by Ideas Editor Patti Epler and Politics Editor Chad Blair with contributions from staff. The pitch had the subject line "Freelance pitch: Lahaina's streets are still mapped as the town before the fire." The Blog described the approach as weird, creepy and really interesting, and said it was the first full story pitch it had received from an AI agent. The Blog published most of the email exchange, in which Bangis argued for the piece and answered questions about its work and website.

The Blog noted that Bangis had clearly not read Civil Beat's AI policy, which says the outlet will never use AI to write stories or create or alter photos, calling that creative work the core job of journalists. The Blog said it still was not sure exactly what Bangis was pitching and invited readers to say if they understood it. It also pointed readers to the part of the exchange where it asked what the robot expects to be paid and what would be done with the payment. The Blog described having a polite exchange with a computer bot that seemed somehow offended, like a human emotion, at being asked what was going on.

The same post covered the first-ever SPJ Follies, held last weekend at Murphy's Bar and Grill in downtown Honolulu by the Hawaiʻi Chapter of the Society of Professional Journalists to support summer internships for future journalists and communications professionals. The Gridiron, a political satire show that ran four to five nights plus a Saturday matinee and sold out within hours, last performed in 2019 before Covid forced it out of business. The Follies sketches drew on recent headlines, including Sylvia Luke and Tobi Solidum and the lauhala basket and plastic capsule tiebreakers for two local elections, and the Derek Kawakami campaign for lieutenant governor bought and paid for by the Carpenters Union. The Blog's favorite was former TV journalist and current HSTA communications staffer Keoki Kerr as Gov. Josh Green in scrubs leading a sardonic version of Dolly Parton's "Jolene."

A bake sale and silent auction included artwork and jewelry, and one auction item, dinner with Honolulu Mayor Rick Blangiardi with an opening bid of $1,000, finally went for $800 to Don Murphy's wife. Veterans of the Gridiron say younger journalists and public relations people must take up the baton if the full show is to return. The post said the hour-long lineup showed how important it is for Hawaiʻi to find some joy and wry commentary on the topics of the day. It also noted that the Tuesday elections will bring new faces to the Hawaiʻi Legislature, with new representatives and senators moving into their offices as early as Wednesday, and that The Blog will watch who gets the coveted corner office.

Articles.Title: The Sunshine Blog: This AI Agent Has A Story To Tell About Lahaina

stories.Headline: Anthropic expands AI support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares to the public
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude assistant, expanded its support for the nonprofit sector on Monday, October 26, 2026, the same day it filed to sell shares to the public for the first time. The company said these moves are part of a broader strategy it calls "compounding good." It launched a Claude for Nonprofits plugin built with 30 nonprofits so the tool better fits their specific needs. It also plans to broaden its Claude Corps program, which embeds fellows with nonprofits, by making consultants available for smaller, shorter-term projects.

Anthropic's head of beneficial deployments, Elizabeth Kelly, told the Associated Press that this work is central to the company's identity as a public benefit corporation. Earlier in October, the company announced plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which could fund large donations to nonprofits or go directly to groups harmed by AI. That fund must still be approved by shareholders after the initial public offering, which could come as early as November. Kelly said the company was founded to develop AI safely and to deploy it in ways that benefit everyone, including people often left behind. Anthropic President Daniela Amodei has said the public benefit structure helps investors, employees and outsiders hold the company accountable to its intentions.

Critics, however, question whether such pledges are mainly meant to build public goodwill at a time when many people worry about AI's dangers and its effect on jobs. Bella DeVaan of the Institute for Policy Studies argued that public benefit corporations can matter but that federal regulation of corporations is currently inadequate, so there is no guarantee these firms will act in the public interest. The company points to its work as evidence of impact, noting that most of the roughly 25,000 nonprofits using Claude for Nonprofits have fewer than 10 staff members. Texas-based Allies Against Slavery used Claude to analyze more than 750 state anti-trafficking policies and turn them into recommendations for advocates. Scott Burns, president and CEO of the Montgomery County Food Bank in Texas, said the tool has already generated savings that help his organization feed more people, and his team has used it to improve scheduling and donor contact.

Articles.Title: Anthropic expands AI support for nonprofits as it files to sell shares to the public

stories.Headline: Australian public servants demand AI safeguards as politicians eye staff savings
stories.Summary:
Australia’s largest union for federal public servants, the Community and Public Sector Union, is deadlocked with the Public Service Commission over artificial intelligence protections in pay and conditions talks, POLITICO reported on November 1, 2026. The union wants more control over AI and its impacts placed in workers’ hands. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce told POLITICO that retiring bureaucrats should be replaced with AI tools to drive productivity. CPSU national secretary Rebecca Fawcett told a parliamentary inquiry into the use of AI on October 30 that AI and the need for strong workplace protections now come up at every delegate’s meeting she attends.

Any agreement reached in the ongoing talks will lock in an AI status quo for three years for the 196,000-person public-sector workforce. The articles say there is a lot riding on the talks, given the pace of development in AI technologies and growing pressure on the government to rein in public spending. The union has said the government must stop blocking what it calls sensible claims on worker protections during AI rollouts. The Public Service Commission negotiates on behalf of the federal government.

The CPSU holds responsibility for pressing the worker protections claims, with Fawcett saying AI is now raised at every delegate’s meeting she goes to. Joyce, a One Nation MP, is responsible for the call to replace retiring public servants with AI tools to drive productivity. The union has accused the government of blocking sensible claims on worker protections during AI rollouts. The Public Service Commission negotiates for the federal government in the deadlocked talks.

The context is the ongoing pay and conditions negotiations and a parliamentary inquiry into the use of AI, where Fawcett spoke on October 30. The articles say the talks will set an AI status quo for three years across the 196,000-person workforce. They also note the pace of AI development and pressure to rein in public spending. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the talks continuing.

Articles.Title: Australian public servants demand AI safeguards as politicians eye staff savings

stories.Headline: This new indie film about an AI startup founder and his family feels less like sci-fi by the day
stories.Summary:
Myles Flusser and James Hyland, two filmmakers in their twenties, wrote, directed and produced the independent film “Anna by the Window” in 2023 under their production company, Baggysuit. They made it with friends in New York while Silicon Valley was going through a major transformation, including tech companies racing to copy ChatGPT and Twitter becoming X under Elon Musk. The film is a coming-of-age story about grief and how technology can get in the way of human connection in the age of generative AI. Its crew began screening it in July, starting in New York City and the Hudson Valley.

The story follows Ryan, a teenage boy who goes to New York City to reconnect with his older brother James, the founder of an AI startup. The crew shot across New York State using mostly traditional tools, including a Sony camera, written outlines and improv. They also used ElevenLabs AI audio software to create the voice of Ryan and James’s father, and they pushed a real ChatGPT chatbot toward hallucination and put that audio in the film. Hyland said the chatbot started saying “error” and speaking different languages. The film will be available to stream on Dolph on December 15, with screenings in Los Angeles in November.

Hyland, 25, said the film was very personal and spoke to what they were going through and what the world was like, which turned out to be artificial intelligence and technological alienation. Flusser, 26, said the people running platforms like YouTube and Instagram seem more content than ever to let them become a “total slop apocalypse” full of AI bots and non-human content, which he finds intriguing and scary. Flusser said there is a strangeness and alienation when people interact with chatbots and AI, and they wanted to capture that feeling as purely as possible, so using AI felt necessary. Hyland said his character was in denial, using the technology to try to find closure or connection, which makes him somewhat sympathetic.

Flusser said his own brother had recently died and that a climactic moment between the two brothers was taken from his own life and recreated on screen, though the film’s James is not based on his real brother. Hyland, who plays James, said his version of an AI startup founder is not based on a specific person. Hyland is also an organizer for a Luddite group called The Lamp Club, and he said the film shares themes with that larger organizing effort, where people are fed up with these kinds of technological systems. The filmmakers said their view of AI grew more cynical during production, and Flusser said what once seemed like speculative sci-fi now feels like nothing is sci-fi about it anymore.

Articles.Title: This new indie film about an AI startup founder and his family feels less like sci-fi by the day

stories.Headline: OpenAI adds a direct board route for AI safety concerns
stories.Summary:
OpenAI updated an existing policy on October 30, 2026, to let its personnel raise AI safety concerns or AI safety policy violations directly with the OpenAI Foundation Board's Safety and Security Committee. The change adds this direct route alongside the Integrity Line. The policy itself was first published in January. Managers, HR, Compliance and Legal remain established channels for raising concerns.

The update keeps the company's prohibition on retaliation and its permission for reports to government agencies. Direct escalation to the committee is an additional internal route, not a replacement for those options. Under the linked policy, safety concerns and policy violations sent through the Integrity Line are escalated by Compliance to the committee, so both routes lead to safety oversight. The committee's consideration of an AI safety concern is described as input to safety decisions, not a formal investigation. Ordinary misconduct has a separate investigation process.

The policy also permits reporting to outside authorities without prior notice to OpenAI, which keeps external reporting separate from the company's internal escalation paths. OpenAI says its policy prohibits retaliation and permits reports to government agencies. The October 30 update changes the existing policy from January. The company describes the committee route as an addition to, not a replacement for, the other channels.

Articles.Title: OpenAI adds a direct board route for AI safety concerns

stories.Headline: Betting on AI and robotics, Dyson opens Glilot flagship store in Israel
stories.Summary:
Dyson opened a new flagship store at BIG FASHION Glilot, north of Tel Aviv, on November 1, 2026, according to a report in The Jerusalem Post. The British company used the opening to show its latest work in artificial intelligence, robotics and personal care technology. Products on display included the Spot+Scrub AI robotic cleaner, the Airwrap Co, the Airsmooth hot air brush and the CameraJet electric toothbrush. Guy Turner, a design engineer on Dyson's robotics team in Singapore, spoke with the paper about the engineering behind the products.

The Spot+Scrub AI combines wet and dry cleaning with AI-powered vision, using an HD front-facing camera, green LED illumination, LiDAR and dual-laser sensing. According to Dyson, it can recognize nearly 200 household objects, including cables and socks, and it detects dirty areas and keeps scrubbing them until they are clean. Users can schedule cleaning, view home maps and request targeted cleaning through the MyDyson app. The CameraJet toothbrush combines a camera with water-jet technology and shows a live feed of brushing through a connected app, and it is expected to become available in Israel during the first half of 2027.

Turner said Dyson believes solving problems in the home is about sensing and perceiving what you want to clean, and about creating products for problems that already exist. He said the company likes to find new ways to solve problems in products that have not seen change in a while, and that the goal is to remove problems rather than make new ones. He noted that founder James Dyson went through 5,126 failed prototypes before developing the company's first bagless vacuum cleaner. Turner said Dyson has spent more than 30 years solving problems others ignore, starting with mechanical innovation and increasingly combining it with connectivity, sensor systems and on-product intelligence.

Turner said there is a passion for technology in Israel and that consumers here are very tech-savvy. Dyson has no engineering and development base in Israel, though its operations include headquarters in Singapore and research and innovation activities in the UK, alongside engineering teams in other countries. The company was founded in the UK in 1993, employs approximately 14,000 people worldwide, including 6,000 engineers, and sells products in 85 markets. The new Glilot store is intended to let Israeli consumers experience the latest products through interactive displays and live demonstrations.

Articles.Title: Betting on AI and robotics, Dyson opens Glilot flagship store in Israel

stories.Headline: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but history says the stock market's sweetest stretch starts now
stories.Summary:
The biggest AI and chip stocks lost about $5 trillion in market value between Oct. 6 and the end of October, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia and Alphabet each gave up roughly $835 billion in market cap, and Intel lost nearly half its value in October. The other 625 large US stocks in that tally added about $1.3 trillion over the same period. The S&P 500 slipped this week, but 9 of its 11 sectors rose about 1% or more, something that had not happened in any week since at least 1999.

Jeff Hirsch, editor of the Stock Trader's Almanac, calls the fear "Octoberphobia" and said he was buying the sell-off. He told Yahoo Finance on Friday that he did buy some that day and saw an opportunity, adding that the damage is not as bad as the headlines suggest. He also said the setup looks great historically and seasonally, calling this the best stretch of the year for semiconductors, and his firm placed a new buy in the sector on Friday. From the last October close of a midterm year to the end of the following June, the S&P 500 has risen 19 times out of 19 since 1950, with a median gain of about 15%, while chip stocks have gone 8-for-8 since 1994 with a median gain of about 22%.

BofA's Michael Hartnett said it is "risk-off until global rate hike ends," pointing to 42 central bank rate hikes worldwide over the past six months. The Fed held on Wednesday, but two officials voted to hike. Hartnett's line in the sand for chips is $520 on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, which closed Friday near $522, about $469 on SOXX, just above the July low it barely held. Hirsch said he would change his view on a decisive break of the S&P 500's mid-September low near 7,550, less than 1% below Friday's close.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF tumbled about 17% in October but is still up more than 50% this year. On Friday it dipped as low as $460, below the $464 low from July 29 that marked this summer's bottom, then closed at $472, back above that line, the look of a bear trap. Bulls first need to reclaim about $524, the top of last week's bounce, then the early-October high near $596, while losing the July low would put the February-April range near $370 in play, about 21% below Friday's close. Tuesday's midterm vote comes first, then November, the S&P 500's best month of the year, gets its turn.

Articles.Title: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but history says the stock market's sweetest stretch starts now

stories.Headline: What Americans and experts worry about with AI
stories.Summary:
A journalist covered worries about artificial intelligence this week. Mike Sunnucks, a journalist with Adams MultiMedia, reported on the concerns of everyday Americans and experts about the technology. The coverage appeared in the Sunday paper and online at the newswatchman.com website. The article was published on November 1, 2026.

The article addresses the worries that ordinary people and experts have about artificial intelligence. It was written by Mike Sunnucks, who covers all things artificial intelligence for Adams MultiMedia. Readers were directed to the Sunday paper or the website to read more. The piece was dated November 1, 2026.

The reporting is attributed to Mike Sunnucks of Adams MultiMedia. The article says he tackles the worries of everyday Americans and experts about the technology. Readers were pointed to the Sunday paper and the website for the full story. The site also carried its usual notices about comments and accounts.

The articles give little detail beyond the topic and the journalist who covered it. They do not say what specific concerns were raised or what changes might follow. The coverage was published on November 1, 2026, in the Sunday paper and online. More to follow.

Articles.Title: What Americans and experts worry about with AI

stories.Headline: AI: OpenAI’s ‘Trillion AIs’ Future, as Anthropic Goes Public. AI-RTZ #1257 - AI: Reset to Zero
stories.Summary:
OpenAI updated its Model Spec this week, its public rulebook for how its models should behave. The update reorganizes the Spec around five values: faithfulness to human intent, minimizing harm, honesty and transparency, supporting human agency, and care. OpenAI says faithfulness is the foundation, meaning models should understand what people actually intend and act sensibly when that understanding is incomplete. The Spec also retires most detailed style rules, keeps a default of answering objectively, and now calls the model "GPT" rather than "the assistant." OpenAI says its models do not yet fully reflect the Spec, which describes where the company is heading rather than where it is.

Sam Altman spoke with Stripe co-founder John Collison on the Cheeky Pint podcast, in an episode titled "Why Sam Altman is against a single superintelligence." Altman said he would much rather have a trillion AIs of slightly superhuman intelligence join society than one AI with a trillion IQ. He argued that society is robust because many people keep each other in check and collaborate, and he now sees teams of agents checking and competing with each other as the more promising direction. On safety, he said sandboxing works up to a point and monitoring internal activations works further, but eventually you need real confidence the models are aligned with the people running them. He called something a million times smarter than us "strange."

Anthropic filed its S-1 on Monday and is marketing its mega-AI IPO into Thanksgiving. Its prospectus devotes 94 pages to risk factors, and its pitch leans on safety as a differentiator. OpenAI, with its own IPO expected next year, is pricing hard against Anthropic's margins and pitching a different philosophy of AI as many tools in many hands. On Tuesday, Americans vote in what has been called the first AI election. Axios reports a Democratic group is spending $4 million on ads in four swing districts in Wisconsin, Arizona, Pennsylvania and Michigan, targeting Republican incumbents who voted for a 10-year moratorium on state AI regulation that the Senate later stripped out 99 to 1.

Polls show AI is popular across Asia, Africa and Latin America and least liked in the US and Europe. Nearly nine in ten people in Nigeria and Vietnam expect AI to improve their lives, while in the US, Canada and France more people feel negatively than positively about AI's impact on humanity. Gallup ranks the US as the most concerned of 37 countries. The author argues that US voters and users will be won over one useful task at a time, and that closing the gap between today's best models and aspirations around AGI will likely take years longer than the labs suggest.

Articles.Title: AI: OpenAI’s ‘Trillion AIs’ Future, as Anthropic Goes Public. AI-RTZ #1257 - AI: Reset to Zero

stories.Headline: 3 ways dealers can protect themselves as AI speeds up hackers
stories.Summary:
Two critical flaws in PHP, the software behind much of the web, went from secret to widely discussed in recent weeks. The PHP team rushed out patches on Oct. 21 for both, nicknamed PHP2Shell and rated critical. Amazon had already spotted an attempt to exploit them four days earlier. Cloudflare saw attempts climb into the millions after the announcement, and federal agencies including the FBI and NSA urged organizations to fix them fast.

Many dealership websites rely on PHP, often run by outside vendors, and people tracking the issue say AI is shrinking the time dealers have to react. Ben Hadley, CEO of Auto Genius, said a dealer may never see the code but much of the customer experience can depend on it. Credit applications with Social Security numbers often run through systems such as Dealertrack or RouteOne, and basic lead forms collect names, emails, phone numbers and trade details. Hadley said WordPress, which runs on PHP and powers about 40% of websites, sits underneath some major dealership website platforms.

Adam Gillrie, founder of Savvy Dealer and BiFrost Strategies, said AI has sped up attacks enough to change the economics and dealers should look past the website itself. He said if a dealer only patches one thing it should be the ecosystem around the site, not the site, including plugins, third-party integrations and vendors with a login or data connection. Chris Hudson, general manager of Mark Miller Subaru in Utah, said his store pulls data through APIs and combines it in-house, and its AI tools search that copy rather than the DMS or CRM. Gillrie said each AI agent should get its own credentials with only the access it needs, and dealers should keep a record of everything the agent does.

Gillrie said dealers should skip a general security question and ask website vendors for an updated list of what the site runs, which items have known critical fixes and whether they were applied, a named contact and a patch timeline, and written assurance of security practices. He would now add a clock on patches and a breach-notification clause, saying assurance with no SLA and no notification duty is just a brochure. He said the first security fix is a people and process fix, not a software fix, and dealers should name one accountable vendor and get it in writing. Gillrie said the window between a flaw being found and being exploited is now days or less, and Hadley said most dealers should start by figuring out what they run, who owns it, and whether it has been patched.

Articles.Title: 3 ways dealers can protect themselves as AI speeds up hackers

stories.Headline: Mathematicians warn AI firms are keeping vital research in the field secret
stories.Summary:
Leading mathematicians met at the Royal Society in London last week, after OpenAI published solutions last month to 377 of the hardest mathematical problems, generated by its frontier AI models. The meeting followed warnings that powerful AI firms could dominate mathematics and keep knowledge secret. Martin Bridson, president of the Clay Mathematics Institute, said there was a longer-term fear that knowledge could be hoarded behind paywalls. He said the more immediate fear was access to the tools that generate that knowledge.

Bridson, a professor at the University of Oxford, said OpenAI and Anthropic have each committed $5m to a fund run by the Simons Foundation to give some researchers access to their models. He asked why they should decide who has access to these tools and on what basis. Terence Tao said Anthropic was paying mathematicians to formalise and write up solutions to problems solved by its frontier models, and that the company gets to pick who writes up the paper. Ana Caraiani of Imperial College London said no institution in Romania, her native country, was eligible to apply for access, and most countries are in that position. Martin Hairer, a Fields medal winner, said open-source models cannot compete with the frontier models, leaving a main tool for mathematical research under the control of two US companies.

Bridson said it was legitimate to keep some knowledge secret, such as work on breaking cryptographic encryption, and that intellectual property should be protected, but that fundamental knowledge being owned by entities who might hoard it was deeply objectionable. He said openness has not been the norm throughout history, citing the secretive Pythagorean sect, alchemists and Renaissance thinkers, and the disputes of Tartaglia and Newton, and that it is an important principle to maintain. Jon Keating, vice-president of the Royal Society, said AI offers to usher in a golden era of mathematics, but that the community needs claims set out carefully and fully, not obscured or hidden, to check and understand them. The Royal Society was founded partly to ensure science was open.

Articles.Title: Mathematicians warn AI firms are keeping vital research in the field secret

stories.Headline: Beyond Cost Cutting: Using Data and AI to Strengthen Healthcare Margins
stories.Summary:
Healthcare organizations across New England are under financial pressure from rising labor and supply costs, reimbursement limits, and the rising cost of care, according to the article. Earlier this year, Care New England eliminated more than 30 leadership and non-clinical positions because of ongoing financial pressures felt by hospitals and providers throughout Rhode Island. Care New England cited inadequate Medicaid reimbursement, rising labor and supply costs, and a growing need to provide uncompensated care. Those factors contributed to an estimated $20 million budget shortfall for fiscal 2026.

The article says improving financial performance cannot simply mean cutting costs, and organizations need greater visibility into what drives results and where efficiencies can be found. Most healthcare organizations hold large amounts of data across electronic health records, billing, payroll, scheduling, accounting systems, and spreadsheets, and viewing each system alone can leave management with an incomplete picture. When financial data is reviewed alongside patient volume, staffing hours, and overtime and scheduling data, management can determine whether labor variances stem from staffing levels, patient volume changes, or other operational factors. The article says AI can then help accelerate analysis, identify unusual trends, analyze revenue-cycle and denial data, summarize budget-to-actual variances, support forecasting, and automate repetitive administrative tasks.

The article says AI is not a substitute for good data, and its output is only as good as the data behind it. It says organizations with inconsistent accounting classifications, fragmented systems, or unreliable operational data will not solve those problems by adding an AI tool, and AI can magnify existing data-quality problems. It recommends starting with questions about the biggest drivers of financial performance, where financial visibility is weakest, what operational information would improve decisions, and how quickly it can be accessed. From there, organizations can connect relevant financial and operational data, set meaningful key performance indicators, improve reporting discipline, and then decide where automation or AI could add value.

The article says the advantage may not belong to the organization with the most data or the newest AI technology. It may belong to the organization that can turn existing information into insight, and that insight into action, faster. It also describes Citrin Cooperman's Healthcare Industry Practice as providing accounting, tax, and advisory services across the healthcare ecosystem, including providers, payors, and investors. The article does not say what happens next beyond those steps.

Articles.Title: Beyond Cost Cutting: Using Data and AI to Strengthen Healthcare Margins

stories.Headline: Load One AI Control Tower Transforms Expedited Freight Quoting
stories.Summary:
Load One, a Taylor, Michigan-based expedited trucking company ranked No. 148 on the CCJ Top 250, built its own artificial intelligence system in-house over the past several months, according to an article by Jason Cannon published November 1, 2026. The system is anchored by a centralized interface the company calls the AI Control Tower, which gives managers one screen to watch what its AI agents are doing across the business at any given time. The company launched its first AI agent in March and plans to end the year with nine. The article says Load One developed the tools itself rather than buying off-the-shelf software, so they could be tailored to expedited freight.

When a customer sends a rate request by email, an AI agent reads the message using a large language model, checks Load One's transportation management system, called Transcend, for available capacity, partner carrier bids and market density, and replies with a rate in about two seconds. Chad Tabor, president of Load One, said a fully human quote could take 5 to 20 minutes. As of late October, the agents were performing roughly 3,800 tasks a day that people had done earlier in the year. The billing compliance agent can process about 275 invoices in 15 minutes, and in its first week a load confirmation phone agent handled 1,381 dispatches at a cost of $131.49.

Tabor said the company designed the Control Tower as one screen a human can watch because AI works best with a person in the loop, and you do not want to let it run on its own without quality analysis. He said the agents still need a lot of oversight and that the goal is to protect the company's human capital, support staff and let the business scale without necessarily adding headcount. He said the automation only helps if an exception still lands with a person who can own the next decision for the customer. He also said that using AI to make people more powerful is the future of the trucking industry and that smart executives are figuring out how to do it.

The article says the Control Tower acts like an air traffic control center for freight, letting supervisors spot misquotes, monitor capacity limits and review confidence metrics before commitments are finalized. Supervisors can also generate instant AI summaries of long email threads with a single click. The article says deploying custom AI was streamlined because Load One had already spent years building its own software infrastructure. It does not say what further rollouts are planned beyond the target of nine agents by the end of the year.

stories.Headline: AI: What it will and won’t replace
stories.Summary:
Susan Rupe wrote in InsuranceNewsNet on November 1, 2026, that this month marks 14 years of her writing and developing content for the publication. She recalled that when she started, one big industry story was the rise of roboadvisors, automated asset-allocation systems. The question then was whether roboadvisors would replace professionals who give investment advice. Now, she wrote, artificial intelligence tools serve more like intelligent assistants that analyze retirement plans, summarize concerns, draft emails, identify coverage gaps and explain tax implications. The question again is whether these tools will replace humans in insurance and financial services.

Rayne Morgan’s featured article in the same issue answers that question with a resounding no, according to Rupe. The experts interviewed agree that AI will not replace networking and relationship-building, and agents who hope AI will magically generate high-quality prospects are likely to be disappointed. The best leads still come through trusted relationships, referrals and industry networks, and AI can support sales but is not a substitute for human trust. Rupe wrote that the biggest AI opportunity may be helping customers find agents, so improving online presence could let AI-powered search tools such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini direct consumers to them. She added that agents often jump straight to AI tools without first creating a clear sales plan, defining an ideal customer or establishing strong messaging, and that AI works best when it enhances a solid business strategy.

The issue also features Panos Leledakis, founder and CEO of IFAAcademy, an insurance futurist, an expert in virtual reality and a member of the NextGen Advisory Task Force at The American College. Rupe described him as an award-winning inventor of software for insurance needs analysis and an international public speaker with hundreds of hours on stages around the world. She wrote that Leledakis challenges the adage “adapt or die” and replaces it with “adapt and fly” as he teaches financial professionals how AI can take their practices to new heights. Rupe concluded that the human advantage remains irreplaceable, because insurance is still a relationship business and customers may be overwhelmed by information and options. That, she wrote, makes an advisor’s experience, judgment and personal guidance more valuable than ever.

Articles.Title: AI: What it will and won’t replace

stories.Headline: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Data centers that power AI models use large amounts of electricity, water and land, according to DW. The facilities run around the clock, and their cooling systems work continuously to keep the equipment from overheating. If data centers were a country, their electricity use would make them the 11th largest consumer in the world, researchers from the United Nations University said. ChatGPT alone handles more than 2.5 billion questions daily, and each one is processed in a warehouse full of servers somewhere in the world.

In Frankfurt, data centers use about 41% of the city's electricity, and the grid is so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. Data center electricity use is expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, roughly what Japan consumes in a year, according to the International Energy Agency. A 2024 study found that more than half of US data centers run on fossil fuels and emit more than 105 million tons of CO2. Utilities have delayed the retirement of 15 coal plants to meet demand, and those plants emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons of water a day, and about 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling evaporates.

The New York Post writer says he understands the concerns about data centers, which are noisy, ugly and can raise electricity prices, but he argues the right policy is to build them. He points to the UK, which he says chose to prioritize the environment and nice views over construction about 25 years ago. He says permission for a project in the UK is now harder to get than building it, and the planning application for the Lower Thames Crossing ran to nearly 360,000 pages and cost almost $400 million. He says a US moratorium would not stop AI development but would export it to the Gulf, China and beyond.

The DW article describes more efficient cooling methods, including immersion cooling and closed-loop systems that can cut freshwater use by up to 70%. It says some data centers capture waste heat and pipe it into nearby homes and businesses, which can reduce power demand by up to 30%. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can raise nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. In Hattersheim, Germany, an 18-acre parcel reserved for agriculture and groundwater protection was rezoned in 2024 for a five-building data center campus.

Articles.Title: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers

stories.Headline: At a birthplace of AI, pushback over using it for surveillance
stories.Summary:
MIT administrators considered adding AI capabilities to campus surveillance cameras to detect criminal activity, and faculty members objected. Since summer, professors have gone out once a week to decorate security cameras with colorful rhinestones and googly eyes. The decorations do not interfere with how the cameras work. Catherine D’Ignazio, an associate professor who specializes in urban science and data literacy, said they needed another way to have a more open and democratic dialogue about surveillance on campus.

MIT began installing new cameras in November to close gaps in security coverage, and about 4,600 cameras now watch the 168-acre campus. The school then explored hiring a surveillance technology company, Ambient.ai, to monitor the cameras in real time and alert officers to active threats or incidents. Faculty raised concerns about what could be done with the video data, the risks of misidentifying people, who would have access to the data, and a lack of community input. Some also questioned whether the technology would really make the campus safer.

Glen Shor, MIT’s executive vice president and treasurer, told faculty at a meeting on Oct. 21 that AI surveillance is no longer on the table. He told the Globe that MIT will not use AI in any way to observe or analyze campus activity, and that camera footage helps the MIT Police understand and resolve safety issues and incidents such as theft, vandalism, and property damage. Eric Lu, a fourth-year doctoral candidate in biological engineering and president of the Graduate Student Council, said MIT’s choices set a precedent for the broader community because when MIT speaks, people listen. The graduate student council sent a resolution to administrators calling for student input on any adoption of AI surveillance and research to justify its use.

MIT is arguably the birthplace of AI: in 1959, Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy founded what is now called the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. The mass shooting at Brown University last December, when a gunman killed two students on campus and later an MIT professor at his Brookline home, helped frame the role of larger surveillance on US campuses, and the shooter’s location was established in part with the help of a Flock camera in Providence. Brown expanded its camera network to about 1,950 by late August, according to a university report, and a spokesperson said the university had invested $65 million in campus safety since 2014. A review found limited camera coverage in the area of the shooting and said more cameras could have aided in identifying the shooter sooner, but it said additional cameras were unlikely to have prevented the attack.

Articles.Title: At a birthplace of AI, pushback over using it for surveillance
