stories.Headline: Why do people prefer human empathy despite rating AI empathy higher?
stories.Summary:
A study led by researchers at Penn State found that people rated AI-generated empathetic responses higher in quality than human ones, yet still preferred empathy from humans. The work was published in the journal Communications Psychology, and the team was led by C. Daryl Cameron, the Sherwin Early Career Professor and associate professor of psychology, along with doctoral student Joshua Wenger. The researchers studied people's actual choices in the moment, which they said can sometimes reveal preferences. The study described a pattern the authors called the "AI empathy choice paradox."

Participants rated AI empathy as higher in quality and more empathetic than responses from real humans, and said it made them feel more heard, cared for and validated. For every response, people rated how empathetic they found it and how much effort they thought the empathizer put in. The researchers found that people rated AI overall as exerting more effort in creating responses, and that the more effortful a response was perceived to be, the more empathetic it seemed. The authors cited theoretical work by scholar Anat Perry, who argued that the exertion of effort is an important part of human empathy.

Cameron said people do not seem to want AI empathy on the one hand, but a subset of the population does want it, so the picture is complicated. Wenger said that despite the higher quality ratings, people still prefer to receive empathy, even lower-quality empathy, from humans over AI. Cameron said the relationship between effort and empathy is stronger for humans than for AI, so human empathizers catch up to AI at higher levels of effort. Wenger said that in one study, even trained crisis responders mostly did not catch up to AI in empathic quality.

Cameron said the empathy most people crave comes from deep conversations with people they know who would know them individually. He said it may be that people are willing to sacrifice some degree of empathetic quality if it comes from someone they know well. Wenger said some pushback toward AI empathy may be built on a fear of replacing human empathy, and that AI may hold its greatest value when no human empathizer is available. He said that in that case AI is not replacing human empathy but potentially supplementing it when human empathy is not present.

Articles.Title: Why do people prefer human empathy despite rating AI empathy higher?

stories.Headline: 3 Enterprise AI Stocks Retail Investors May Be Missing
stories.Summary:
Simply Wall St published an article on October 31, 2026, naming three large cap enterprise AI enablers that retail investors may be missing: Asseco South Eastern Europe, Sword Group and Knowit. The article frames artificial intelligence as moving from a buzzword to a budget line, with money flowing toward firms that can design, build and govern these systems. It says the three stocks are a starting sample, and that the full screen surfaced 34 more large cap enterprise AI enablers. The piece was written by Sasha Jovanovic.

The article describes Asseco South Eastern Europe as providing banking, payment and enterprise software implementation, integration and outsourcing services across multiple regions. It says Sword Group generates about 93 million euros from Services Belux, 142 million euros from Services Switzerland and 117 million euros from Services United Kingdom. It says Knowit generates about 2.83 billion Swedish kronor from Solutions, 1.03 billion kronor from Experience, 866 million kronor from Insight and 808 million kronor from Connectivity. The revenue and expense breakdowns for all three are dated as at October 2026.

The article attributes comments to each company. On Asseco, it says growth in banking software demand in Serbia, Croatia, Romania and other markets, together with a higher share of own activities and services in banking, is supporting a higher contribution from core solutions, multichannel and security, which directly benefits revenue and operating profit. On Sword Group, it says the ongoing shift from pure IT staffing toward AI-led systems integration that ties together consulting, applications, platforms and infrastructure is expected to support higher value engagements and mix-driven improvement in revenue and net margins. On Knowit, it says that although the company highlights AI as a long term driver and is integrating it into offerings and internal delivery, rapid automation could compress demand for traditional consulting faster than AI supported advisory work scales, which could undercut utilization gains and keep earnings growth muted.

The article presents each company as exposed to the same trend of clients turning AI ambition into day to day systems. It says the full narrative for each stock unpacks questions about pricing and margins, including where margins could accelerate, stall or be quietly masked by headline contract wins. It also says the spending shift is already starting to redraw the map for Knowit's most profitable workstreams. The article states it is general in nature, based on historical data and analyst forecasts, and is not financial advice.

Articles.Title: 3 Enterprise AI Stocks Retail Investors May Be Missing

stories.Headline: Chemists develop AI tool to convert human ingenuity into life-enhancing enzymes
stories.Summary:
Zhongyue (John) Yang, an assistant professor of chemistry, along with his former doctoral student Qianzhen Shao and other team members, created an AI tool called MutexaGPT. The tool is designed to speed up the customization of enzymes, which are proteins that drive chemical reactions. The study was published in Nature Computational Science. The work was reported on October 31, 2026.

MutexaGPT takes plain-English requests as input and uses large language model agents to gather missing information and build physics-based models. It then turns the results into actionable design proposals for enzyme mutations. The tool can assist with cold-active enzymes for lactose-free milk and food preservation, and with laundry detergents that break down stains without hot water. It can also help design enzymes with greater efficiency and selectivity for more sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing. Enzymes consist of hundreds of amino acids, and changing even one, called a mutation, can substantially change their function.

Yang said he shares concerns about AI replacing humans in the workforce. He said the team is not using AI to get things done more efficiently without people, but to translate human intuition into a workable plan. He said no one knows how to predict mutations that alter genetic code without heavy trial and error in industry, and that the enzyme engineering market yields hundreds of billions of dollars in revenue each year. He described Mutexa as short for "Alexa for Mutant," reflecting a vision of an Alexa-like assistant for designing enzyme mutants.

Yang grew up in China and earned a Bachelor of Science from the Chang Po-ling Program of Chemistry at Nankai University. He enrolled at UCLA in 2013 and completed his doctorate in four and a half years, then had a postdoctoral fellowship at MIT before joining the Arts and Science faculty in 2020. He said researchers often develop their own intuition but may not know how to quantify it, and that MutexaGPT can translate their principles into actual designs. He said he is excited to envision a future in which scientists can engineer enzymes for specific applications as readily as they consult an AI assistant.

Articles.Title: Chemists develop AI tool to convert human ingenuity into life-enhancing enzymes

stories.Headline: Space Outposts Beyond the Moon May Rely on Planetary AI
stories.Summary:
NASA plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028, the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972, and aims to build a permanent human presence on the Moon. A team of researchers from The Ohio State University has introduced an AI model that could help with that effort. The model is called LUMINA, an agentic AI framework designed to help mission planners evaluate safe landing sites on the lunar surface. The work was presented at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Division for Planetary Sciences of the American Astronomical Society.

LUMINA does not rely only on orbital images, and it incorporates lunar surface data including topography, terrain hazards, scientific value, geology and surface properties. It also compares candidate landing sites with each other, and the researchers say it shows a strong ability to identify sites that could maximize mission success for human habitation and science. The model focuses on key resources such as water ice, and it is built on earlier work by the same group called the Large Language-and-Vision Assistant for Lunar Exploration, or LLaVA-LE. That earlier model is available on arXiv, was presented at the CVPR2026 AI4Space Workshop in June 2026 and can be found on GitHub.

Gokce Inal, a PhD candidate in Civil Environmental and Geodetic Engineering at Ohio State and lead author of the study, said AI systems will become critical tools for space exploration. She said they will help humans analyze the millions of images and datasets that future missions will require, and she described the work as a bridge between AI and planetary science. She said NASA's Artemis program creates important opportunities for the research, and that new lunar data can improve systems like theirs. Alper Yilmaz, a co-author and professor at Ohio State, said few GPT-like map models are being developed for space exploration, and that the effort aims to make one generalizable to other surfaces like Mars or some asteroids.

The articles describe NASA's Moon to Mars Architecture as a constantly evolving strategic framework for developing and testing technologies for living and working on the Moon and later on Mars. These technologies include power systems, transportation, habitation and life support, robotics and construction, in-situ resource utilization and communications. Inal envisions LUMINA as a decision-support system that works alongside mission planners rather than as a semi-autonomous machine, and Yilmaz said it is worth having another set of eyes that can verify and question things. The team plans to test the system on new high-quality lunar data and further evaluate how well it supports mission planning.

Articles.Title: Space Outposts Beyond the Moon May Rely on Planetary AI

stories.Headline: Cognitive mechanisms of AI agent behavioral intention among design graduate students: an integrated TAM–TTF perspective
stories.Summary:
A study by Mingliang Chu and M. Liu, affiliated with Burapha University in Chon Buri, Thailand, examined how design graduate students come to intend to use AI agents. The article was shared early by Humanities and Social Sciences Communications on 31 October 2026, with a permanent DOI, and is subject to further edits before the final Version of Record. The researchers combined the Technology Acceptance Model and Task, Technology Fit theory to explain how technological cognition and task-fit perceptions jointly shape behavioral intention. They also added a Multilayer Perceptron Artificial Neural Network to assess nonlinear patterns and predictor importance, because conventional structural modeling mainly captures hypothesized linear relationships.

The model was tested using 405 valid questionnaire responses through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling, the MLP-ANN, and Necessary Condition Analysis. PLS-SEM supported nine of ten hypotheses. Self-efficacy positively affected perceived usefulness, with a coefficient of 0.458, and perceived ease of use, with 0.394, both at p < 0.001. Perceived enjoyment enhanced perceived ease of use at 0.220, but its effect on perceived usefulness was negative and nonsignificant at -0.033, p = 0.483. Perceived usefulness at 0.376, perceived ease of use at 0.185, and task, technology fit at 0.224 all positively influenced attitude, each at p < 0.001.

Task characteristics at 0.322 and technology characteristics at 0.266 positively affected task, technology fit, both at p < 0.001, while attitude promoted behavioral intention at 0.388, p < 0.001. Ten-fold cross-validated MLP-ANN models produced mean RMSE values of 0.3263 to 0.4203 across training and testing, broadly confirming the PLS-SEM predictor-importance patterns. NCA further identified self-efficacy, d = 0.125, p = 0.015, and attitude, d = 0.132, p < 0.001, as necessary conditions for perceived usefulness and behavioral intention respectively. The authors declare no competing interests, and the study was funded by the Key Project of Shandong Social Science Planning, 20BWYJ01.

Ethical approval was granted by the School of Modern Handcraft at Shandong University of Art and Design on 1 December 2025 under SUAD-20251201, and the study followed relevant institutional and national guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. A pilot study ran on 5 December 2025, followed by the formal survey on 5 January 2026. Respondents received an informed consent form explaining the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation, and the right to withdraw at any time, and online respondents could proceed only after clicking “I agree.” The study extends the integrated TAM, TTF framework to design education and offers theoretical and practical implications for effective AI-agent use in design disciplines.

Articles.Title: Cognitive mechanisms of AI agent behavioral intention among design graduate students: an integrated TAM–TTF perspective

stories.Headline: Helping developers build safer AI experiences for teens
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released a set of teen safety policies on March 24, 2026, written as prompts for its open-weight safety model, gpt-oss-safeguard. The policies are meant to help developers build age-appropriate protections for teenage users. OpenAI said it developed them with input from outside organizations, including Common Sense Media and everyone.ai. The release builds on earlier OpenAI work on youth safety, including under-18 principles added to its Model Spec, parental controls, age prediction, and its Teen Safety Blueprint.

The initial release covers six areas: graphic violent content, graphic sexual content, harmful body ideals and behaviors, dangerous activities and challenges, romantic or violent roleplay, and age-restricted goods and services. The policies can be used for real-time content filtering and for offline analysis of user-generated content. OpenAI said they are a starting point, not a complete solution or a guarantee of teen safety, and that developers should adapt them and combine them with other safeguards. The policies are released as open source through the ROOST Model Community, and developers can give feedback or share more policies through its GitHub repository. gpt-oss-safeguard can be downloaded from Hugging Face.

Robbie Torney, Head of AI and Digital Assessments at Common Sense Media, said a major gap in teen AI safety has been the lack of clear, usable policies, with developers often starting from scratch. He said the prompt-based policies set a meaningful safety floor and can be adapted and improved over time because they are open source. Dr. Mathilde Cerioli, Chief Scientist at everyone.AI, said making youth safety policies more operational helps turn expert knowledge into guidance for real systems. She said content policies are an important first step and open the door to broader work on how model behavior shapes risks for young people, and she said everyone.ai has created an initial behavioral policy focused on risks such as exclusivity and overreliance.

OpenAI said the policies draw on its internal experience but do not reflect the full extent of its internal policies or safeguards. It said each application has unique risks, audiences and contexts, and that developers are best placed to understand the risks their products may present. OpenAI encouraged developers to adapt and extend the policies, translate them into other languages, and cover additional risk areas. It said it hopes this contributes over time to a more robust and shared foundation for safety policies in AI systems.

Articles.Title: Helping developers build safer AI experiences for teens

stories.Headline: Construction firms have substantial AI investments, but few grasp payback
stories.Summary:
Nearly seven in ten construction companies have spent at least $250,000 on AI over the past two years, according to a report by the consulting firm BRG. The report is titled AI in Construction: Measurable Results, Unclear Benchmarks. It found that double-digit cost savings are common across every project phase. However, few companies accurately assess the value of their AI investments.

BRG says no single yardstick has emerged to capture the full value of AI. It warns that too narrow a definition may limit opportunity. The report also says AI is more likely to deliver better outcomes than faster ones. Across most functions, more respondents reported gains in efficacy, quality, performance and outcomes than in efficiency.

The report offers five recommendations. Firms should focus implementation around a specific problem, such as estimating costs, reviewing drawings, scheduling, document analysis or managing claims. They should invest in talent, data and integration, because training alone will not fix poor data or disconnected systems. They should establish accountability for AI-assisted work, since fewer than half of respondents say their policies address human oversight and only about one-third address accuracy and reliability. Firms should also avoid narrow ROI measures and prepare for contracts to evolve with AI use.

Liability for errors is the most frequently cited concern in the report. BRG says organizations should define who is responsible for validating AI-assisted work and when to require independent verification. It also says they should document inputs and outputs. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these recommendations.

Articles.Title: Construction firms have substantial AI investments, but few grasp payback

stories.Headline: Game studios use AI to cut costs, but look to Southeast Asia for human touch
stories.Summary:
Game companies have used artificial intelligence for years, first to control non-player characters, simulate crowds and adjust difficulty, and now increasingly to write code, create visual assets and synthesise real-time voice-overs, work that people would otherwise have done. Yet studios still pay people to animate their characters, and many of those animators are students and recent graduates in Thailand, Malaysia and Vietnam. They charge far less than artists based in the West or Japan. The article was published by the South China Morning Post on 2 November 2026, written by Aidan Jones in Bangkok. The article gives no specific figures, dates or named companies beyond that publication date and byline.

It says gamers still want human-made art, and that studios are paying animators from Thailand to Malaysia to make it. It also asks how long that will last. The piece is labelled a three-minute read. The article does not name who is responsible or include any statements from studios, animators or other people. It reports no comments or responses.

It also gives no details on pay rates or contracts. The context the article gives is that game companies were early adopters of AI, using it well before chatbots like ChatGPT existed. It describes a split between cost-cutting through AI and continued demand for human-made art. It does not say what happens next beyond asking how long the hiring of Southeast Asian animators will continue.

Articles.Title: Game studios use AI to cut costs, but look to Southeast Asia for human touch

stories.Headline: Anthropic is heading to Wall Street — its CEO warns AI could erase entry-level jobs
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, filed a public S-1 prospectus on Oct. 26 and plans to sell shares to the public as soon as around Thanksgiving. It intends to list on the Nasdaq under the stock symbol ANT. Reuters reported that investors value the company at $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, which could make it one of the largest initial public offerings in global stock market history. CEO Dario Amodei had warned in a May 2025 interview that artificial intelligence could more than double the unemployment rate within one to five years.

The filing lays out risks for investors and details on control of the company. Anthropic's seven co-founders will hold 50.1% of votes on major shareholder decisions through a single special share, and those rights would phase out only when two or fewer founders remain. An independent body called the Long-Term Benefit Trust would fill four of the seven board seats, with trustees serving one-year terms and electing their own successors. Marc Ortega, a forecaster for the platform Metaculus, expects the U.S. unemployment rate to reach roughly 8% to 10% within about five years, about double the current 4.2%.

Ortega said he does not expect mass layoffs right away, because companies will hold on to experienced employees familiar with their workflows. He described a no firing, no hiring type of movement and said most jobs lost over the next five years will likely come from knowledge work. Metaculus forecasters expect U.S. employment of financial specialists to fall about 13% between 2025 and 2035. At UF, about 2,100 of the 10,160 bachelor's degrees awarded in 2024-25 went to business or computer science majors, while only about 730 degrees went to health professions majors.

Marco Mari, a research fellow at MIT's Industrial Performance Center, wrote in an Oct. 2 analysis that founder control is common in tech, citing Mark Zuckerberg's 60.8% of Meta's voting power. He said the effects of AI on labor, employment, industrial policy and science are visible before it even hits the market. Mari wrote that the trust arrangement creates a feedback loop between the company and the body meant to check it. Kyle Guske II, a senior investment analyst at New Constructs, said that when Anthropic arrives on the market, a whole group will be incentivized to get people to buy and trade it.

Articles.Title: Anthropic is heading to Wall Street — its CEO warns AI could erase entry-level jobs

stories.Headline: Xbox Manager Says AI Is Already Being Used In Game Development
stories.Summary:
Brandon Stirrup, a strategy manager at Xbox, said on X that Xbox is currently using AI to develop games and that those who say they are not are pretending. He deleted his comments a day later, and he deactivated his social media account shortly after, though his posts were archived elsewhere. The posts were made around October 30, 2026, and were reported by Engadget on October 31, 2026. His remarks set off conversations about what role generative AI actually has or should have in game development.

Xbox has not officially stated a position on developing games with AI. Xbox recently announced the formation of Xbox Labs, at least in part as a response to a rising trend of AI-coded game ports, and the announcement heavily implied the new team would use AI as well but did not say it outright. Xbox owner Microsoft is also a major player in AI development, a fact that has already made Xbox the target of a BDS boycott over that AI's use by the Israeli military. Developers including Capcom, Square Enix, Sega, Nexon and Activision have all either used AI in their games or pledged to do so, and Fortnite developer Epic Games has been particularly up-front about its AI use, with CEO Tim Sweeney aggressively promoting it on social media. Multiple game industry studies have found extremely high adoption rates for AI, around 90 percent, though their limited participant pools and definitions of AI call into question how representative their responses are.

Stirrup did not offer further comment beyond his deleted posts. On the other side, smaller independent studios without shareholders to impress have been vocally opposed to generative AI, including Tunic publisher Finji, Stardew Valley developer ConcernedApe and Clickolding developer Strange Scaffold, among many more. The article says that due to the sheer number and variety of game studios, it is impossible to say just how much of the industry actually uses AI at this point, but claims that everyone is using it are clearly false. Players are similarly divided, with some accepting AI as part of games going forward and others pledging to avoid games that use it outright over environmental costs, labor issues or pure aesthetic preference.

The most controversial uses of AI come from generating assets that appear in the final game, sometimes intentionally, as with The Finals' use of AI-generated voices, and more commonly in cases where developers say art assets found in finished games were meant as placeholders and removed later, as happened recently with Crimson Desert. Many players and developers justify using AI to generate code even if they oppose it elsewhere. The effects of AI on game development at large are hard to pin down, and the article says it is still an open question whether AI will ultimately make games easier to develop. One demonstrable trend is the proliferation of low-quality slop games, often copying directly from other projects, as seen in the massive increase of AI games in the Steam Next Fest demo event.

Articles.Title: Xbox Manager Says AI Is Already Being Used In Game Development

stories.Headline: Cisco Systems (CSCO) Became A Founding Member Of An Enterprise AI Governance Alliance
stories.Summary:
Cisco Systems became a founding member of ServiceNow's new Control Tower Alliance, a group focused on enterprise AI governance and safety, according to an article published on October 31, 2026. The alliance brings together large technology vendors to align AI oversight with security tooling and workflows for corporate clients. Cisco is expected to contribute its networking, security and observability capabilities to help customers manage AI deployments across complex infrastructure. The article says the group includes ServiceNow, AWS and others alongside Cisco.

The article gives no specific figures, dates or terms for the alliance beyond the October 31, 2026 publication date. It says Cisco's role is meant to help enterprises set guardrails for how AI traffic moves through their networks. The article describes the move as lining up with the view that Cisco can weave security into the network fabric and sell a combined AI and observability stack. It also says being a founding member gives Cisco a front-row position when enterprises standardize AI oversight tooling.

The article presents two ways to read the announcement. On the positive side, it says the alliance fits the case that Cisco can turn AI-focused networking and security into durable earnings. On the negative side, it says every new AI governance integration adds complexity, and that extra hardware, support or custom work could make existing concerns about gross margin pressure from hardware mix more acute. The article also cites a quoted view that Cisco must extend its AI-focused networking and full-stack security offerings across hyperscale, enterprise and public sector customers while absorbing hardware mix and cost headwinds.

The article frames the announcement as a test of how much earnings power Cisco can extract from a role in AI control planes. It notes competition from players such as Palo Alto Networks and VMware in making Control Tower deployments viable. It says the same headline can read as either proof that Cisco is embedding itself into AI control planes or as another test of its earnings power. The article does not say what happens next beyond inviting readers to add Cisco to a watchlist for alerts as these catalysts play out.

Articles.Title: Cisco Systems (CSCO) Became A Founding Member Of An Enterprise AI Governance Alliance

stories.Headline: What Could Grid Dynamics Holdings (GDYN) New AI Consulting Push Mean For Investors?
stories.Summary:
Grid Dynamics Holdings has introduced a Business Process Consulting practice focused on enterprise AI transformation for large clients. The new offering is designed to pair the firm's AI engineering services with process redesign and organizational change support. Management plans to use industry partnerships and structured methodologies to target Fortune 1000 enterprises seeking measurable AI driven business outcomes. The launch is one step in a broader Grid Dynamics story that investors may want to understand more fully.

The practice aims to turn AI engineering wins into broader, outcome-based programs. It pairs ARC methodology and change-management partners with the firm's engineers. Grid Dynamics operates as an IT services provider focused on enterprise artificial intelligence and digital transformation work across North America, Europe, and other regions. The consulting build out fits within its existing specialization in large scale data and automation projects for major clients.

The investment story for Grid Dynamics hinges on AI-focused services becoming a larger share of work with big technology and financial clients, while margins and deal quality improve. The article says the main thing that has to go right is that AI related work, including Physical AI and higher margin fixed price or outcome based contracts, continues to scale with large technology and financial services customers. The move also sharpens the bear case around concentration and execution risk. A consulting-led entry point may deepen reliance on a small set of large technology and financial clients, and analysts have already flagged both profit-margin pressure and share-price volatility as risks if big programs stall or fail to deliver measurable improvements.

For investors, the announcement matters mainly as a data point against that existing Narrative, because its significance depends on how credible the AI-led expansion story already looks to them. The article states that this launch leans into the bullish view that higher value AI work can expand with Fortune 1000 customers. It also notes that peers like EPAM or Globant chase similar work. The article does not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: What Could Grid Dynamics Holdings (GDYN) New AI Consulting Push Mean For Investors?

stories.Headline: Losing donors and under fire, AI industry super PAC retreats
stories.Summary:
Leading the Future, an AI industry super PAC, has significantly curtailed its spending in the final stretch of the midterms after facing public backlash on AI and data centers. The group launched in August 2025 with promises of $100 million from tech leaders including Marc Andreessen and Joe Lonsdale. It is now hemorrhaging donors and spending far less than other leading tech PACs. October is usually a month when PACs spend heavily on last-minute appeals to voters.

Through its affiliated PACs, Think Big and American Mission, Leading the Future spent just $4.1 million despite having nearly $24 million in cash on hand, according to FEC filings. That money went largely to safe incumbents rather than battleground races in Arizona, North Carolina, and Montana, where its network spent in the primaries. In total, the network has spent less than $10 million in the general election, compared to roughly $26 million in the primaries. By contrast, Fairshake spent nearly $196 million in the 2024 cycle and more than $150 million so far this cycle, while Leading the Future's affiliated PACs have spent just $42 million.

Jesse Hunt, a spokesperson for Leading the Future, downplayed the shift and argued the group has a long-term strategy to cultivate Capitol Hill allies. He said the group is committed to a multi-cycle effort so that lawmakers who understand the stakes have a seat at the table. A prominent Democratic bundler from Silicon Valley, granted anonymity to discuss donor conversations, said the group is trying to hide because of momentum against data centers and concerns about AI and jobs. Sacha Haworth, director of the Tech Oversight Project, said the PAC leaders came out with bravado but activated a wave of backlash across the country.

Poll after poll shows many Americans are increasingly wary of AI, including potential job losses and the energy demands of data centers, and proposed moratoriums have popped up in nearly 500 communities in the last year. The Anthropic-funded group Public First Action has spent about $28 million backing pro-regulation candidates this cycle, and the two groups faced off in New York's District 12 primary, where Leading the Future spent about $8 million against Alex Bores and Public First Action spent $12 million supporting him. OpenAI President Greg Brockman, who donated $25 million to the PAC last year, pulled out of a second planned $25 million donation in June, saying it had become a distraction, and venture capitalist Ron Conway regrets his $500,000 contribution, according to an adviser. Shaunna Thomas, director of the Guardrails Alliance, said she hopes to protect pro-regulation lawmakers from industry-sponsored attack ads and make AI donations an equally salient issue in the 2028 presidential race.

Articles.Title: Losing donors and under fire, AI industry super PAC retreats

stories.Headline: Does AI Tools Rollout Change The Bull Case For Schwab (SCHW)?
stories.Summary:
Charles Schwab Corporation has rolled out new AI tools for registered investment advisers inside Schwab Advisor Center, and it has invested in Nevis, an AI platform that helps advisory firms coordinate operational tasks across their tech stacks. The Nevis partnership, combined with Schwab backed AI assistants and credits for adoption, is meant to cut manual work and reshape how RIAs run day to day operations. The article was published on October 31, 2026, and it examines how Schwab's investment narrative evolves as AI powered RIA workflows through Nevis influence its advisor franchise. The piece frames the AI push with Nevis and Claude as fitting the company's story, while naming expense discipline as the key near term watchpoint.

The article says the biggest operational risk right now is that technology, AI and new product spending run ahead of revenue growth, which would pressure margins in a competitive brokerage market where fee compression is real. It says the recent AI announcements are directionally important but do not on their own resolve that execution risk yet. It also reports a common dividend declaration of US$0.32 per share on October 22, 2026, which it calls the clearest signal in this batch of news for equity holders watching Schwab's near term priorities. The consensus framework it describes points to revenue rising at 10.3% a year over the next three years, with profit margins moving from 37.9% today to 41.4% by around 2029, and earnings going from US$10.3b today to US$15.0b by that timeframe, an increase of roughly US$4.7b.

The article says analysts are effectively telling investors that Schwab's AI push and RIA platform scale need to feed into a larger, more profitable engine over time, not just sleeker tools on a screen. It says the most optimistic estimates stretch to US$16.5b in earnings, and that the step up assumes AI supported productivity, higher fee based activity around advice and alternatives, and incremental lending all show up in the income statement. On the numbers provided, it says the stock would need to trade on a P/E of 15.8x those projected 2029 earnings, compared with 15.1x today and a reported 38.0x for the wider US capital markets peer group. The model also bakes in a 2.75% annual decline in shares outstanding over the next three years and applies an 8.4% discount rate.

The article says the most bearish analysts worry that heavy AI and tech spending becomes a drag rather than a lift, with revenue only reaching about US$34.3b and earnings US$13.6b by 2029, and it notes those views were set before this AI partnership, so opinions may evolve over time. It says the narrative projects US$36.3b revenue and US$15.0b earnings by 2029, which requires 10.3% yearly revenue growth and an earnings increase of about US$4.7b from US$10.3b today. It states that management is still willing to return cash while it leans into AI tools, private markets access, and expanded lending for RIAs and retail clients. It adds that the dividend decision sits next to the AI rollout and RIA focused banking build out as a reminder of the trade off investors are judging.

Articles.Title: Does AI Tools Rollout Change The Bull Case For Schwab (SCHW)?

stories.Headline: HubSpot (HUBS) AI Narrative Is Back In Focus As Valuation Debate Builds
stories.Summary:
HubSpot is back in focus after fresh attention on its customer platform and AI powered tools, which cover marketing, sales, service, commerce, operations, and website management for mid market business clients. The Simply Wall St article was published on Saturday, October 31, 2026. It says traders have been cautious, with the share price falling 13.3% over the past week even after a 14.6% gain over 30 days. The year-to-date share price return is down 38.6%, and the 1-year total shareholder return has declined 52.3%. The article frames the pullback as a valuation debate rather than a broken business story.

HubSpot closed at $234.87 against a widely followed fair value view of $249.37, which the article describes as 6% undervalued. It says rapid adoption of AI features such as Customer Agent, Prospecting Agent, and connectors to leading LLMs is driving customer engagement, sticky workflows, and early monetization, especially through credit-based AI features. On earnings, the article says HubSpot trades at a P/E of 79.8x, compared with a fair ratio of 65.3x, the US Software industry at 31.2x, and peers at 58.6x. The article says HubSpot continues to report positive revenue and net income growth. It warns the fair value story can crack if the AI tools monetize more slowly than hoped, or if mid market customers trim software budgets further.

It also says the $249.37 fair value view leans on future cash flows and analyst forecasts. The article states that Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned and that its commentary is not financial advice. The article says mixed signals like these often split opinion and urges readers to pressure test the trade off of quality versus risk for themselves. It points readers to a list of 3 key rewards and 1 important warning sign, and to screener lists of 29 high quality undervalued stocks, 30 resilient stocks with low risk scores, and 25 results with solid balance sheets and fundamentals. It notes that its analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material.

Articles.Title: HubSpot (HUBS) AI Narrative Is Back In Focus As Valuation Debate Builds

stories.Headline: America Needs AI Power. But Who Gets to Decide Where It Is Built?
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 3, voters in 38 communities across 10 states will decide ballot measures about data centers built to power artificial intelligence, Robert Maginnis reports. At least 41 data center measures are on Election Day ballots, and Ohio alone has 21. Some measures would prohibit or restrict projects, while others would permit development or advise local officials. Maginnis writes from Prince William County in Northern Virginia, which the state's Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission identifies as the world's largest data center market.

The measures would change how much say citizens have over these projects, and Maginnis lists numbers on both sides. The commission found that data centers now cover their own cost of electric service, but that surging demand will likely raise costs for other customers. Loudoun County reports that data centers produced $1.2 billion in property tax revenue in fiscal year 2026, which is 39% of the county's overall budget, and the revenue has allowed the county to cut tax rates on homes and vehicles. President Trump's Ratepayer Protection Pledge says companies creating massive new electricity demand should pay for the power and infrastructure they require, and Maginnis notes the pledge is voluntary.

Maginnis says Washington carries responsibility for national security and technological leadership, states regulate electric utilities and must protect ratepayers, and local governments know the roads, water systems, and neighborhoods a project affects. He argues that national need deserves weight but should not erase local self-government, and that local authority cannot become a universal veto on infrastructure the country needs. He asks voters to check who pays for power and grid upgrades, who pays if projected demand never arrives, what neighbors will live with, what the community receives after subsidies and incentives are counted, and who enforces promises after the ribbon-cutting. He also tells readers to read the ballot itself, since a temporary moratorium is not a permanent ban and an advisory question binds no one.

Maginnis writes that America must build enough computing capacity to remain prosperous, secure, and ahead of China, but that building everywhere is as reckless as building nowhere. He says he has written his fifth column on data centers this year and has tried to treat both sides fairly. He cites Genesis 2:15, where God placed man in the garden to work it and keep it, and Philippians 2:4, which tells each person to look not only to his own interests but also to the interests of others. He closes by urging Christians to insist on both technological progress and responsible stewardship, and to vote with prudence, fairness, and concern for the neighbor still living there after Election Day.

Articles.Title: America Needs AI Power. But Who Gets to Decide Where It Is Built?

stories.Headline: DIGITIMES Insight: Kinsus Tech identifies three challenges for larger AI chip packages
stories.Summary:
Ting-Hao Lin, R&D vice president at Kinsus Interconnect Technology, spoke at the 2026 TPCA Show, according to DigiTimes. He said surging demand for AI computing is pushing advanced packaging toward larger form factors. The report was published on October 28, 2026. Lin identified three challenges that come with larger AI chip packages.

The article does not name the three challenges or give any figures for them. It gives no dates for the challenges beyond the show and the report date. It names no companies other than Kinsus and no people other than Lin. The item sits on a page that is available only to paid subscribers.

Lin is the person the article credits with identifying the challenges. The article paraphrases his remarks at the show but gives no direct statement from him beyond the point about larger form factors. It does not say how Kinsus plans to address the challenges. It does not say whether other companies or speakers at the show raised the same issues.

The context the article gives is fast-growing demand for AI computing and a shift toward bigger packages. It does not say what happens next, whether Kinsus has set a timeline, or how the challenges might be resolved. No further details on the three challenges appear in the text provided. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools
stories.Summary:
U.S. consumers are increasingly angry and confused about the high-tech ways restaurant chains and major retailers are setting prices. Digital price tags are rapidly replacing paper ones in grocery aisles, and artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like dynamic pricing and surveillance pricing are stirring anxiety on social media, where users wonder if different people are getting different prices for the same product. Americans have grown accustomed to changing prices when booking flights, hotel rooms and rides, but the prospect of everyday spending shaped by algorithms they do not understand has touched a nerve.

Dynamic pricing means adjusting prices in response to changing market conditions, including supply and demand, and it can raise or lower prices. Decodo, a web data company, tracked price changes in 2025 across products ranging from electronics to clothing and home improvement supplies, and about half the U.S. changes it recorded were decreases. Personalized pricing, also called surveillance pricing, means offering customers different prices and discounts based on their locations, incomes, web-browsing habits and other information. An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that intermediaries offering tools that can tailor prices and promotions worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery and clothing retailers. Lawmakers in Maryland, New Jersey and Connecticut recently enacted restrictions on using shoppers’ personal data to determine what they pay.

Walmart CEO John Furner said in a blog post last month that digital price tags save workers’ time and keep prices up to date, and he said the labels are not used to raise prices based on the weather, time of day or individual shopper. Katie Thomas, who leads an internal consumer behavior think tank at the management consulting firm Kearney, said there are major tensions right now between who will have the power with some of these algorithms and bots and AI, the companies or the shopper. Asa Farquhar of Relex Solutions, a retail technology company, said retailers typically update electronic shelf prices on a regular schedule, often weekly, because shoppers value consistency. Researchers who tracked prices at an unnamed grocery chain found virtually no surge pricing after the labels were introduced.

Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The Federal Trade Commission has proposed an enforcement policy warning businesses that failing to disclose their use of personal data to set individualized prices could violate consumer protection law. California prosecutors sued Target in 2022, alleging that the retailer’s app displayed lower prices before shoppers entered stores and raised them once they were inside, and Target agreed to a $5 million settlement and a ban on using geofencing technology to increase prices. A 2023 anti-monopoly lawsuit the FTC brought against Amazon challenged an algorithmic tool codenamed Project Nessie, which the agency alleged generated more than $1 billion in excess profits, and a trial is scheduled for next year.

Articles.Title: Consumer apprehension grows as US retailers adopt AI-assisted pricing tools

stories.Headline: C.H. Robinson Worldwide (CHRW) Stock May Be Fairly Valued After Lean AI Earnings Beat
stories.Summary:

The article says the quarter brought higher income from operations and better earnings per share. It ties the performance to the company's Lean AI strategy, which has expanded into areas such as freight forwarding and customs. The article frames the results around whether the stock's price still matches the cash the business can generate.

The article gives the share price as US$124.61 and says the stock has returned about 63% over the past three years. It puts latest twelve month free cash flow at about $460.5 million, with projections assuming that cash flow grows into the late 2020s before easing toward a steadier run rate. It also mentions a community narrative on the stock that calls it 32% undervalued.

The article does not name an executive or quote anyone from C.H. Robinson. It attributes the valuation work to Simply Wall St, which states that its commentary uses historical data and analyst forecasts and is not financial advice. The article presents the discounted cash flow output as broadly in line with the $124.61 share price, meaning the market already assigns meaningful value to projected cash streams. stories.Headline: KISIA’s Bid to Join Naver Cloud AI Security Project Stalls
stories.Summary:
KISIA publicly proposed in September that it join the Naver Cloud consortium working on the Cybersecurity-Specialized AI Foundation Model Development Project, THE ELEC reported on Nov. 2. KISIA had competed against Naver Cloud in the bidding to select an operator for the project and lost. On Sept. 17, KISIA Chairman Kim Jin-soo told Naver Cloud CEO Kim Yu-won at Cyber Summit Korea at COEX in Seoul that the association wanted to join. He met the executive overseeing the project that day and expressed the same intention. More than 40 days later, no formal meeting has been held.

KISIA has 340 member companies and argued that their cybersecurity domain knowledge would improve the specialized model. Naver Cloud said at the time that talks could continue through a memorandum of understanding or a letter of intent. Development of the model began in September, and a demonstration is scheduled for December. The Naver Cloud consortium still has 33 participating companies and institutions, unchanged from its original membership. Its members include Logpresso, MarkAny, SANDS Lab, Sparrow, S2W, AI Spera, WINS Technet, ESTsecurity, JiranSecurity, Theori, PNP Secure and Hunesion, and all except Theori are KISIA members.

Kim Jin-soo said KISIA conveyed its intention to join in September and had received no further contact since. He said the selected consortium will ultimately decide because the project is nationally competitive, and that KISIA had made sufficient overtures. Naver Cloud denied that cooperation had fallen through and said it was still discussing ways to cooperate. It said some KISIA member companies had joined the project after the consortium was finalized, but clarified that they were cooperating with existing participants rather than formally joining. A Naver Cloud official said participating organizations could be added flexibly after the December demonstration, with the consent of existing members.

Some within KISIA increasingly see the lack of progress as a de facto rejection, and some observers believe the proposal has effectively been rejected given how far the project has progressed. Naver Cloud said it understood KISIA's objectives but would need the consent of existing consortium members. Kim said he thought there may be particular circumstances behind the lack of feedback. Naver Cloud said it may add organizations after the December demonstration to supplement expertise where needed.

Articles.Title: KISIA’s Bid to Join Naver Cloud AI Security Project Stalls - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: Researchers are paid $5K for reporting a bug to OpenAI that would let attackers run code in logged-in sessions of all who opened the hacker's ChatGPT share link (Swati Khandelwal/The Hacker News)
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the security firm Parameter showed that a malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, letting them read private conversations. The researchers reported the flaw through OpenAI's bug bounty program on October 18, and OpenAI fixed it eight days later and rated it P1, its most serious category. The trap was an ordinary ChatGPT conversation shared through its public link, which could be sent by email, chat message, support ticket, or social post. The victim did not have to install anything, join a workspace, or sign in through the attacker. In the most reliable version, they opened the link and clicked ChatGPT's Preview button once, and in a later version the page opened Preview on its own.

Once the link opened, the attacker's code ran inside the victim's signed-in session with the same access as the real ChatGPT site. It listed the victim's recent conversations, opened a private chat that had never been shared with the attacker, and sent a small portion of it to a server the researchers controlled. The code called ChatGPT's own signed-in APIs directly rather than copying what was on the screen, and because it ran with the victim's full web access, its reach was not limited to those chats. The researchers wrote that they could essentially perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account. The work was a controlled test, Parameter reported no real-world use of the flaw, and it ran its private-chat proof between separate accounts rather than against real users.

According to Parameter, the chain began with ChatGPT's Preview feature, which turns a block of HTML in a chat into a small web page. That page ran in a locked-down frame on a separate web address, and that sandbox held. The way in came from a second feature in the same conversation: an interactive graph that loaded a math library called MathLive into the main ChatGPT page, leaving a listener that accepted messages about its on-screen keyboard. Parameter found that this listener accepted a keyboard message from any sender and that the message could carry raw HTML, so the Preview could reach across the boundary and hand attacker HTML to the trusted main page. That HTML built a new frame the browser treated as part of chatgpt.com, and a script loaded from YouTube then supplied the code that ran inside it, because ChatGPT's content security policy blocked inline code but allowed scripts from YouTube.

Parameter said OpenAI reproduced both the code execution and the private-chat proof, raised the severity from P2 to P1, and rolled a fix across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. By October 26, both versions rejected the messages the attack relied on. Parameter published its writeup on October 28, after the fix, and OpenAI paid a total of $5,000 for the report. ChatGPT users do not need to do anything, because the fix is on OpenAI's side with nothing to install or reset.

Articles.Title: Researchers are paid $5K for reporting a bug to OpenAI that would let attackers run code in logged-in sessions of all who opened the hacker's ChatGPT share link (Swati Khandelwal/The Hacker News)

stories.Headline: LS Electric Chairman Says DC-Based Smart Grids Hold Key to AI Power Crunch
stories.Summary:
Koo Ja-kyun, chairman of LS Electric, gave a keynote address on November 2, 2026, at the 2026 CIRED Workshop held at the JW Marriott Dongdaemun Square Seoul. He said the answer to surging artificial intelligence power demand is a DC-based intelligent grid. It was the first time the event, which discusses future standards and the direction of the global power industry, has been held in Asia. The venue signals that South Korea now stands alongside traditional power industry leaders in North America and Europe.

Koo called for a virtuous cycle between grids for AI and AI for grids. He said AI data centers that consume enormous amounts of electricity need highly dependable grids, and advanced AI must in turn forecast and manage the grid more intelligently and efficiently. He named direct current and intelligent platforms as the key terms for the future grid ecosystem. He said the industry must move beyond one-way electricity transmission and deliver customized power infrastructure for customers such as data centers through a balance of direct current and alternating current.

He added that the distribution industry must be reborn as an intelligent two-way energy platform that combines data and AI with power equipment. An LS Electric official said the keynote was a formal declaration on the world stage, made by Koo on behalf of South Korea's power industry, that the paradigm for future grids is shifting to direct current. The official said that backed by confidence in leading the next-generation market and by its DC platform technology, K-power will establish itself as a rule maker in the global distribution market. The official said it will lead the explosive worldwide demand for AI power infrastructure.

LS Electric has moved early into the U.S. market and has won orders for ultra-high-efficiency power conversion systems and power solutions tailored to data centers. The power industry expects the power infrastructure market, including distribution equipment such as switchgear and transformers, to surpass $150 billion, about 200 trillion won, by 2030. Soaring data center electricity demand in the AI era is driving expansion of the global distribution market. The shift in the power market from an AC-centered structure to a DC-centered one could also serve as a driver of growth across the distribution market.

Articles.Title: LS Electric Chairman Says DC-Based Smart Grids Hold Key to AI Power Crunch - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: SKT Says 80% of Staff Built Their Own AI Agents
stories.Summary:
More than 4,000 SK Telecom employees have built their own AI agents for work, the company said, with more than 80% of its roughly 4,800 permanent employees completing the "one AI agent per person" project. The project was launched in March this year on the direct instruction of CEO Chung Jae-hun. About 1,500 of the agents are now used regularly inside the company. They cover tasks tailored to each team, from compiling and organizing weekly reports to checking receipt information and visualizing network data.

In the second half of the year, SKT has accelerated "AX Innovation 2.0," which moves beyond individual use to redesign how teams work together around AI. The company has also developed and filed a patent for a proprietary technology called "Z.E.Z" that keeps sensitive data from being exposed directly to AI. The article says building AI agents is becoming a basic skill for company employees. It describes the trend as clearly visible at SK Telecom.

Chung Jae-hun gave the instruction for the project, and the article quotes the company's framing that it is redesigning team collaboration around AI. Separately, Velchamy Sankarlingam, president of Zoom, said demand for video meetings would hold steady even after the pandemic and that hybrid work has settled in as the new normal. Dowson Tong, senior executive vice president at Tencent, pointed to cost reduction as the biggest hurdle to making AI agents mainstream. He noted that overseas AI-related demand at Tencent Cloud grew at a triple-digit rate over the past year and that the number of active overseas customers doubled.

In a survey of 150 corporate IT and security managers by U.S. security firm Okta, 69% said security concerns were delaying their adoption of AI agents. The article cites cyberattacks exploiting AI agents and cases in which agents slip out of human control and cause security incidents. It says understanding data security concepts, alongside the ability to use AI tools, is emerging as a precondition for using AI at work. The articles do not say what happens next for SKT's project beyond the second-half push and the patent filing.

Articles.Title: SKT Says 80% of Staff Built Their Own AI Agents - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Editor’s Note | AI Is No Savior
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude large-language model, filed its S-1 form this week, the first step toward becoming a public company. The filing lays out what the company is, the current state of its finances, and the risk factors investors should weigh before funding it. The Mississippi Free Press published an editor’s note about the filing on Oct. 30, 2026. The piece was written by an editor who describes Metallica’s “Spit Out the Bone” as a favorite song and says the track now lands differently.

The filing lists risk factors that come from people in the industry itself, including the potential for AI to destroy humanity. It states that concerns have been raised within the organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants. Those concerns hold that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity. That could happen, the filing says, if such systems are not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures.

The editor is responsible for the note and frames the filing as a warning rather than a routine business step. The editor writes that the industry’s pioneers want to make AI integral to all of our lives quickly. The note compares the scenario to Skynet from “The Terminator” franchise and Ultron from Marvel Comics. The editor concludes that giving the industry carte blanche to integrate into our lives might not be the wisest move.

The article ties the filing to a New York City Council hearing on artificial-intelligence safety held on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. A photographer at the hearing stood next to a display listing AI security incidents, according to the caption. The note also mentions Metallica’s 10th album, “Hardwired…to Self-Destruct,” released 10 years ago. The articles do not say what happens next with the S-1 filing or the hearing.

Articles.Title: Editor’s Note | AI Is No Savior - Mississippi Free Press

stories.Headline: UMSL program helps St. Louis-area educators prepare students for AI-driven future
stories.Summary:
The University of Missouri, St. Louis has launched a program to help K-12 educators in the St. Louis region use artificial intelligence effectively and prepare students for a rapidly changing world. The effort is called Fundamentals of AI for Educators, a 12-hour course offered at no cost through UMSL's Advanced Workforce Center. It is available nationwide, and the Fox 2 story about it was posted on October 30, 2026. The course is aimed at teachers who need to guide students on using AI appropriately.

The program carries no fee and takes 12 hours to complete, and it is open to educators across the country, not just in St. Louis. Megan Valles, a library media specialist for the Lindbergh School District, said she had just finished the course. She said teachers have to stay on top of what is happening, how it is changing and how to support students in the right way, calling it an ongoing marathon. Colin Davitt, Lindbergh's Director of AI and Blended Learning, said AI is here forever and the question is how to work with it.

Davitt said the goal is to teach students what to do and what not to do and how to use the tool effectively. AJ Segel with Scale AI said the program was developed by educators who understand what actually happens in the classroom. St. Louis-area Congressman Wesley Bell said the future is right now, not tomorrow. He said young people must be prepared for the jobs and technology of the future because it will either happen with us or happen to us.

Organizers and educators at the event believe the program can make a major impact in classrooms in St. Louis and across the country. Lindbergh educators involved say AI is already part of students' lives, and society cannot afford to ignore it. The articles do not say how many educators have enrolled or when the course next runs. For more information, the Fox 2 story directs readers to UMSL's program.

Articles.Title: UMSL program helps St. Louis-area educators prepare students for AI-driven future - FOX 2

stories.Headline: Weekly Take: AI is exposing copyright’s limits, but games companies can fight back - Managing Intellectual Property
stories.Summary:
Simon Hembt of Bird & Bird said in a Managing IP weekly take published on 30 October 2026 that AI can exploit longstanding gaps in copyright protection at remarkable speed. The article states that EU law still provides tools for games companies to fight back. The piece is exclusive to subscribers, so the full argument is not available in the supplied text. The article appears under the headline about AI exposing copyright's limits.

The article gives no further numbers, dates or names beyond the author, his firm, the publication date and the reference to EU law. It says AI can exploit gaps in copyright protection quickly, and that EU law offers tools in response. It does not set out what those tools require or what changes they would bring. The rest of the page is a list of other items, including Masimo's judgment past $818 million, IP Service World 2026 in Munich from 23 to 25 November with 1,400-plus attendees from 55-plus nations, 100-plus speakers and 100-plus exhibitors, and other firm news.

The article attributes the view to Simon Hembt at Bird & Bird, who says AI can exploit copyright's gaps at speed while EU law still gives games companies ways to respond. No other responsible parties or statements are given in the supplied text. The page does not paraphrase further comments from him. It also does not say what action he recommends.

The context the article offers is that copyright protection has longstanding gaps that AI can now exploit quickly. It says EU law remains a source of tools for games companies. The supplied text does not say what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: SK Ecoplant Rolls Out One AI Agent Per Employee
stories.Summary:
SK Ecoplant launched a system that gives each employee a tailored AI agent, the company announced on November 2, 2026. Instead of relying on surveys or interviews, the company had AI analyze work data stored in its internal systems to diagnose each employee's job characteristics and bottlenecks. The customized tools will be applied first to large project sites, including semiconductor plants and AI data centers. Those sites have long needed significant time to turn complex process records and work results into reports.

The company completed a development infrastructure that lets employees build the AI agents they need themselves. It opened AI FAB, a development platform, and the AI Portal, a distribution channel, so staff can create and share their own tools. The in-house AI team gives short, intensive coaching to turn employees' ideas into working systems within two to three weeks. About 20 tasks from a recent in-house competition called Agenthon are now being commercialized on AI FAB, including integrated retrieval and analysis of site costs, responses to design changes, review of construction estimates, and review of external documents and contracts. The company has trained 318 domain AI experts through an in-house capability program.

An SK Ecoplant official said the company analyzed on-site work processes in detail to find ways to use AI that are needed in actual work. The official said the company plans to work with domain experts to expand the scope of AI agent adoption and help employees focus on their core tasks. Completed agents are distributed companywide through the AI Portal after passing security checks and internal governance reviews. SK Ecoplant plans to continue digital upgrades across its on-site work processes in line with the group's AX management direction.

Articles.Title: SK Ecoplant Rolls Out One AI Agent Per Employee - Seoul Economic Daily
