stories.Headline: AI, Lean, and the Future of Formal Verification, with Lean Creator Leo de Moura
stories.Summary:
Leo de Moura, creator of Lean, VP and Distinguished Scientist at AWS, and Chief Architect of the Lean Focused Research Organization, spoke with Ben Lorica on the podcast about AI and formal verification. Lean is both a programming language and a theorem prover, and its proofs are machine-checked. To trust a result proved with Lean, you need to trust only the kernel, where the proof is checked. Lean has more than one checker, and two of them are now verified, with a third coming soon.

The conversation covered several examples and numbers. Kim Morrison ported zlib, a compression library, to Lean and proved that compressing and then decompressing data returns the data without loss. Aeneas is a tool that verifies Rust code using Lean, and the SymCrypt team at Microsoft uses Aeneas plus Lean to verify its crypto library. The human-built Lean mathematical library Mathlib has 2.5 million lines and took 10 years to build. There are now published Lean proofs of 50 million lines, and the Fermat's Last Theorem proof written by Anthropic AI is 13 million lines.

De Moura said AI is now fully capable of writing code that satisfies stated properties and proving it in Lean. He said that when AI builds a model of your program in Lean, there is always the question of whether the model is faithful to your code, and some people use differential testing to find discrepancies. He said he sees this happening incrementally, citing the Claude Code main developer Boris, who asked Claude to check Claude Code for bugs using Lean, and Claude found real bugs and filed pull requests that Boris merged. De Moura said Boris noted he does not even know Lean. De Moura said this works reasonably well for bug finding, but to say there are no bugs you have to check that the model is accurate and keep it in sync.

De Moura said that if someone had told him last year that AI could build a Lean model of code in any language, he would have said it was science fiction. He said the frontier models became capable of this on their own, without involvement from the Lean side. He said he expects people to focus much more on specifications, models, and the properties they want software to have in the next few months and years. On Navier-Stokes, he said a human-curated statement of the problem already existed before OpenAI directed the models, so there was no doubt the statement was correctly formalized. He said there is some controversy because OpenAI presented an informal proof in natural language and a formal proof in Lean.

Articles.Title: AI, Lean, and the Future of Formal Verification, with Lean Creator Leo de Moura

stories.Headline: Greece's AI Strategy: How DAEDALUS and PHAROS Could Shape Its Future
stories.Summary:
Greece’s DAEDALUS supercomputer was inaugurated in Lavrion on 19 October 2026, according to EuroHPC and GRNET. EuroHPC launched the tender in June 2024 and announced the signed contract with Hewlett Packard Enterprise on 28 March 2025. In June 2026 the system appeared in the TOP500 ranking, while EuroHPC still described wider European availability as forthcoming. The October inauguration is a further milestone, and the article says procurement, contractual commitment, benchmark performance and public inauguration should remain distinct in the record.

At inauguration, EuroHPC reported sustained performance of 85.69 petaflops and peak performance of 115 petaflops. The system uses HPE infrastructure and more than 2,000 NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips. The acquisition cost was €36 million, with 35% funded by EuroHPC and 65% through the EU-financed Greece 2.0 recovery plan. Cyprus, Montenegro and North Macedonia also participate in the consortium, and access is jointly managed by EuroHPC and the DAEDALUS consortium in proportion to investment.

DAEDALUS is operated by GRNET within an international arrangement. The article says the machine’s location does not give every Greek institution unrestricted or immediate access, so ministries, universities and firms need to understand allocation routes, eligibility conditions and support arrangements. It adds that hardware from HPE and NVIDIA ties parts of the system’s operation and renewal to those suppliers. The policy response should concern support continuity, staff competence and credible options for future workloads, the article says.

PHAROS describes its purpose as connecting academia, industry and the public sector through computing infrastructure, services and expertise. It identifies health, culture and language, and sustainability as priority domains. The article proposes four indicators for judging progress: published access and utilisation records, completed projects reporting task-specific results including failures and costs, repeated use by public bodies and firms, and staff retention and maintained software. It says Greece can develop a meaningful role as a location for selected AI applications and regional collaboration if it converts the new infrastructure into dependable institutional capability.

Articles.Title: Greece's AI Strategy: How DAEDALUS and PHAROS Could Shape Its Future - HackerNoon

stories.Headline: How to Secure AI-Generated Code Across an Enterprise SDLC
stories.Summary:
The article is a guide to securing AI-generated code across an enterprise software development lifecycle, published by DevOps.com on October 27, 2026 and written by Anastasios Arampatzis. It reports that AI coding assistants produce code faster than teams can review it, and that people who accept the output often cannot judge its security. It cites Aikido's 2026 State of AI in Security and Development report, which found that 1 in 5 respondents had experienced a serious incident linked to AI-generated code. It also cites a 2021 study by Pearce et al. in which roughly 40% of 1,689 programs produced by GitHub Copilot contained the targeted weakness.

The article lists four main risks and the checks for each. On invented package names, it cites a 2026 test of five frontier models that still made up nonexistent packages in roughly 5% of cases, and it recommends checking every package at install time and holding back versions published in the previous 48 hours. On leaked secrets, it cites GitGuardian's State of Secrets Sprawl 2025 report, which found a 6.4% leakage rate in public repositories using AI assistants compared with 4.6% overall, and it recommends a pre-commit hook plus a server-side backstop. On agents bypassing checks, it recommends connecting scanning to the agent environment and gating every pull request with a mandatory scan of the branch diff. On broken access control, it recommends functional access control tests, including cross-user and cross-tenant checks.

On responsibility, the article says enterprises must assign an owner to each check, or the checks stall in a backlog or disappear. It cites Aikido's 2026 State of AI in Pentesting report, which found that only a third of security teams hold both the authority to stop a release and responsibility for the outcome. It says security tools must record who overrode a block, why, and where a finding was raised, so auditors have a reliable record. It also says over half of respondents to that report said logic flaws, broken access control and multi-step vulnerabilities are always or often missed in manual testing, rising to 92% among teams shipping daily or faster.

The article describes the pull request as the final point where security findings match the exact code about to merge. It says autonomous agents often rewrite code before delayed scan results arrive, so scheduled scans alone are not enough. It recommends layering context-aware AI and agentic code reviews on top of the pull request gate. The article does not say what happens next beyond these recommendations.

Articles.Title: How to Secure AI-Generated Code Across an Enterprise SDLC - DevOps.com

stories.Headline: Hatch Center announces lineup of contributors to 2026 Policy Review on Copyright, AI, and American Innovation
stories.Summary:
The Orrin G. Hatch Foundation announced on October 30, 2026, the contributors to the seventh volume of its annual Hatch Center Policy Review. The volume is titled "The Future of Creativity: Copyright, AI, and American Innovation." U.S. Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri will write the introduction. The publication is scheduled for release in early January 2027.

The volume will include essays by eight named contributors. They are Senator Hawley, U.S. Representative Ben Cline of Virginia, Shira Perlmutter, Maria A. Pallante, Karyn A. Temple, Mitch Glazier, Tracey Armstrong, and Michael D. Smith. Three of them, Perlmutter, Pallante, and Temple, are current or former Registers of Copyrights. The essays will examine copyright law and artificial intelligence from legal, economic, and policy perspectives.

The foundation said the contributors represent institutions and industries central to the future of American creativity. Hawley is a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee and chairs its Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism. Cline sits on the House Judiciary subcommittee on courts, intellectual property, artificial intelligence, and the internet, and co-chairs the Congressional Songwriters Caucus. The foundation said the volume reflects the legacy of the late Senator Orrin G. Hatch, who helped shape the nation's intellectual property laws during more than four decades in the Senate.

The foundation said artificial intelligence is changing how creative works are produced, distributed, and consumed. It said policymakers face questions about using copyrighted works to train generative AI systems and about ownership, licensing, compensation, and protection of human creativity. The foundation said the volume builds on its longstanding commitment to discussion of complex public policy challenges. The articles do not say what happens after the release.

Articles.Title: Hatch Center announces lineup of contributors to 2026 Policy Review on Copyright, AI, and American Innovation - Utah Policy

stories.Headline: Black Duck Adds AI Agent to Triage and Fix Vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Black Duck this week added an artificial intelligence agent to its portfolio that triages vulnerabilities and then generates and validates fixes for DevSecOps teams to review before applying them. The agent is called Signal Agentic Fix. Patrick Carey, vice president of product marketing for Black Duck, described how it works. The company announced the addition in an article published on October 30, 2026.

The agent uses Black Duck's static application security testing and software composition analysis engines to find vulnerabilities in proprietary code and open source dependencies. It then validates any fixes the agent generates. Fixes can be generated using AI models made available by Black Duck or a supported model that DevSecOps teams prefer to invoke. Rules can be configured to define what the agent is allowed or required to fix and how to do it, and those rules can also set coding and compliance standards the agent must follow. Any generated fix is rescanned to confirm it does not introduce new defects or vulnerabilities.

Carey said the goal is to make it simpler to reduce a growing backlog of vulnerabilities requiring remediation as AI models are increasingly used to discover them. He said the only way to burn down that backlog will be to rely more on AI and automation. He noted that AI now enables cybercriminals to reverse engineer a vulnerability and create an exploit in a matter of minutes. He said AI agents provide the additional headcount needed to scan and review code faster, whether it was created by a human or another AI agent. Signal Agentic Fix follows Black Duck's introduction of its AI Fix Pull Requests capability earlier this year, and the company expects to add more AI agents for threat analysis, penetration testing and, longer term, other aspects of software supply chain security.

Mitch Ashley, vice president and practice lead for software lifecycle engineering at the Futurum Group, noted that the bottleneck in application security has moved from finding vulnerabilities to fixing them, and AI is speeding up both discovery and exploitation. He said Black Duck checks every AI-generated fix with the same scanners that found the flaw, which gives teams evidence to review before anything ships. He noted that the configurable rules matter more than the model because they determine what the agent is allowed to change. He said the next test is whether teams apply those rules where code is written, so flaws never reach the backlog. The article says it is not clear to what degree DevSecOps teams are revisiting existing workflows to better secure applications in the AI era, but given the rate at which vulnerabilities are being discovered, it is now more a question of when rather than if.

Articles.Title: Black Duck Adds AI Agent to Triage and Fix Vulnerabilities - DevOps.com

stories.Headline: Nearly 1 in 3 District and School Leaders Skip AI for Operations. Here’s What the Rest Do - Education Week
stories.Summary:
A nationally representative survey of 852 educators, including 262 district and school leaders, asked administrators which business or operational purposes their school or district uses generative AI for. The EdWeek Research Center conducted the survey between Aug. 26 and Oct. 6 of this year. Nearly one-third of respondents said they do not use AI for any school or district operational purposes. Among those who do use it, the top five answers were school or district communications, foreign-language translation, strategic planning, employee evaluation, and class scheduling.

Ronn Nozoe, the CEO of the National Principals Association, said the results did not surprise him and matched what he hears and has seen across the country. He said the big issue is making sure school leaders protect student privacy, so he was not surprised that much of the operational use of AI is about communications. Krestin Bahr, the superintendent of Peninsula school district in Washington state and a member of the AASA executive team, said she is not hearing a lot of conversation among district leaders about using AI in operations. She said their focus has been on the screen time debate, getting resources for teachers to receive professional development about the technology, and ensuring students' safety and privacy.

Nozoe and Bahr both said a challenge in unlocking AI's potential for operations is that there are not always employees who know how to use the technology effectively. In the Peninsula district, Bahr has made AI a priority, giving her staff time and training opportunities to learn the technology, especially AI agents. The district uses AI for routing efficiencies, optimizing enrollment reporting, and analyzing substitute teacher rates. Bahr said the intent is to optimize when you can and to use tools so the district can be ahead of the curve with problems instead of being reactive.

Nozoe said the absence of national guidelines might also be slowing down the uptake of AI in school operations. He said not everybody has to do the exact same thing, but there should be some national guidelines that everybody knows. From there, he said, schools and districts can adjust accordingly based on their particular context. Otherwise, he said, everybody is iterating on their own, and that is probably not the best use of everyone's time.

Articles.Title: Nearly 1 in 3 District and School Leaders Skip AI for Operations. Here’s What the Rest Do - Education Week

stories.Headline: Deep fakes on screen: what the EU's new AI labelling rules mean for sport, media and entertainment
stories.Summary:
The EU AI Act's rules on labelling deep fakes have applied since 2 August 2026. They require production companies, rights holders and others who deploy AI systems to generate content to disclose when that content is a deep fake. The Act defines a deep fake as AI-generated or manipulated content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear authentic or truthful. The rules can catch any business anywhere in the world that uses AI to generate content it foresees being disseminated in the EU, including by posting it online.

The Act requires disclosures to be clear, distinguishable and accessible, including to vulnerable groups such as children and persons with disabilities, at the latest when someone first sees the content. It does not set the form of the label, but the voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content, approved as adequate by the Commission and the AI Board, says signatories should use an icon or label at the start of content and at regular intervals where possible, and after breaks such as ad breaks at a minimum. The default position is somewhere clear of other on-screen graphics, for example the top right corner. Evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works get a lighter-touch approach, such as notes or opening or closing credits, but the disclosure must be noticeable without the viewer doing anything, and sports content will rarely qualify as creative or fictional.

The obligation falls on the deployer, which the Guidelines describe as the party with authority over the decision to use AI and how it is used, and which does not need technical control. Businesses that only passively disseminate content, which can include broadcasters, are not deployers, though they are encouraged to preserve labels applied by others. A production company is typically the deployer, a broadcaster or platform that directs or signs off the AI use may also be a deployer, and rights holders and federations distributing direct via OTT or social channels are plainly deployers, including those outside the EU. For live real-time graphics the host broadcaster or the production entity commissioning them will usually be the deployer, even where an outside vendor develops or operates the tools.

The Guidelines expect deployers to make sure their labels survive distribution, including through contractual conditions with distribution partners. Commissioning and licensing agreements should therefore cover who assesses each asset, which label is used, where it sits, who preserves it downstream and who bears the risk. Fines can reach 15 million euros or 3% of global turnover, whichever is higher. A label does not cure other potential liabilities, and IP, image, personality and data protection rights always need to be considered when generating deep fakes.

Articles.Title: Deep fakes on screen: what the EU's new AI labelling rules mean for sport, media and entertainment - Lewis Silkin

stories.Headline: Nvidia to prop up British AI giant as data centre boom unwinds
stories.Summary:
Nvidia is reportedly in talks to provide financial backing for a new flagship US data centre being built by the British AI company Nscale, which Anthropic plans to use. The support would take the form of credit backing to cover the construction and electricity costs of the complex in West Virginia, which will be equipped with Nvidia chips. The discussions were first reported by The Information. Nscale and Nvidia were both contacted for comment.

The backing would give Nscale a boost after Microsoft pulled out of a separate agreement for a major data centre in Essex. Microsoft, one of Nscale's two largest customers, had been set to become the anchor tenant at Nscale's first UK data centre as part of a wider pledge to invest £22bn in the UK. The Telegraph revealed this month that Microsoft had withdrawn from the project, which has faced delays and is now in limbo. The decision has cast a shadow over Nscale's plans to list on the New York Stock Exchange in a flotation worth up to $35bn, or £26bn.

Nscale was founded by Australian entrepreneur Josh Payne, a former coal miner, and has appointed Sheryl Sandberg and Sir Nick Clegg, both former Facebook executives, to its board. The company has been privately valued at $15bn, and a stock-market float could make it one of Britain's most valuable AI firms. Nvidia is already an investor in Nscale. Investors such as Michael Burry, who was depicted in the film The Big Short, have warned about an AI bubble and the threat of a market crash.

The talks come amid wider concerns about whether AI infrastructure businesses will deliver sufficient returns. Australian rival Firmus cancelled plans for a $30bn initial public offering earlier this month, citing market conditions, while neocloud companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius have seen their shares and bonds slump. Soaring interest rates have driven up the cost of debt-funded AI infrastructure projects. The success of Nscale's listing will be seen as a critical test of investors' appetite for debt-fuelled AI businesses.

Articles.Title: Nvidia to prop up British AI giant as data centre boom unwinds - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: BE Stock Recovers After 10% Selloff: Morgan Stanley Says Crusoe Project Pause Does Not Break AI Power Thesis
stories.Summary:
Bloom Energy shares fell nearly 10% on Wednesday after Crusoe announced it had paused a data center project in Wyoming at the request of its customer. The project was expected to be powered by a mix of Bloom Energy's fuel cells and grid electricity. The stock then recovered in the overnight session and edged more than 1% higher at the time of writing. Crusoe was working with Blackstone-backed energy company Tallgrass to develop a 1.8-gigawatt campus in Cheyenne, Wyoming, for an undisclosed tenant.

The project had planned to deploy 900 megawatts of behind-the-meter fuel cells from Bloom Energy, in addition to grid power. Crusoe said in a statement on Tuesday that at the request of its customer it had paused its development activities on the site. Morgan Stanley said the paused project represented approximately $2.65 billion in revenue potential for Bloom Energy. The analyst said that amount had been allocated from the 1-gigawatt master supply agreement signed with AEP in December 2024.

Morgan Stanley said it remains optimistic about Bloom's overall bullish thesis despite the pause. The analyst said it believes contractual protections within Bloom's agreement should help safeguard earnings over the planned delivery period. Morgan Stanley maintained its Overweight rating and $310 price target on the stock. RBC Capital also reiterated its Outperform rating and $335 price target on Bloom Energy.

Morgan Stanley maintained its confidence in Bloom's full-year and longer-term outlook. Retail sentiment around BE stock remained in bearish territory amid high message volumes at the time of writing, according to Stocktwits. One user said the stock was totally oversold and pointed to a massive backlog, expecting another great quarter in July. The company's shares have surged 137.34% so far this year.

Articles.Title: BE Stock Recovers After 10% Selloff: Morgan Stanley Says Crusoe Project Pause Does Not Break AI Power Thesis - Stocktwits

stories.Headline: Pope Leo says AI ‘must be disarmed’ ahead of weapons talks
stories.Summary:
Pope Leo XIV called on Friday for artificial intelligence to be “disarmed,” urging governments meeting in Geneva in November to take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons systems. He made the call in a post on X, saying the future of AI is not pre-determined and depends on the people who develop, deploy and regulate it. He said decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must always remain under effective, informed and responsible human oversight. He also said machines are tools, not persons, and rejected proposals to grant such systems rights or legal personhood.

The pope’s intervention comes ahead of international discussions in Geneva over lethal autonomous weapons, which are systems that can identify and attack targets without human control. In a joint statement in August, UN Secretary-General António Guterres and Mirjana Spoljaric, president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, renewed a call made three years earlier for specific prohibitions and restrictions on autonomous weapon systems. They said the risks have intensified and that the world is dangerously close to crossing a moral red line, the autonomous targeting of humans by machines. They said the Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in November offers the clearest path for states to decide to negotiate a legally binding instrument.

Leo also called for AI to be developed for the common good rather than mainly for a privileged minority, and for international oversight so that AI decisions can be examined, challenged and met with remedies for harm. He said the decisive question is not simply what AI can do but what purpose it should serve. He has raised similar concerns before, warning at UNESCO in Paris in September that AI could become an instrument of domination, and in June 2025 that it could be misused for selfish gain or to foment conflict. He recalled that Pope Francis told G7 leaders in 2024 that a machine should never be entrusted with the decision to take a human life.

The warnings come amid alarm inside the AI industry. Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who previously worked at OpenAI, resigned in September and accused both companies of racing toward self-improving superintelligence. Anthropic said it has been transparent about AI’s benefits and risks and maintains strong safeguards, while OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman has backed calls to slow frontier development and warned AI could go very badly if humanity loses control of the future to it. President Donald Trump has taken a more optimistic view, signing an executive order in September directing executive-branch agencies to use “super intelligence” and “SI” instead of “artificial intelligence” and “AI” in official communications. Newsweek said it reached out to the United Nations and the White House by email on Saturday.

Articles.Title: Pope Leo says AI ‘must be disarmed’ ahead of weapons talks - Newsweek

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Expands AI Cloud Footprint With Denmark Data Center — Plans Global Network Expansion Across 4 Continents
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave said it has brought most of its planned 22.5 megawatts of computing capacity online at its DEN01 data center in Copenhagen, which is operated with a company called North and is the firm's first deployment in Denmark. The facility runs Nvidia Blackwell systems and high-speed networking to handle demanding AI workloads. The announcement came on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, and CoreWeave stock was trading about 1% higher in premarket. Separately, in India, E2E Networks said on October 26 that it plans to add roughly 5.4 megawatts of capacity to meet rising demand for AI computing.

The Copenhagen site lifts CoreWeave's European footprint to nine data centers across five geographies, and it has an agreement to send surplus heat to a local district heating network. CoreWeave is also building what it calls the first global AI backbone network, designed for petabit-scale transfers of large datasets between regions. New connection points are planned in the United Arab Emirates, India, Indonesia, Singapore, Australia, Korea and Japan, with deployment starting later in the fourth quarter of 2026 and a complete network loop targeted for mid-2027. As of June 30, the company ran 51 data centers with more than 1.5 gigawatts of active power, and its contracted power reached about 4.2 gigawatts as of August 11. E2E Networks' addition would build on its existing capacity of about 9.2 megawatts and is meant to host Nvidia HGX B300 systems and other Blackwell GPUs.

CoreWeave Chief Operating Officer Sachin Jain said customers increasingly need reliable computing capacity and infrastructure that lets them move data and workloads wherever their business requires. E2E Networks said the build-out will follow its infrastructure deployment plan and expected demand for AI services. It has not given a fixed investment amount or a completion date, and it expects to fund the work through a mix of internal accruals and debt. Its shares rose 5% to ₹594.35 on October 26, up from a previous close of ₹566.05, though the report noted the announcement alone does not establish the cause of the rise.

The CoreWeave news follows a rough stretch for its shares, which are down nearly 70% from the all-time high reached in June 2025 and down over 30% so far this year. UBS said its 37% October decline reflected weaker investor confidence in AI infrastructure providers and a move toward defensive investments, and cut its price target to $105 from $120 while keeping a Buy rating. Morgan Stanley lowered its target to $70 from $99 with an Equal Weight rating, calling CoreWeave the speed and scale leader among specialized AI cloud providers. The firm warned, however, that financing uncertainty clouds the company's ability to deploy contracted capacity and eventually reach eight gigawatts of active capacity. The network rollout is the next milestone to watch, beginning later this quarter.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave Expands AI Cloud Footprint With Denmark Data Center — Plans Global Network Expansion Across 4 Continents - Yahoo Finance

stories.Headline: Cover Story: The Global Tech Selloff Tests the Economics Behind AI Boom
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, a San Francisco-based AI model developer, published its preliminary prospectus on Oct. 26, 2026, nearly five months after confidentially submitting a draft to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on June 1, 2026. The filing gave battered global technology shares a temporary lift, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rising 2.82%, Japan's Nikkei 225 up 1.73% and South Korea's Kospi up 3.09%. The lift interrupted two severe selloffs in July and October 2026 that erased hundreds of billions from the AI supply chain. Losses were steep: Nvidia surrendered more than $200 billion from its $5.43 trillion peak, SK Hynix tumbled over 50%, CoreWeave shed over $35 billion, and Hong Kong-listed Zhipu AI and MiniMax fell more than 80% from their peaks, with MiniMax sinking below its HK$165 offer price.

Anthropic's planned offering could raise tens of billions near a $100 billion valuation. CoreWeave's revenue surged sevenfold to $1.9 billion in 2024, with 62% from Microsoft, but filings showed about $51.6 billion in total debt and lease obligations against only $5 billion in equity. Its second-quarter operating cash flow of $679 million fell far short of $9.4 billion in adjusted capex, and Bernstein estimated $76 billion in additional outside capital is needed. Hyperscalers also increased spending sharply: Alphabet spent $51.4 billion, Amazon $77.3 billion (up 120%) and Microsoft nearly $116 billion (up 80%). Meta posted negative third-quarter free cash flow of $2.12 billion and unveiled a $35 billion equity offering on Oct. 26.

JPMorgan strategist Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou said October's downturn showed no floor, with dip-buyers absent, corporate buybacks scaled back and lean short positions precluding short-covering rallies. GF Securities' Kuang Shi attributed the decline to capital flows and sentiment rather than deteriorating fundamentals, noting investors now scrutinize capex sustainability, ARR at Anthropic and OpenAI, and commercially viable enterprise applications. LSEG characterized Nvidia's more than $50 billion in commitments across model developers, neocloud operators and optical suppliers as an interconnected network obscuring end-user demand, and Nomura likened the capex race to a prisoner's dilemma. On Oct. 27, Nvidia announced a $3 billion investment in new Meta equity.

In Hong Kong, 116 debuts in the first nine months raised HK$387.9 billion, up 76% year on year, but by September four out of five mid-month debutants broke offer prices, and more than 380 companies were awaiting listing hearings. Foreign funds logged HK$15.9 billion in net outflows in early October. Physical bottlenecks compounded financial risks: NEXTDC cut A$140 million from fiscal 2027 guidance after grid delays and its stock plunged 41.7%, Thailand suspended 49 data centers, and Microsoft terminated its Nscale agreement in the UK. Moonshot AI confidentially submitted a Hong Kong application and DeepSeek is preparing for Shanghai's STAR Market, while robotics startups faced skepticism, with Leju Robotics suspending its Shenzhen IPO review and Fine Motion withdrawing its Shanghai application.

Articles.Title: Cover Story: The Global Tech Selloff Tests the Economics Behind AI Boom - Caixin Global

stories.Headline: China Focus: AI drives digital transformation in China's primary care - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China is introducing AI-powered tools in community health centers to speed up the digital transformation of grassroots healthcare, improve primary care, expand equitable access and enhance public well-being. AI assistants that support voice-based consultations, automated medical records, medication-risk screening, follow-up reminders and health education are appearing in community health centers. They are becoming a key part of the digital transformation of grassroots healthcare. The push comes as family doctors in China take on a wide range of duties, from resident registration and chronic-disease follow-up to initial screening and public-health record keeping, often burdened by heavy paperwork and limited staffing. AI-assisted family-doctor services have been introduced in many cities and provinces this year.

In May, the Longgang District of Shenzhen in south China's Guangdong Province launched the "Ant Afu" app, allowing residents to check medical reports, obtain AI-assisted interpretations, sign up for family-doctor services and link family members' health information. In Beijing's Fengtai District, the Majiapu Community Health Service Center has deployed an AI family doctor and an AI health steward. Built on large models and AI-agent technologies, the system supports chronic-disease management, wearable-device monitoring and automatic risk alerts, with high-risk cases forwarded to contracted family doctors. In Wuxi, east China's Jiangsu Province, AI was used in a citywide cancer screening campaign, and residents completed risk self-assessments through a mobile app or an AI-powered voice questionnaire.

Big-data models identified high-risk groups for follow-up screening at 49 institutions equipped with AI-assisted imaging, ultrasound and endoscopy systems. According to the Wuxi Municipal Health Commission, the AI-enabled screening significantly improved cancer detection among high-risk groups, with liver and lung cancers detected at markedly higher rates than in the general population. Industry insiders say the most significant shift is that AI is moving from isolated add-on tools into routine clinical workflows in some community health centers. Earlier systems often required doctors to open separate applications for image reading or diagnostic support.

The newer AI systems are being integrated with hospital information systems and health-checkup platforms, so that AI prompts appear within the interfaces doctors already use. Nie Chunlei, vice president of the Community Health Association of China, said AI used to seem lofty and unrelated to primary care but has now taken root at the grassroots level. With growing demand and expanding real-world deployments, more tech companies are entering the sector, further driving the digital upgrade of grassroots healthcare services. Ant Group's Ant Afu health app has rolled out its "AI agent plus human doctor" model in more than 40 cities, and tens of thousands of grassroots doctors use the platform, which had served more than 5 million residents by mid-August this year.

JD Health, Runda Medical and others are also ramping up investment in primary-care AI, each drawing on its own strengths. In October 2025, five national agencies issued guidance identifying intelligent clinical decision support, AI-enabled family-doctor services and coordinated chronic-disease management as priority areas, with a goal of basically achieving full coverage of AI-assisted diagnosis and treatment in primary care institutions by 2030. Industry insiders caution that scaling AI across primary care requires careful adaptation, because AI must be tailored to frontline needs, embedded in daily workflows and built into applications that are replicable, scalable and can be regulated. Sun Dehui, R&D director at the Beijing Medical Robotics Industry Innovation Center, said primary-care AI is a clear long-term direction for public health, and with policy support increasingly focused on the grassroots level, the sector is poised for rapid growth in the coming years.

Articles.Title: China Focus: AI drives digital transformation in China's primary care - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Chinese experts train Tanzanian media professionals in AI applications - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
China's National Radio and Television Administration held a two-day training program for Tanzanian media professionals in Dar es Salaam, starting on Sunday, November 1, 2026. The program was called "The China-Africa AI Media Training." It brought together around 30 professionals from media production, programming, creative, digital and technical departments. The training was run by Chinese experts.

The training focuses on practical uses of generative AI in media production, tourism promotion, cultural storytelling, television commercials and content commercialization. It uses a "train-the-trainer" approach to develop local trainers and spread AI skills to more African media professionals. Chinese Ambassador to Tanzania Chen Mingjian said AI was rapidly changing media through automated translation, proofreading, text-to-video generation, digital presenters and virtual studios. She said China was committed to helping African countries strengthen digital capabilities and bridge the digital divide, and that AI development should be inclusive and benefit all.

Yang Yong, deputy director-general of the Department of International Cooperation of the NRTA, said the initiative aimed to strengthen technical capabilities, nurture talent and promote joint storytelling between China and Africa. Sheba Kussaga, director of business development at Clouds Media Group, said the training will enhance employees' efficiency, productivity and competitiveness. Mbarouk Khan, a radio presenter and digital content creator attending the training, said AI skills would help him produce higher-quality social media content, improve productivity and potentially increase his income. He called for more training opportunities to help young Tanzanian media professionals adapt to emerging technologies.

stories.Headline: Cohere + Aleph Alpha: €500M Canada-Germany AI Deal [2026] - tech-insider.org
stories.Summary:
Canada announced on October 29, 2026 that it would invest up to C$1.6 billion in Cohere, the Toronto-founded enterprise AI company, according to AFP copy carried by Digital Journal. Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the investment ahead of a Canada-EU summit in Montreal. AFP described the move as the government buying a stake in Cohere to bolster tech sovereignty. The investment sits inside a larger Series E target of C$7 billion and values Cohere at C$35.7 billion after the government money goes in, both figures coming from a single wire report.

Cohere announced its plan to acquire Germany's Aleph Alpha on April 24, 2026, in an event in Berlin, CNBC reported. Aleph Alpha was founded in 2019, the same year as Cohere, and builds language models for European enterprises and public institutions. TechCrunch counted about 250 employees at the German company and named its PhariaAI suite as the main product line. The combined company will use the Cohere name, with headquarters in Toronto and Berlin, and Aleph Alpha's Heidelberg office will focus on research. CNBC reported that the financial terms of the acquisition itself were not disclosed, and a September 2026 report says the deal still needs regulatory approval and shareholder votes.

Schwarz Group, an existing Aleph Alpha shareholder, plans to invest about US$600 million in Cohere's Series E, which TechCrunch converts to roughly €500 million. TechCrunch described the Schwarz money as structured financing alongside a lead-investor role in the round, and CNBC confirmed the US$600 million figure. TechCrunch reported that the group expects the combined company to run on STACKIT, the sovereign cloud platform operated through its Schwarz Digits division. Carney framed the moment in strategic terms, saying per AFP that this is the moment that decides where AI gets built, how it gets governed, and who it serves. Cohere's CEO Aidan Gomez warned, per AFP, that Europe risks falling into total technological irrelevance without sovereign capabilities.

The deal followed roughly ten months of political groundwork between Ottawa and Berlin. The Government of Canada's February 2026 release shows that Evan Solomon and Karsten Wildberger signed an AI joint declaration at the Munich Security Conference on February 14, 2026, and launched the Sovereign Technology Alliance. Solomon said at the signing that AI is becoming foundational to economic strength and national security, and the alliance targets secure compute infrastructure, faster AI research and commercialization, and talent development. The release listed no funding amounts, so the October cheque is the first hard dollar figure tied to the alliance's logic. The reports reviewed do not say how much Cohere capacity will land on Canadian soil versus German soil.

Articles.Title: Cohere + Aleph Alpha: €500M Canada-Germany AI Deal [2026] - tech-insider.org

stories.Headline: DeepSeek Open-Sources dsh-superagent, a Router-Worker Coding Agent
stories.Summary:
DeepSeek's DeepSeek Harness team released dsh-superagent, an MIT-licensed research prototype, on November 1, 2026. It is a proactive coding agent for a single GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness. It listens to GitHub and optionally Feishu, and turns allowed requests into parallel work items, each in its own agent session. The release shipped alongside a design post titled Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System.

The bundle is a TypeScript release, v0.1.0, shipped as one commit under the MIT license, and it uses whatever model the Harness profile is set to. It runs on your own machine as a dedicated DeepSeek Harness profile and needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24+, git 2.32+, Python 3.8+, tmux and GitHub CLI 2.48+. In DeepSeek's simulation it finished tasks far faster than a single-session agent under a noisy message stream. Its best result was a p95 task completion of 15.7 minutes against 29.5 minutes for the baseline, about 1.9 times faster, though it was tested only on synthetic messages and simulated tools and real coding quality was not measured.

The README states the core rule as taking as little human attention as possible and giving as much value as possible. The team argues that mainstream agents treat one session as the basic unit, while a person can actively follow only 3 to 5 sessions at once, so human attention becomes the bottleneck. The architecture has two layers, a long-running Router that handles interaction and dispatch and isolated Worker sessions that do the actual work. Proactive work is gated by three accept modes, off, observe, which is the default, and auto, and in observe the agent only records what it would have accepted.

DeepSeek tested with simulated group chat and GitHub CI streams, with each run having about 300 messages, of which about 20 were real work requests, and each scheme ran 5 times. The super-agent had a p50 of 12.4 minutes and a p95 of 15.7 minutes, while the single session plus subagents with a neutral prompt had a p95 of 29.5 minutes and no p50 was given. Under the neutral prompt the baseline called a subagent 0 times in 5 runs. As arrivals rose from about 1 to 40 per minute, batch size grew from 1.0 to 2.8 and per-request latency rose from 2.5 to 3.9 seconds, and an ablation that removed direct event pass-through raised Router decisions about 30% and cache-read tokens about 37%, from 23.23M to 31.77M, with all figures self-reported.

Articles.Title: DeepSeek Open-Sources dsh-superagent, a Router-Worker Coding Agent

stories.Headline: Nace AI Open-Sources Drex Max v1: A 27B Decision Model That Runs Locally on Apple Silicon
stories.Summary:
Nace AI released Drex Max v1 as open weights on November 1, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. It is the company's most capable decision model, and it now runs on a user's own hardware. The release includes bf16 weights, a Q8_0 GGUF, an affine Q4 checkpoint, and forks of llama.cpp and Ollama. Nace AI says developers can keep routing, classification and policy checks on a local machine.

The model is a dense 27B-parameter system with a 262,144-token window, 16,384 by default, and up to 255 options per question. It runs on an NVIDIA GPU with Python, on Apple Silicon Macs with 24 GB or more for the affine Q4 or 48 GB for the Q8_0 GGUF, and on CPU through llama.cpp and Ollama. Nace reports 67.52 on the public Decision Index 0.4, 6.27 points ahead of Drex v2.0, and 97.3 skill on InfographicVQA. The model answers typed questions about a given context by returning a probability for every option in one forward pass, with no text generated.

Nace describes the model card as a dense 27B backbone with 64 layers, 48 of them Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers and 16 full-attention layers placed every fourth layer. Images pass through a native vision tower, and a 255-way readout head turns the last hidden state into option probabilities. Nace says quantization held up in its tests: on a 48 GB Apple M5 Pro, the Q8_0 GGUF matched H100 bf16 within 0.02 per probability, and the affine Q4 stayed within 0.0329 of Q8_0 with no choice flips. The articles do not say what happens next.

Articles.Title: Nace AI Open-Sources Drex Max v1: A 27B Decision Model That Runs Locally on Apple Silicon

stories.Headline: Microsoft’s big buyout, Amazon’s trillion-dollar future, and an AI wearable reviews our show
stories.Summary:
Microsoft is offering buyouts to about 60,000 employees, about a quarter of its workforce, including some executives. The offer was reported by GeekWire in an episode published on October 31, 2026. Unlike the retirement program Microsoft offered in the spring, this one has no age or tenure requirement. Business leaders decide whether their groups take part. The buyout comes as Microsoft reports a blockbuster quarter, including $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI, more than the company made from Xbox or Bing.

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy predicts that AWS and Amazon’s stores business could each reach $1 trillion in annual revenue in the next five to 10 years. AWS grew 39% in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years. Amazon’s profit fell short of expectations as the cost of its AI buildout and growing debt cut into earnings. On the GeekWire Podcast, Todd Bishop and John Cook discuss what is behind the offer and why buyout stories draw so much interest from readers. Todd also tests Amazon’s new Bee AI wearable, which listens to the first part of the show, summarizes the conversation and offers a critique of its own.

The hosts talk about what it is like to wear a device that records the people around you, a concern raised by a former AWS security engineer. John starts to come around on the device, with reservations about its shopping features. The episode also includes the hosts’ Halloween costumes and a Trivia Challenge inspired by T-Mobile’s new T-Mix plans. The show was edited by Curt Milton, with music by Daniel L.K. Caldwell.
